articles.title: What a British think tank gets wrong about Russia’s ultimate weapons
articles.body:
What a British think tank gets wrong about Russia’s ultimate weapons
A few days ago, the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) released a report titled ‘Russia’s Nuclear Deterrent and Its Weapons Procurement’. The report examines the development of Russia’s nuclear triad amid stringent financial constraints and the rising threat of a potential US non-nuclear counterforce strike.
The author of the report, Sidharth Kaushal, makes conclusions based on the publications of Russian military experts in the journal ‘Voennaya Mysl’ (Military Thought), as well as established Western practices for analyzing Russia’s nuclear capabilities.
A British diagnosis of Russia’s nuclear future
Here are the key takeaways from the report:
- Paradigm shift: Russia is being compelled to shift its focus from a posture of “assured retaliation” (increasing the survivability of mobile missile systems and submarine-launched ballistic forces to effectively counter a first strike) to a Launch on Warning (LOW) posture (employing its arsenal early against an enemy attack).
- Vulnerability of mobile forces: Advancements in US space reconnaissance make the concealment of mobile ground-based systems increasingly ineffective.
- Greater reliance on silo-based launchers, which are viewed as more secure bases for strategic missiles. Silo-based systems will comprise a greater proportion of throw weight, particularly since RS-28 Sarmat heavy intercontinental ballistic missiles are silo-launched to ensure instant readiness.
- Economic challenges: According to the report, modern Russia cannot pursue a large-scale quantitative increase in its missile arsenal due to the enormous costs associated with developing and maintaining the conventional armed forces amidst the ongoing military operation in Ukraine.
- Due to cost parity, the domestic production costs of strategic missile systems compete with conventional weaponry – for example, producing one Yars missile is equivalent to the cost of 15 T-72 tanks.
- A labor shortage in the nuclear and missile industries is unavoidable in the current conditions and necessitates a significant increase in wages.
The author also provides interesting assessments of specific weapons systems:
- RS-28 Sarmat: The report projects no quantitative increase in the deployment of these missiles. Emphasis is placed on a short boost phase and a high payload capacity for overcoming missile defense systems.
- The medium-range Oreshnik missile is seen as a priority in the European theater of operations and as a tool for preemptively neutralizing US Dark Eagle systems in Europe. Given manufacturing shortages, it is expected to be deployed primarily in its nuclear variant.
- The long-range KH-BD air-launched cruise missile (with a range up to 6,500 km) is designed to be carried by Tu-95 and Tu-160 bombers, in light of the lack of progress on the PAK DA next-generation stealth strategic bomber.
- Burevestnik and Poseidon programs are considered technically unfeasible by the author of the report; due to the high costs, they are perceived primarily as methods of psychological intimidation
- Space-based warfare: The report highlights the jamming of US missile defense systems as a major priority for Russia. It predicts the launch of nuclear electronic warfare satellites into orbit and the eventual deployment of full-scale space-based nuclear weapons to create massive plasma fields in the ionosphere.
How can we assess this report? Generally, the picture is more complex than described. Like in the Indian parable about the blind men and the elephant, the author of the report sees certain aspects of the ‘elephant’ but fails to see the general picture, which may be quite different. Let’s take a closer look.
The logic behind Russia’s nuclear shield
Regarding the structure of the strategic nuclear forces and the shifting balance between mobile and stationary systems, the distinctive feature of the Soviet, and now Russian, approach lies in balancing mobile and stationary strategic missile systems. Despite advances in satellite reconnaissance, mobile missile systems hold certain advantages: for example, hundreds of them are deployed over vast territories. Moreover, several Peresvet laser weapon systems have already been deployed; these can blind potential adversaries’ optical reconnaissance systems at a critical moment. While reliance on space-based systems is understandable, it’s important to note that these technologies are also vulnerable to various factors, as we have seen recently.
Stationary missile systems come with a significant drawback: it’s relatively easy to spot their location. However, they offer a high level of protection against non-nuclear strikes and maintain relatively high (though not absolute) survivability in the event of a nuclear exchange. Russia’s strategy combines hard-to-detect mobile missile systems with stationary systems that can be employed in response to a nuclear attack. This combination allows for greater flexibility and multiple operational scenarios. Considering this strategy, it’s likely that a large inventory of Sarmat missiles isn’t necessary – two regiments with 50+ missile silos might suffice. This doesn’t indicate a shift in priorities but rather reaffirms a conservative and justified traditional approach.
We must also note the naval component, which ensures reliable retaliatory capability. Both Russian and Western analysts have grown accustomed to the fact that the Bulava submarine-launched solid-fuel missile has been deployed and will eventually replace other ballistic missiles in the Russian Navy. However, that’s not entirely true. Project 667BDRM DELTA-IV submarines equipped with liquid-fueled R-29RM missiles remain on duty. These missiles are among the most effective strategic systems in terms of their energy-mass efficiency. Judging by statements from 2022, it seems that Russia may very well renew its interest in liquid-fueled sea-based missiles. Maintaining two centers for naval missile production is more expensive than having just one, but if it results in a higher number of warheads with fewer missiles, financial concerns could be overlooked.
Lastly, the demonization of the Oreshnik missile in the West is understandable and, overall, justified. Its minimal flight time presents a significant threat. There’s also the option for hybrid use – deploying it with non-nuclear payloads to signal intentions or for use in low-intensity conflicts. The existence of such a missile system increases the range of potential scenarios for employing strategic forces and provides substantial flexibility.
Even a few launch facilities would suffice for these purposes, which raises questions about the costly deployment of multiple brigades. Most likely, we’re talking about the deployment of divisions with 3-4 TELs instead of full brigades consisting of 12 TELs. This strategy also allows to increase the number of deployed missiles, should the need arise.
Beyond the bluff: Weapons built for retaliation
The assessment of the aviation component of the strategic nuclear forces seems fairly accurate, but it’s necessary to note that several other weapon programs are also being developed alongside the KH-BD missiles. Russian defense contractors consistently work on multiple projects, regardless of the current financial climate. It’s reasonable to assume they’re developing air-launched hypersonic missile systems for both tactical and strategic aviation, as well as various types of cruise missiles for strategic use. Additionally, it’s highly likely that a range of tactical munitions for front-line aviation is also under development. Similarly, work on the new PAK DA strategic bomber is probably ongoing, even if the urgent need for this expensive project has diminished.
I’d like to highlight the assessments regarding the Burevestnik nuclear-powered cruise missile and the Poseidon nuclear-powered UUV. Both systems boast practically unlimited range and the ability to remain airborne/underwater for extended periods of time. There’s a lot of speculation and publicity surrounding these projects, and it makes sense to leverage such groundbreaking initiatives for propaganda purposes. However, this doesn’t negate their real military significance or the seriousness of intentions regarding their deployment.
Infrastructure for these projects wouldn’t be carried out solely for PR purposes. At least one major base with several launch systems is being constructed for Burevestnik missiles, and for the Poseidon UUV, basing facilities are being built in the Pacific Ocean, and it is set to be deployed to the Northern Fleet.
Experts monitor progress and construction through satellite imagery. Tracking testing activities is more complex, but there are signs that work continues in this direction as well. Most importantly, these combat systems possess an unknown yet potentially immense retaliatory capability, which is difficult to evaluate due to the absence of analogues. What’s certain is that their potential is significant. Poseidon UUVs may not be able to target naval fleets, but their true purpose is to ensure guaranteed retaliatory strikes capable of causing total destruction along an adversary’s coastline.
In summary, despite economic and financial challenges, Russia will undoubtedly find the resources necessary to maintain and advance its nuclear triad, or even the more powerful new strategic nuclear forces.

articles.title: US delays the Patriot missiles Ukraine needs against ballistic strikes but keeps sending older PAC-2s
articles.body:
The US is delaying PAC-3 interceptors for Ukraine’s Patriot air defense systems while older PAC-2s keep arriving, a NATO source told Radio Svoboda on 29 October. PAC-3 is the Patriot missile built mainly to stop ballistic missiles.
The delay comes as Russia leans on ballistic missiles against the capital. In two weeks, Russia launched more than 100 at Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in his 27 October evening address. “And above all, we do not have enough missiles for Patriots,” he added. On 29 October, Zelenskyy said Ukraine has intelligence that Russia is preparing new ballistic missile attacks. Kyiv is “awaiting the relevant decisions” on interceptor packages, “primarily for Patriots,” he said.
A question for politicians
The PAC-2s, used mostly against aircraft and cruise missiles, arrive through PURL, the NATO mechanism under which allies pay for US weapons for Ukraine. The PAC-3 delay is under discussion at a high political level, the NATO source said. It is unclear when the situation will change.
What Washington said before
On 20 October, Hegseth said in Wisconsin: “We haven’t changed our posture in any way toward the Ukrainians, but certainly with things like interceptors, we want to make sure our guys have the most possible as well.”
“We haven’t changed our posture in any way toward the Ukrainians, but certainly with things like interceptors, we want to make sure our guys have the most possible as well.” Hegseth said in Wisconsin
The same day, Secretary of State Marco Rubio conceded that some interceptors bought for Ukraine through PURL may not have been delivered, Reuters reported. “There’s nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” he said, adding: “We have our own needs, too.”

- Russia used everything but nuclear weapons against civilians in Ukraine’s Kherson Oblast, its governor says. Drones strike up to 6,500 times weekly
- Drones have not killed tank: Ukrainian analyst says Operation Vivaldi shows NATO how to make armor work again
- “We have been killed”: Novaya Gazeta, the last major independent newsroom still working from inside Russia, closes after losing its Moscow office and its reader donations in the same week

articles.title: North Korea tests attack drones as Kim calls for 'absolute superiority'
articles.body:
North Korea tests attack drones as Kim calls for 'absolute superiority'
North Korea has tested attack drones, cruise missiles and rocket launchers at a weapons demonstration, state media reported Friday, as Kim Jong Un called for faster development of military drone and artificial intelligence technology. The tests follow a series of weapons trials and rising tensions with South Korea.
North Korea has test-fired attack drones, missiles and a multiple rocket launcher at a weapons demonstration, state media reported Friday, as leader Kim Jong Un called for faster development of drone and AI technology for military use.
The event came a day after Seoul said Pyongyang had fired 'around a dozen' short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast, though it was not immediately clear whether the launches were linked to the demonstration.
At the event, Kim stressed the "aim to seize the absolute superiority in the drone technology is an indispensable option in the light of the ever-changing patterns of modern warfare", according to KCNA.
He added: "Strength precisely means peace and peace is guaranteed only by strength."
The demonstration featured suicide attack drones, multipurpose drones firing air-to-surface missiles, cruise missiles and 600mm multiple rocket launchers. KCNA said the drones and cruise missiles hit an island target with 100 percent accuracy.
The event follows a slew of recent weapons tests by Pyongyang, including a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, both of which were said to employ AI technology.
Read moreNorth Korea fires 'around a dozen' ballistic missiles amid rising tensions with South Korea
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said its military detected "around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles fired from the Wonsan area of North Korea towards the East Sea", also known as the Sea of Japan.
The missiles flew about 250 kilometres (155 miles), and "South Korea and the United States are conducting a detailed analysis of their exact specifications", Seoul's military said, adding it had stepped up surveillance of possible additional launches.
Seoul's National Security Office, meanwhile, said the launches violated UN Security Council resolutions, labelling them "serious acts that do nothing to help manage the current situation".
Thursday's missile flurry comes against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between the two Koreas that saw three South Korean soldiers wounded.
A joint Seoul-UN investigation earlier this month concluded that North Korea planted the landmines over a year ago.
Seoul accused Pyongyang of "a clear violation of the Armistice Agreement" and demanded an apology, something the North has mockingly dismissed.
Read moreNorth Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
'Show of force'
Last week, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said the North would place loudspeakers on standby along the border "within days" and had put unspecified "new counter means" on alert.
Both countries have occasionally turned to loudspeakers blaring propaganda across their shared border and other psychological warfare methods.
South Korea days later proposed military talks with the North to "mutually confirm the precise location" of their border and discuss restoring communication channels, but Pyongyang has yet to respond.
The DMZ is one of the world's most heavily fortified frontiers, and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war, as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce rather than a peace treaty.
The ratcheting tensions come as US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to North Korea have raised concerns that Seoul – an ally of Washington – could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving Pyongyang.
In his most recent comments, Trump seemingly downplayed the possibility of a summit while insisting his relationship with Kim Jong Un was "very good".
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: U.S. clears sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine
articles.body:
- The U.S. State Department approved a possible $2.1 billion sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptors to Ukraine on Oct. 30.
- Canada, Germany and Norway are funding part of the sale through JUMPSTART, with the rest financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan.
The U.S. State Department has approved a possible sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE interceptors to Ukraine for its Patriot air defense systems, a package worth an estimated $2.1 billion that will be paid for entirely by Ukraine’s allies and partners. The department notified Congress of the decision on Oct. 30.
Canada, Germany and Norway are contributing donations through JUMPSTART, a U.S. Foreign Military Sales mechanism for donor-funded Ukraine purchases, and Ukraine will cover the rest with national funds financed by the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan. No U.S. funds are involved. Besides the missiles, the package includes classified and unclassified PAC-3 MSE spare parts and logistics and program support. Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor.
The notification is not a contract. It opens a congressional review period, after which Ukraine and the U.S. government can sign a letter of offer and acceptance and the U.S. Army can place the order with Lockheed Martin. The State Department gave no delivery schedule, and it did not say how the cost will be split among the three donors and the EU-financed share. Divided evenly, the total comes to about $4.2 million per missile, but that figure also covers spares and support.
The State Department said the missiles will help Ukraine sustain its existing Patriot operations against ongoing aerial threats, and that Ukraine will have no difficulty absorbing them into its armed forces. The sale will not require any additional U.S. government or contractor personnel in Ukraine.
The approval comes days after Ukrainian officials publicly pressed Washington on interceptor supplies. On Oct. 26, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had waited nearly a month for U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to sign off on missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS systems, including transfers from allied stocks that require U.S. approval. A day later, he told journalists that Ukraine had received an average of 12 Patriot interceptors a month from the United States in 2026, while Russia launches about 150 ballistic missiles a month that Ukraine needs to intercept.
PAC-3 MSE is the Patriot system’s main weapon against ballistic missiles. Unlike the older PAC-2 interceptors, which detonate a blast-fragmentation warhead near the target, the PAC-3 family destroys targets by direct impact, a method known as hit-to-kill. The Missile Segment Enhancement version adds a larger two-pulse solid rocket motor, with the second pulse firing late in the flight to extend range and altitude against maneuvering threats. That makes it the interceptor Ukraine relies on against Russian Iskander ballistic missiles and Kh-47M2 Kinzhal air-launched missiles. Ukrainian officials have described PAC-3 as their only effective defense against Russian ballistic missiles.
Ukraine received its first Patriot battery in April 2023, and in May of that year Ukrainian crews shot down a Kinzhal over Kyiv, the first publicly confirmed combat interception of the missile. Ukraine has since received further batteries from the United States, Germany, the Netherlands and Romania, and in July 2025 Germany and Norway agreed to pay for three more systems to be bought from the U.S. manufacturer. Interceptor supply has been a tighter constraint than launchers. In February 2026, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius offered five PAC-3 rounds from German stocks if other allies together supplied 30 more, and in July, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said it was using about $1 billion from the EU loan to buy roughly 100 Patriot missiles.
The financing reflects how Ukraine’s air defense is now paid for. The U.S. Defense Security Cooperation Agency describes JUMPSTART as a channel that lets allies and partners finance Ukraine’s Foreign Military Sales cases with their own donations. Norway reported routing about NOK 10 billion through the mechanism in 2025, much of it for F-16 support. In September 2026, Canada said it would put about C$350 million toward air defense interceptors for Ukraine through JUMPSTART. Separately, NATO allies buy U.S. weapons for Ukraine through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, known as PURL.
EU governments agreed in early 2026 on a €90 billion loan for 2026 and 2027, with €60 billion set aside for defense, and the first disbursements went out in June 2026. The loan gives priority to weapons built in Ukraine, the EU and the European Economic Area, but allows purchases elsewhere when no European alternative exists. Patriot interceptors are one case where none does.
Production is the main limit on how fast the missiles can arrive. Lockheed Martin delivered 620 PAC-3 MSE interceptors in 2025, a company record. In January 2026, the company and the U.S. Department of War signed a seven-year framework agreement to raise annual output from about 600 to roughly 2,000. In April, the U.S. Army awarded Lockheed a $4.76 billion PAC-3 MSE contract, most of it funded through Foreign Military Sales customers. Demand has also climbed since the United States drew on its own Patriot inventory during this year’s conflict with Iran.
At 2025 production rates, the 500 missiles approved for Ukraine equal about 10 months of Lockheed’s output. Where Ukraine’s order falls in the production queue, and when the first missiles from this sale will reach Patriot batteries in Ukraine, has not been disclosed.

articles.title: When Will US Transfer Operational Control to South Korea? Debate Rages
articles.body:
For years, U.S. and South Korean officials have said they want to reach an arrangement where, should war break out on the peninsula, Seoul’s military commanders would have operational control of American forces there.
Such a setup would be unprecedented in modern times, and what it would mean for U.S. Airmen, Guardians, and other troops remains to be seen. But recent comments from U.S. and Korean leaders underscore just how complex and even controversial the idea remains.
Since World War II, the U.S. has been the ultimate authority for all its combined forces’ wartime operations. But South Korea—officially called the Republic of Korea—has been pressing to finalize the transfer of wartime operational control, or OPCON. Since taking office last year, President Lee Jae Myung has publicly stated his goal is to reach OPCON before his term ends in 2030, and likely earlier.
But the commander of U.S. Forces Korea, Army Gen. Xavier T. Brunson, sounded far more cautious at a Center for Strategic and International Studies summit on Oct. 14. Evolving security concerns, such as recent ballistic missile launches, have created “new standards” that must be met before OPCON can be transferred, Brunson said.
Brunson said the transfer must be “conditions-based” and not follow a political timeline.
His comments spurred immediate backlash from Korean officials, including Defense Minister Kan Shin-chul and National Security Advisor Wi Sung-lac, who claim that Brunson’s remarks about new conditions amount to shifting the goalposts and will make the planned transfer impossible.
On Oct. 29, Sung-lac said during a parliamentary audit that the government had been consulting with Washington to complete the transfer by or before 2030. But a planned Security Consultative Meeting scheduled for December in Washington to discuss various alliance and security concerns has been postponed to next year.
A U.S. Pacific Command spokesperson declined to respond to specific questions regarding the conditions required for transfer but did provide a statement to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“The transition of wartime operational control (OPCON) remains a conditions-based process mutually agreed upon by the United States and the Republic of Korea,” Navy Lt. Cmdr. Chloe Morgan wrote. “Both nations remain committed to ensuring that the necessary conditions are met before any transition occurs. We will not prejudge decisions or outcomes of this bilateral process.”
While the OPCON process continues and Korean leaders push to move forward, not all American experts agree that it’s a good idea. During an Oct. 27 symposium hosted by the Institute for Korean-American Studies, former USFK commanders Walter Sharp and Paul LaCamera, both Army four-stars, critiqued the weakening of the U.S.-Korea alliance, the Korea JoongAng Daily reported.
“That whole combined nature goes away and … [I] really do see it as a doorway to greatly reducing the alliance, greatly reducing our work with Korea,” Sharp said.
LaCamera was even more pointed.
“It will be suboptimal when the fighting starts, and then we will quickly get to optimization because it is adapt or perish,” he said.
As the debate continues, South Korea is leading combined missions during a two-week, biannual, air-focused Freedom Flag exercise.
The top ROK air commander, Col. Lee Seung-hwan, emphasized his airmen’s role and its ultimate goal.
“While using this as an opportunity to build teamwork among South Korean and U.S. pilots and polish combat skills, we will also cultivate capabilities in preparation for the OPCON transfer,” Seung-hwan said.
To Transfer or Not
The idea behind transferring OPCON to South Korea dates back to the 1980s when President Roh Tae-woo made it a campaign promise in 1987, driven by a desire to strengthen South Korean sovereignty. The United States didn’t transfer peacetime control to Seoul until 1994. Wartime control was expected to soon follow but was derailed during the 1993-1994 North Korean nuclear crisis.
The South Korean push renewed under President Roh Moo-hyun in 2003. Then-U.S. Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld championed the idea, calling it “pushing on an open door” to free up U.S. forces on the peninsula and give the Pentagon more strategic flexibility.
The pair formalized an agreement in 2006 to begin the wartime OPCON transfer.
But getting to the point where the transfer makes sense for both sides isn’t so simple, multiple retired commanders with deep experience on the peninsula told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“Conditions should determine the timeline,” retired U.S. Army Special Forces Col. David S. Maxwell told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “The timeline should never determine the conditions.”
Maxwell explained that target dates help drive budgets, procurement, training, and accountability, but can’t substitute for demonstrated combat capability.
“If political leaders want to accelerate transition, they must accelerate the fielding of equipment, development of personnel, and combined exercises required to meet the agreed conditions,” Maxwell said. “Political authority cannot manufacture readiness.”
Retired Lt. Gen. David Deptula, Dean of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, also emphasized the importance of not rushing the transfer.
“My principal concern would be any arrangement that sacrifices combat effectiveness to satisfy an arbitrary political timeline or the symbolism of transferring command,” Deptula said. “We cannot afford to discover deficiencies in command and control after a conflict begins.”
Still, Maxwell, now vice president of the Center for Asia Pacific Strategy, said changing conditions “cannot become an unexplained justification for indefinite delay.”
“Both allies must identify what has changed, which operational requirements it affects, and what capabilities will close the resulting gaps. We should distinguish the agreed conditions from the evolving military capabilities required to satisfy them,” Maxwell said. “The objective is a successful transition that strengthens deterrence and combined defense. Most importantly, political leaders cannot base decisions on threat assessments from five, 10, or 20 years ago.”
Maxwell and Deptula highlight several critical conditions before OPCON transfer should go through:
- South Korea should demonstrate the capability to lead a combined defense and coordinate offensive actions at scale.
- There should be comprehensive alliance capabilities to respond to North Korean nuclear and missile threats.
- A stable security environment
- Integrated architecture for intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and early warning for near-real-time actionable data
- Integrated air and missile defenses across U.S. and ROK forces
- Secure, resilient command and control in the face of cyber and electronic attacks.
- Sufficient munitions, logistics, infrastructure protection, and sustainment capabilities.
- Certified initial operational capability, full operational capability, and full mission capability assessment results for readiness.
While wartime control of the entire combined U.S.-ROK force is in question, more complex considerations apply to the use of the 7th Air Force, USFK’s air component based at Kunsan and Osan Air Bases in South Korea.
The Air Side
If conflict were to break out today, U.S. and ROK forces would be controlled by a Combined Forces Command that has existed since 1978. The commander of U.S. Forces Korea is dual-hatted as the head of the CFC and has a Korean deputy.
Once the OPCON transfer occurs, that arrangement would flip: a South Korean four-star commander with a U.S. four-star deputy. But even with that combined arrangement, the Pentagon doesn’t cede control of its forces entirely, and it does not give the Korean commander authority over U.S. aircraft in the Pacific.
Retired Lt. Gen. Jeffrey A. Remington, who commanded the 7th Air Force from 2008 to 2012, explained that under the new arrangement, the 7th Air Force commander would still oversee the air component for the Korean general in charge, informing the general on the status of air forces, personnel, and wartime options.
“[The 7th Air Force commander] would continue to be the air component commander, not a Korean, … a U.S. Air Force three-star general,” Remington said.
The commander would then come to the Korean four-star and say, ““Here’s the options, here’s what I can do for you. Here’s the implications of those options,’ and we’ll come to an agreement,” he said.
Even in that arrangement, Remington said Washington likely wouldn’t be involved directly in any major decision involving U.S. forces, especially major airpower assets.
Deptula stressed that in hammering out the details of this arrangement, “the issue is not whether a South Korean general is capable of commanding American airpower. It’s whether the command structure provides the authority, experience, capabilities, and operational flexibility necessary to employ airpower effectively.”
The ROK military is highly professional and capable and a solid U.S. ally in the region, Deptula added. But such a transfer requires more.
“Commanding a modern, integrated air campaign involving hundreds of aircraft, sophisticated intelligence and surveillance capabilities, electronic warfare, space-based systems, and long-range strike assets requires far more than flying airplanes or managing individual missions,” Deptula said.
Day-to-day operations running an Air Operations Center and delivering air tasking orders already happen in a combined way through the AOC at Osan Air Base, Deptula said.
“The real issue is creating a master air attack plan,” he said. “That is the mechanism through which an air campaign translates strategic and operational objectives into coordinated tactical actions. It integrates offensive counterair, defensive counterair, strategic attack, interdiction, close air support, intelligence collection, electronic warfare, air refueling, and other capabilities into a coherent campaign.”
While the U.S. has participated in combined forces operations in World War II and with NATO in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo, it has never been in a combined force operation without being the ultimate authority for wartime OPCON.
Most U.S. operations during the Global War on Terror and since have been in coalitions. Those typically operate with separate militaries covering different areas, such as the British contribution to the invasion of and early stages of the Iraq War, where their forces were concentrated near Basra and controlled the southeastern section of the war effort near Kuwait.
Combined warfare is different.
“Combined warfare means you’re there together. You’re executing together. You’re mixed and making things happen,” Remington said. “Whereas in a coalition it’s not all that combined, especially from a command-and-control perspective.”
In a very technical sense, for U.S. aviators that might mean being controlled through another nation’s airborne early warning or air battle management systems.
That has been somewhat common with NATO combined forces arrangements in past operations and exercises and with South Korea via their ROKAF Master Control and Reporting Centers. Those two MCRCs serve as nerve centers for all air ops on the peninsula and have operated since the mid-1980s, preceded by a Tactical Air Control Center that ran from the early 1980s until the advent of MCRC.
One MCRC, call sign Watchman, is at Osan. The other, call sign Acacia, is at Daegu Air Base and serves as a reserve aerospace operations center.
Beyond the Peninsula
While 7th Air Force is the USFK air component with primary duties to defend South Korea, it also relies on Pacific Air Forces for support and contributes to PACAF’s needs to support U.S. Pacific Command. U.S. Forces Korea are not on a proverbial island, focused solely on local security concerns.
Should a conflict with China or other regional problems erupt, USAF may need to draw upon 7th Air Force.
“The U.S. military is operating with declining force structure and must meet growing global requirements,” Deptula said. “Aircraft, aircrews, munitions, tankers, intelligence platforms, and other assets cannot be committed to two different campaigns simultaneously without accepting significant operational risk.”
That fact means that contingency planning, force allocation, and command relationships take on even more significance when looking to transfer operational control, Deptula said
“Both nations must understand in advance what capabilities are committed, what reinforcements may be available, and under what circumstances U.S. forces might be required elsewhere,” he said.
Any such transfer “must preserve” U.S. commanders’ ability to employ their capabilities where they can achieve the greatest strategic effect, he said.
“Any future defense of South Korea must begin with an appreciation for the fact that air superiority provides the freedom to attack and the freedom from attack,” Deptula said. “It enables all other military operations. The campaign must be designed to achieve the degree of air superiority necessary to permit the joint force to operate effectively, rather than simply contest the airspace.”

articles.title: Ukraine Destroys Russian Iskander-M Launcher Near Key Transit Point
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck a Russian Iskander-M ballistic missile launcher near a missile transshipment point in Russia’s Kursk region early on Friday, Oct. 30, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
“An Iskander-M tactical missile system launcher was struck in the vicinity of a ballistic missile transshipment point, near Fatezh in the Kursk region of the Russian Federation,” the General Staff said on Telegram.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The military said the strike would reduce Russia’s capacity to launch ballistic missile attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces also struck several other Russian military targets, including ammunition depots near Maloyanysol in the Donetsk region, Novoiehorivka in the Kharkiv region, and Hanusivka in the Luhansk region.
Other targets included a logistics and supply depot near Bilovodsk, an enemy repair unit near Rubizhne, and a repair and restoration base near Pysarivka – all in the Luhansk region.
The General Staff said destroying ammunition depots reduces Russian forces’ firepower, while strikes on repair facilities make it harder for them to restore damaged equipment and return it to the battlefield.
In a separate attack, Ukraine struck a Russian Iskander ballistic missile launcher and destroyed two Su-34 fighter-bombers on Thursday, Oct. 29, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The Ukrainian Navy’s Neptune coastal missile system hit the aircraft at the Marinovka airfield in Russia’s Volgograd region, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) reported. The Su-34s are used by Russian forces to launch guided and unguided aerial bombs, including KABs.
Russian Ballistic Missile Strike on Kyiv Kills One, Sparks Fires
Zelensky added that Ukrainian intelligence had information indicating Russia was preparing to launch another wave of ballistic missile attacks.
He urged international partners to provide additional interceptor packages for Patriot air defense systems, warning that Ukraine faced a critical shortage.
“We are waiting for the relevant decisions,” Zelensky said.
He made a similar appeal during his visit to the Netherlands on Wednesday, Oct. 28, describing Patriot interceptors as Ukraine’s most pressing weapons shortage.
He urged Washington not to delay deliveries under the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a mechanism through which allies fund purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine.
As winter approaches, Russia is increasingly using ballistic missiles to target Ukraine’s critical infrastructure, including electricity and water supply facilities. Kyiv had reportedly depleted its stocks of Patriot interceptors as of Oct. 15, amid limited deliveries from allies.
PAC-3 interceptors are among the few weapons capable of destroying Russian ballistic missiles, including the Iskander-M, which carries a warhead weighing around half a ton and can cause extensive damage to residential buildings.
“Another aspect of our anti-ballistic work is the interceptor packages, primarily for Patriots, that partners can provide to us,” Zelensky said on Wednesday.

articles.title: “We need asymmetric effect,” Defense Minister Khmara says, as Ukraine funds its own missiles and radars to stop burning costly interceptors on cheap Russia’s drones
articles.body:
Ukraine is opening grant money for home-built air-to-air missiles and radars, aiming to shoot down Russia’s fastest drones without paying a huge price. The Defense Ministry, the Ministry of Digital Transformation, and the Brave1 defense-tech cluster are launching the competitions, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara announced in an address to manufacturers, adding that a grant contest for turbojet engines will follow.
Ukraine is being forced to use expensive air defense missiles against relatively inexpensive Russian drones and cruise missiles. Developing cheaper interceptors, domestically produced radars and engines could change the economics of warfare.
The move comes as Russia leans harder on faster, jet-powered drones that strain the cheapest layer of Ukraine’s defenses. It also follows an earlier round of Brave1 grants that had already flagged anti-bomb systems and Ukrainian radars as priorities.
What Kyiv wants built, from navigation to radars that see the faint targets
Khmara laid out the threats the money is meant to answer: ballistic missiles, cheap cruise missiles, high-speed drones and guided bombs.
From Ukrainian producers, the ministry wants domestic navigation systems, stronger electronic warfare, radars able to pick out low-signature targets, and affordable designs that can be developed in quantity.
“Our requirements are clear: effectiveness, affordable cost, interoperability between systems, and sufficient volume of supply,” Khmara says.
The grants are one tool among others, meant to carry developments that can later scale for the Security and Defense Forces. Earlier, the ministry and Brave1 ran a large-scale test of drones with AI-assisted targeting.
The next contest targets the guided bombs Ukraine still cannot reliably stop
The minister singled out a separate job for manufacturers: new ways to counter Russia’s guided aerial bombs, known in Ukraine as KABs, and to blunt their use.
These are the glide bombs Russian aircraft release from a distance, and Ukraine has struggled to answer them without reaching the launch aircraft themselves.
“It is important to create innovative solutions that let us act ahead and prevail. We need asymmetric effect. We need technologies that change the rules of the game in our favor,” he argues.
Grants for turbojet engines, the ministry says, are the next step after the missiles and radars.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia strikes Dnipro railway station again, day after attack killed 15
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Russia strikes Dnipro railway station again, day after attack killed 15
Key developments on Oct. 30:
- Russia strikes Dnipro railway station again, day after attack killed 15
- Evacuation convoys from Russian-occupied Oleshky split toward Ukraine and Russia, officials say

Russian forces launched new strikes on the railway station in Dnipro on Oct. 30, Ukrainian Railways (Ukrzaliznytsia) reported.
Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said that a fire had broken out at the station and that a woman had been injured.
The station came under attack for the second day in a row, after a Russian drone strike on Oct. 29 killed 15 people and injured 14 others.
Ukrzaliznytsia said an evacuation had been announced ahead of the strikes. The company added that areas for extended stays had been set up in the station's underground facilities to accommodate passengers sheltering from the attacks.
Ukrzaliznytsia warned that trains arriving in and departing from Dnipro could face significant delays due to repeated Russian attacks on the station and locomotives.

Evacuation convoys from Russian-occupied Oleshky split toward Ukraine and Russia, officials say
Evacuation convoys carrying residents of Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast have separated, with some heading toward Ukrainian-controlled territory and others toward Russia, Ukrainian and Russian officials said on Oct. 30.
Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said he was continuing to personally coordinate the humanitarian mission and was heading back to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Earlier, Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova said that buses carrying evacuees had reached Armiansk in Russian-occupied Crimea, where they were to split into two convoys.
The Ukrainian delegation had traveled to Oleshky via Anapa in Russia's Krasnodar Krai, from where they reportedly flew to Belarus before continuing by bus to Ukrainian-controlled territory, David Arakhamia, head of President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary faction, said earlier on Oct. 30.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion. Located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, the city has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, which have prevented humanitarian aid from reaching residents.
Residents have faced severe shortages of food, water, and electricity. Mined roads and constant drone attacks have made safe evacuation virtually impossible, and civilians trying to flee on the only roads in and out of the city have frequently been targeted by drones.
Despite efforts by the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and even Pope Leo XIV, a ceasefire agreement has only come about since the intervention of Melania Trump.
Twenty-five buses with a combined capacity of 750 passengers, along with ambulances for people with limited mobility, had been prepared to evacuate residents from Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, Lubinets said.
Lubinets's statement came amid reports that Russia had begun evacuating residents ahead of the agreed date.
"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to leave safely. At the same time, those who have decided to stay can stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian support," Lubinets said.
Lubinets and Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova held a joint press briefing in Armiansk, Russian-occupied Crimea, ahead of the evacuation from Oleshky.
Lubinets said the Ukrainian and Russian delegations were accompanied by media representatives from three countries. However, photos published by Ukraine's Ombudsman's Office show predominantly Russian media outlets.
Around 11:30 a.m. Kyiv time, the Ukrainian delegation had safely reached Oleshky, and the ceasefire had been in effect for 80 hours and was still holding, Lubinets said.
Lubinets added that he was speaking with local residents to hear about their needs and understand what kind of assistance they required most.
Arakhamia said around noon that humanitarian aid had been delivered to Oleshky and that "technical support" was being provided to those wishing to evacuate.
Lantratova also confirmed on social media that the evacuation from Oleshky had begun, with people gradually boarding buses. She added that some residents wanted to travel to Russia, while others wished to go to Ukrainian-controlled territory, without specifying how many people were in each group.
Following the separation of the convoys, Lubinets proposed making humanitarian missions coordinated by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump a regular initiative, saying the operation in Oleshky demonstrated that such agreements could help civilians.

Ukraine destroys Iskander-M missile launcher in Russia's Kursk Oblast, General Staff says
Ukrainian forces struck an Iskander-M missile launcher in Russia's Kursk Oblast, along with several ammunition depots and repair facilities in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories between Oct. 29 and Oct. 30, the General Staff said.
Ukraine struck the missile launcher near the town of Fatezh, at a site used to reload ballistic missiles, the General Staff said.
The Iskander-M is a short-range ballistic missile system that Russia uses to attack Ukrainian cities. During its overnight attack on Oct. 30, Russia launched ballistic missiles from Voronezh, Kursk, and Bryansk oblasts as part of a combined assault that mainly targeted Kyiv, Poltava, and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts, Ukraine's Air Force said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 5 that Ukrainian forces would prioritize strikes on Russian missile launchers as Moscow steps up its use of ballistic missiles. Zelensky also said international deliveries of air-defense interceptors to Ukraine had fallen threefold from 2025 levels.
Ukraine's military also reported strikes on Russian ammunition depots in the occupied parts of Donetsk, Kharkiv, and Luhansk oblasts.
Ukrainian forces hit several other Russian military targets in occupied Luhansk Oblast, including a logistics depot near Bilovodsk, a repair unit near Rubizhne, and a repair and recovery base near Pysarivka, the General Staff said on Oct. 30.
The General Staff did not specify which weapons were used in the strikes.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the extent of the damage.
Zelensky said on Oct. 29 that Ukraine had carried out two missile strikes, destroying an Iskander-M missile launcher and two Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber jets.
On Oct. 29, Ukraine's Navy also struck two Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber jets at the Marinovka military airfield in Russia's Volgograd Oblast using domestically produced Neptune missiles, the Navy reported.

Russia has damaged more than 800 Ukrainian energy assets since September
Russia has carried out more than 350 attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure since September, damaging more than 800 pieces of equipment, Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said on Friday.
The strikes are increasing pressure on the country’s power system as the heating season approaches. Ukraine is stepping up efforts to protect energy facilities while expanding generation capacity to reduce the impact of further attacks on an already crippled system after years of Russian missile and drone attacks.
Speaking during a question-and-answer session with the government in parliament, Shmyhal said the damaged equipment included facilities at substations and power generation sites.
He said a second level of physical protection had been built for 235 transformers. According to the minister, only one piece of protected equipment had been hit by a ballistic missile over the past six months.
"Without this protection, restoring energy facilities under the current intensity of Russian attacks would take months," Shmyhal said.
Alongside protecting existing infrastructure, Ukraine is working to expand its electricity generation capacity through smaller, decentralized power plants.
On Oct. 29, the government approved the mechanism and terms for providing almost Hr 939 million ($20 million) in loan financing from the Finnish-Ukrainian Investment Fund to state-owned energy company Ukrnafta.
The funding will support four projects to install gas-engine power plants in the western Ivano-Frankivsk and Lviv oblasts, adding around 60 megawatts of capacity to Ukraine’s power system, Shmyhal reported.
The money will cover the purchase of the power plants and related equipment, as well as installation, testing and commissioning. The loans were raised for Ukraine’s state budget under a framework agreement between the Ukrainian and Finnish governments signed in November 2024.
The projects are part of broader efforts to develop distributed generation, spreading electricity production across multiple locations rather than relying solely on large power plants.

Russian deputy PM confirms strikes on 3 refineries, gas-chemical complex
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Ukraine had attacked three Russian oil refineries and a gas-chemical complex on Oct. 30, Russian state news agency TASS reported.
"Today, there was another attack on Russian refineries, four processing plants. More precisely, three refineries and one gas-chemical complex. There was minor damage at one plant, but overall, our defense system, the air defense system, worked," Novak said, without specifying the locations of the facilities.
"We had a brief pause, but today, attacks on refineries have resumed, and our facilities are working to protect themselves," he added.
Kyiv had not commented on the reported strike at the time of publication.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the footage or establish the extent of the damage.

The Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ published photos and videos submitted by local residents that appear to show fires burning in the area around the refinery, alongside reports of drones flying overhead.

Schemes, an investigative journalism project by Radio Free Europe's Ukrainian service, shared a satellite image of the Novokuybyshevsk refinery taken on Oct. 30. The image shows a large fire still burning at the facility, with thick black smoke covering much of the surrounding area.
"We are repelling an attack by the Ukrainian Armed Forces on our territory. Air defense and mobile fire teams are operating. Remain calm and remain in a safe place," Samara Oblast Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said.
The governor did not specify which facilities in the city were targeted.
Fedorishchev later said that two people died in Samara Oblast while clearing up the aftermath of the drone attack.

articles.title: Kim Jong Un calls for rapid development of drone technology after North Korea launches ballistic missiles
articles.body:
Kim Jong Un calls for rapid development of drone technology after North Korea launches ballistic missiles
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has called for the rapid development of drone technology in the country and watched tests of various weapons systems as tensions with South Korea continue to mount along the border.
Source: Associated Press, citing North Korea's state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA)
Details: Acquiring advanced drones is a key priority for Kim, who is seeking to strengthen both the country's conventional and nuclear capabilities. Experts believe that North Korean troops sent to Russia to support its war against Ukraine have likely gained valuable experience in drone warfare from the Russian Armed Forces.
KCNA reported that Kim visited an exhibition of various attack and other drones on Thursday 29 October, showcasing the latest advances in uncrewed aeronautical technology.
According to KCNA, in a speech at the exhibition, Kim stressed the need to achieve "absolute superiority in the drone technology" and announced unspecified measures required to "rapidly expand and strengthen the unmanned aeronautical technology".
KCNA also reported that North Korea later conducted test launches of various drones, missiles and munitions from 600mm ultra-precision multiple-launch rocket systems.
Photographs released by KCNA show Kim watching missiles in flight or clenching his fist, while his teenage daughter, standing beside him, applauds.
South Korea's military said earlier that it had detected the launch of around 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the North Korean east coast city of Wonsan on Thursday. These were North Korea's first ballistic weapons launches in 17 days.
AP noted that tensions between the two Koreas remain high following landmine explosions along the border last month that injured three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of laying mines south of the military demarcation line and demanded an apology. Pyongyang denied responsibility for the explosions and warned that it would take retaliatory measures in the event of provocation.
North Korea threatened last week to resume propaganda broadcasts over loudspeakers and deploy new weapons systems along the border.
North Korea withdrew from talks with the US and South Korea after Kim's high-stakes diplomatic initiative with US President Donald Trump collapsed in 2019. In recent weeks, North Korea has stepped up weapons testing, apparently seeking to strengthen its position in potential diplomatic negotiations with the US after Trump expressed a desire to resume talks with Kim.
Kim made an unexpected visit to a Chinese border city via a newly opened bridge on 24 October and pledged to develop bilateral relations. Kim has recently taken steps to strengthen ties with China, North Korea's economic partner, after prioritising relations with Russia for several years. This included sending thousands of troops and munitions, apparently in exchange for economic and military assistance.
Meanwhile, Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis arrived in North Korea on Thursday to attend a ceremony marking the reopening of Switzerland's diplomatic mission in Pyongyang and meet North Korean officials. He is due to travel to South Korea on Friday 30 October.
Background: North Korea conducted test launches of two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles off its east coast in mid-October.

articles.title: ‘Entire Country, Not Just Oleshky’ – Zelensky Presses US Over Delay of Missiles

Russian strikes killed at least 20 people across Ukraine on Thursday, Oct. 29, as a US-brokered humanitarian ceasefire held in Russian-occupied Oleshky and President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Moscow was preparing new ballistic missile attacks.
The deadliest strike hit a railway station in Dnipro, where a Russian jet-powered drone struck a platform beside a commuter train and a scheduled passenger train bound for Zaporizhzhia, killing 14 civilians and injuring 14.

Two 15-year-old girls were killed in Chernihiv, while three people died in strikes on residential buildings in Kremenchuk. A late-night attack in Kyiv killed another person.
“Today, the Russians carried out extremely brutal strikes on Dnipro, Chernihiv, Kremenchuk. Against civilians – ordinary people,” Zelensky said in his evening address.
Nationwide de-escalation, not just Oleshky
The US-brokered ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky, negotiated with the involvement of First Lady Melania Trump, continued without reported major violations, allowing humanitarian aid and preparations for civilian evacuations.
Zelensky welcomed the initiative while urging Washington to address the continuing violence elsewhere in Ukraine.
“It is also important that America not remain silent about the killings that continue unabated,” he said.
“We must act and turn the situation around so that Russia moves toward de-escalation and so that this applies to our entire country, not just Oleshky.”
Russia Strikes Kremenchuk Again: Kills 3, Injures 32
Russian, Ukrainian, and US delegations arrived in the Oleshky area as preparations continued for aid deliveries and evacuations.
An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 civilians remain trapped there, including about 50 children.
A bipartisan group of US lawmakers welcomed Melania Trump’s initiative but warned against forcibly transferring residents to Russian-controlled territory.
Patriot missiles await Pentagon approval
Zelensky renewed his urgent appeal for Patriot interceptors, citing Ukrainian intelligence indicating that Russia was preparing further ballistic missile attacks.
“We now have intel about the Russians preparing new ballistic missile attacks. We need the capabilities to shoot down this Russian evil and are awaiting the decisions,” he wrote on social media.
Condemning the Dnipro railway station attack as “horrific,” Zelensky challenged Western governments over sanctions relief for Moscow while Russian forces continued killing civilians.
“Just how many terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on certain Russian oligarchs and the Russian energy sector, rather than de-escalating?” he wrote.
“It is time for new, stronger sanctions steps by the EU, the US, and the G7.”
On Oct. 26, Zelensky said Ukraine had been waiting nearly a month for US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to authorize shipments of Patriot and NASAMS interceptors already paid for by NATO allies.
The missiles were purchased through NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), which allows European allies and other partners to finance US-made weapons for Ukraine. Despite the funding being secured, the shipments still require Washington’s approval.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged that some interceptors might not have arrived but denied that delays were politically motivated.
Meanwhile, The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Ukraine had informally suspended strikes on Russian oil refineries following pressure from President Donald Trump over fuel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 US midterm elections.
The reported US pressure comes as Russian attacks continue to kill Ukrainian civilians and damage energy infrastructure, while Kyiv awaits American approval for critical air defense supplies.

articles.title: North Korea’s Reaper copy Saetbyol-9 fires a new cruise missile
articles.body:
- North Korea released the first images of its Reaper-like Saetbyol-9 drone firing an air-launched tactical cruise missile during an Oct. 29 demonstration.
- The drone carried Korean People’s Army Ground Force markings, and KCNA claimed drone-fired missiles hit an island target with 100% accuracy.
North Korea has released new images of its Saetbyol-9 attack drone, a near copy of the U.S. MQ-9 Reaper, firing an air-launched tactical cruise missile during a live-fire demonstration Kim Jong Un watched, state news agency KCNA showed on Oct. 30.
A KCNA photo taken from the drone’s own wing shows a black cruise missile with a pointed nose and a yellow band mounted under the wing, while a second cruise missile streaks away below the clouds after launch. The drone carries the markings of the Korean People’s Army Ground Force, the North’s army, and the serial number 2101003 on its nose, which suggests the aircraft is assigned to ground units for reconnaissance and strike missions rather than only to the air force. KCNA said missiles fired from drones and ground-launched cruise missiles hit an island target with 100% accuracy, a claim that cannot be independently checked.
South Korean analysts at the Korea Defense and Security Forum said the weapon is a tactical air-to-ground cruise missile with a seeker in the nose to guide it onto its target, Financial News reported, and called it the first time North Korea has shown a Saetbyol-9 launching such a missile. North Korea has not given the missile a name or released its range, warhead size or guidance method.
The launch was part of a firepower demonstration that followed North Korea’s “Unmanned Aeronautical Technology Development-2026” exhibition, where Kim called for the country to seize “absolute superiority” in drone technology. The drill also involved tactical suicide drones, ground-launched cruise missiles and a battalion of 600 mm multiple rocket launchers, and South Korea’s military detected around 10 short-range ballistic missiles fired from the Wonsan area the same day.
The Saetbyol-9, or “Morning Star-9,” is propeller-driven and closely mirrors the shape of the MQ-9 Reaper, with a wingspan of roughly 20 m (66 feet), the same as the American drone. It first appeared in July 2023 alongside the larger Saetbyol-4, a long-range reconnaissance drone modeled on the U.S. RQ-4 Global Hawk, which North Korea also put on display at this week’s exhibition. A brief North Korean video from 2023 appeared to show the Saetbyol-9 firing a pair of missiles that resembled the U.S. Hellfire, and a U.S. Army general said in 2024 that North Korea was arming its drones with reverse-engineered copies of the Hellfire.
The new photos show a different, larger-looking store under the wing. A cruise missile flies on wings and an engine for most of its flight, which typically gives it longer range than a rocket-powered missile like the Hellfire and lets a drone fire from farther away from enemy air defenses. Without official data, it is not possible to say how far the North Korean missile can fly.
South Korean officials have questioned how much combat value the Saetbyol-9 adds. In March, the South Korean military said the drone barely imitates the Reaper’s appearance without matching its capabilities, while noting it had spotted new aircraft in the same category with a modified shape and paint scheme. In September, state media showed Kim touring production lines with airframes matching the Saetbyol-4 and Saetbyol-9, the clearest sign yet that North Korea intends to build both in numbers.

articles.title: Ukrainian Neptune strike destroys two Russian Su-34 bombers used to attack frontline cities, Ukraine’s Navy says

Ukraine’s Navy said on 29 October that it destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers in a Neptune missile strike on Marinovka airfield in Russia’s Volgograd Oblast.

Neptune strike hits Russian military airfield

The Navy said the strike destroyed two Su-34 fighter-bombers belonging to Russia’s 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment, based near the settlement of Oktyabrsky in Volgograd Oblast. The regiment is part of the 4th Mixed Aviation Division of Russia’s 4th Air and Air Defense Forces Army.
The Ukrainian Navy did not provide further details about the strike.
Su-34s are key to Russia’s guided bomb attacks
Russia uses Su-34 fighter-bombers to launch guided aerial bombs, known as KABs, against Ukrainian military positions and settlements, particularly in frontline areas. These attacks threaten both Ukrainian troops and civilians in communities near the front.

articles.title: Germany is accelerating military preparations amid the threat of a possible Russian attack on the Baltic states - media
articles.body:
Germany is accelerating military preparations amid the threat of a possible Russian attack on the Baltic states - media
Kyiv • UNN
More than 70 generals assessed the defense of the Baltic states and urged NATO to prepare more quickly for a confrontation with Russia. Germany plans to reinforce its troops and stockpiles.
More than 70 generals and senior officers from Germany and the Netherlands visited Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania to assess potential combat areas on the border with Russia. The military leadership believes that NATO needs to accelerate preparations for a possible military confrontation. Die Welt reports this, UNN writes.
Details
According to the publication, since Tuesday, military leaders from both countries have been visiting border areas with Russia. The trip, which was largely organized in secret, is being called unprecedented. It is intended to demonstrate the seriousness of the European NATO members' intentions to fulfill their mutual assistance obligations.
Germany's Inspector of the Army, Christian Freuding, together with his Dutch counterpart, Jan Swillens, is studying possible areas for operations in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
We have all reached the shared conclusion that we need to prepare even faster for an immediate response, improve our capabilities every day, and only in this way will we be able to fulfill our great responsibility
Germany has already deployed the 45th Armored Brigade in Lithuania, whose formation is still under way. In addition, since July, the German-Dutch Corps has been responsible for the possible conduct of NATO ground operations in Estonia and Latvia.
Thus, the Baltic countries have become the main area of responsibility for the German Army. If necessary, German troops are to be rapidly redeployed there in large numbers.
Freuding said that he currently sees no indications that Russia is preparing for a possible limited attack on NATO territory. At the same time, he does not consider such a scenario entirely implausible.
According to him, Vladimir Putin could potentially use captured Alliance territory as an instrument of political pressure on the allies, demanding that they end support for Ukraine in exchange for ending the offensive.
The Russian armed forces will probably have a numerical advantage over us in this region
Among the preparation priorities, he named protection against threats in low-altitude airspace, countering electronic interference, and the development of unmanned systems and digital communications supported by artificial intelligence.
Germany also plans to pre-position weapons and material stocks in the Baltic countries to ensure that its troops are ready for prolonged defense.
Particular attention is being paid to long-range strike capabilities. The German Army is considering purchasing cheaper cruise missiles with a range of up to 1,500 km. They are planned for use in strikes against troop concentration areas and the enemy's supply routes. According to the publication, the purchases could be made both in Ukraine and in Germany.
Meanwhile, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are building the "Baltic Defense Line" along NATO's eastern flank. It involves constructing military obstacles and communications infrastructure, as well as deploying unmanned systems for attacks, defense and reconnaissance.
Directly near the Russian border, the Baltic countries are also digging trenches and building bunkers. One potential flashpoint is said to be the Estonian border city of Narva, where about 87% of the 52,000 residents are of Russian origin.
During the visit, the German and Dutch generals were presented with a detailed report on the defense preparations. At the same time, details of the military planning remain classified.
According to Die Welt, Estonian troops play loud music by the German band Rammstein from loudspeakers. The noise is intended to prevent Russian border guards from eavesdropping on conversations. Their post is reportedly located just over 100 meters from the site of the work.

articles.title: Drones have not killed tank: Ukrainian analyst says Operation Vivaldi shows NATO how to make armor work again
articles.body:
The lesson for NATO is not to abandon armored warfare, but to rethink how it is conducted. That is the argument Ukrainian military observer Oleksandr Kovalenko draws from Operation Vivaldi, the Third Army Corps’ counteroffensive near Lyman, which he says proves tanks still have a place on a battlefield many had already written them off.
Vivaldi is Ukraine's counteroffensive aimed at disrupting Russian forces' plans to encircle the fortress-belt cities in Donetsk Oblast from the north and south that protect the region from the entire occupation. Among them are Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka. These cities have helped hold back Russian forces since 2014.
Kovalenko's claim runs against a view that hardened as drones came to dominate the front: that massed armor is finished, kept alive only by habit.
It matters because NATO’s own recent exercises have fed that view, with small Ukrainian drone teams beating Alliance armor again and again. Kovalenko says the Alliance now risks taking the wrong lesson from its own defeats.
What NATO’s war games got wrong about the tank
Kovalenko points to two drills. At Estonia’s Hedgehog exercises in May 2025, Ukrainian FPV-drone units ran rings around NATO troops, who he says lost vehicles by the dozen and failed one task after another.
In one episode, Ukrainian pilots notionally knocked out a large combat group built around a British brigade.
A year later, during the Aurora 26 exercises on the Swedish island of Gotland, the pattern repeated, and the NATO units, in his telling, in a sense lost control of the island.
The skeptics’ case leaned on exactly these results, Kovalenko says, with many concluding that the Alliance faltered in part because it still fielded large amounts of armor, a tool they believe has lost its relevance in modern warfare.
How the Third Army Corps made armor move again
Vivaldi is the counterexample, Kovalenko argues. During it, the Third Army Corps carried out two mechanized assaults that pushed into the Russian rear, not armor used the old way.
A similar idea appeared in the 2024 Kursk operation, he notes, paired there with intense electronic warfare; Vivaldi widened the package, with deeper reconnaissance and dedicated work against the enemy’s own strike systems.
The vehicles carried extra passive and active protection, and crews trained for the task, and Ukrainian forces moved to suppress Russian surveillance and communications.
None of these ingredients is new on its own, he says. What mattered was adapting the working formulas to attack a heavily outnumbered enemy.
“Ukrainian forces are showing that even what seems at first glance to be a battlefield anachronism can be adapted and given a new function,” Kovalenko says.
The corps’ commander made the same point about armor specifically.
“These operations prove that maneuver by armor remains possible on a battlefield increasingly dominated by reconnaissance drones, loitering munitions and precision weapons,” Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, who leads the Third Army Corps, said in a comment Kovalenko cites.
His own conclusion is a warning: NATO armies are stuck near Cold War templates for attack and defense, and unless they study and absorb what Vivaldi did, the Alliance could one day find itself routed not in an exercise but on a real battlefield.
