articles.title: Report: US deploys 10 military cargo planes to Israel amid preparations for possible strike on Iran
articles.body:
The US has transferred 10 military cargo aircraft to Israeli air bases in the southern Negev region amid preparations for a possible military strike against Iran, the Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported Thursday, Anadolu Agency reported.
The broadcaster said the aircraft landed at Ovda and Nevatim air bases, while additional US military planes were reportedly dispatched to bases in Jordan, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.
According to KAN, the planes departed from Fort Bliss in the US state of Texas, which houses one of the US military’s largest air defense centers, including facilities associated with interceptor missiles and air defense batteries.
There was no immediate US confirmation of the reported deployments, and it remained unclear what cargo the aircraft were carrying or whether Washington had decided to launch an attack against Iran.
An Israeli official told the broadcaster that Israel and the US were closely coordinating their military preparations.
“Israel and the United States are coordinating closely, and although no decision has yet been made on the matter, the Americans and Israel are preparing for any decision President Donald Trump makes,” the official said.
The official did not specify the nature or timing of any potential decision.
Earlier this week, KAN reported that Washington had warned Gulf countries about the possibility of a short, limited military campaign against Iran.
According to the broadcaster, the US military has also transferred a Patriot missile defense system from Texas to reinforce its air defenses in the Gulf region.
The report said US troops stationed at bases across the region had been instructed to leave as a precaution against a possible military escalation.
It added that US forces were replenishing their weapons stockpiles, with an additional aircraft carrier and Marine Corps unit expected to arrive in November.
The reinforcements would reportedly join approximately 20 US warships already operating in the Middle East.
Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier Thursday that US Central Command (CENTCOM) Commander Gen. Brad Cooper had briefed Trump on options for potential strikes against Iran.
The newspaper suggested that the briefing could indicate that Washington was moving closer to launching major military operations.
Democratic US Sen. Chris Murphy said he and several other senators had received a briefing on possible plans to attack Iran, describing them as “insane.”
Murphy warned that such an operation would lead to a devastating escalation and could undermine the US commitment to the rule of law.
The US and Israel launched attacks against Iran on Feb. 28, prompting Tehran to retaliate against Israel and US targets across the region before a ceasefire agreement was reached in April.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, but its implementation has stalled over disagreements related to the waterway’s security.
The latest reported military deployments come amid renewed concerns over a possible escalation between the US and Iran.

articles.title: Russian attacks across Ukraine kill 27, injure 128 over past day as 'horrific attack' strikes Dnipro train station
articles.body:
Russian attacks across Ukraine kill 27, injure 127 over past day as 'horrific attack' strikes Dnipro train station
At least 27 people were killed and 127 injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, with a daytime drone strike on Dnipro's train station accounting for the highest number of casualties, local authorities said.
A Russian attack struck a platform at Dnipro railway station on the morning of Oct. 29, killing at least 15 people and injuring at least 14 others, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
A passenger train was preparing to depart for Zaporizhzhia when the station was struck by a Russian jet-powered drone, Ukrainian Railways wrote on social media. According to Ukraine's Air Force, Dnipro was targeted by four Russian jet-powered drones at around 11 a.m., three of which were shot down by Ukrainian air defenses before reaching their targets.
"A horrific Russian attack on Dnipro train station," President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on social media in response to the attack. "The Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing."
International leaders reacted throughout the day, condemning the attacks against the backdrop of reported progress in peace negotiations.
Later in the day, Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov reported that a Russian drone struck the dormitory of a vocational school in Dnipro, setting the entire fifth floor on fire. There were no injuries, Filatov said, as the students had managed to reach the shelter before the strike.
Throughout the day, Russian attacks across Dnipropetrovsk Oblast injured four more people, including a 15-year-old girl, Hanzha said in an evening statement on Oct.29.
Following the Russian attacks overnight, about 350,000 people in the oblast were left without electricity, Hanzha said in the early morning.
Beyond strikes on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russia launched ballistic missiles, four guided aerial missiles, and 113 Shahed-type drones, including 83 jet-powered drones, against Ukraine overnight on Oct. 30, according to Ukraine's Air Force.
The main targets of the attack were in Kyiv, Poltava, and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts, according to the Air Force.
Ukrainian air defenses intercepted or suppressed three of the guided missiles and 96 Russian Shahed-type drones, including 71 jet-powered drones, across 17 locations, the Air Force said.
The Air Force did not specify how many Russian ballistic missiles were launched or how many were intercepted.
In Chernihiv Oblast, Russian forces struck central Chernihiv in northern Ukraine around noon on Oct. 29 with Banderol cruise missiles, killing two 15-year-old girls, regional governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
The attack injured 25 other people, including four children, Chaus said. The youngest child is 10 months old, while the others include a 10-year-old girl and boys aged 16 and 17, he added. Eight people remain hospitalized.
Oct. 30 has been declared a day of mourning in Chernihiv.
In the city of Kremenchuk in Poltava Oblast, at least three people were killed and 32 injured, including six children, after Russian drones struck an apartment building in a residential area, regional governor Vitalii Diakivnych said.
Oct. 30 has been declared a day of mourning in Poltava Oblast.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Russian attacks killed two people and injured 23 others, including a child, over the past day, the local authorities said.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks over the past day injured five people, regional governor Vadym Filashkin said.
Russian attacks over the past day killed four people and injured 21 others in Kharkiv Oblast, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
Four people were killed and 12 others injured in a Russian attack on the city of Izium, while six people were injured in Lozova. Three more people were injured in separate attacks in the city of Kharkiv, the village of Shevchenkove, and the village of Zatyshshia.
Russian forces attacked the oblast using FPV drones, other types of drones, glide bombs, and missiles, Syniehubov added.
In southern Kherson Oblast, a localized ceasefire aimed at allowing the evacuation of people from Russian-occupied Oleshky remains in effect. Regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin reported that one person was injured by the explosion of a Russian mine. No shelling or strikes targeting civilian or critical infrastructure were recorded over the past day, he said.
In Kyiv, Russian ballistic missile and drone attacks overnight killed one person and injured another, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration. In the Dniprovskyi District, a residential building was damaged in the attack, while a fire broke out at a non-residential building in the Darnytskyi District.
In Sumy Oblast, Russian attacks over the past day injured one person, according to the regional military administration. Russian forces attacked nine communities in the oblast using artillery, mortars, FPV drones, other drones, and glide bombs.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1709: Russian jet drone kills 14 on Dnipro railway platform beside a Zaporizhzhia-bound train
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
“The enemy has changed tactics”: Zaporizhzhia faces record number of Russian FPV drone attacks, hitting public transport 3 times in one day. The attacks injured 14 people, including a 14-year-old boy, and damaged residential buildings, warehouses, and vehicles.
Ukrainian Neptune strike destroys two Russian Su-34 bombers used to attack frontline cities, Ukraine’s Navy says. The aircraft are a key part of Russia’s tactical aviation fleet, used to launch guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian military positions and settlements near the front line.
Russia’s October losses hit record high of 49,040 with three days left, Ukraine says. Russia’s estimated personnel losses reached a new monthly high by 29 October, surpassing the previous record set in December 2024.
Russian jet drone hits Dnipro railway platform, killing 14 people next to a Zaporizhzhia-bound train. An air alert was on and the railway had ordered an evacuation, but many passengers were still beside the train when the drone struck.
Baking soda by day, armor chemistry on contract: drones reportedly strike Russia’s Bashkir Soda Company. The plant, which Russian Telegram channel Astra says sits on a closed register of defense suppliers, is the country’s only producer of a chemical used in bulletproof fibers.
Russia may use the Oleshky truce to rebuild its forces, ISW warns, as evacuees face a route through Russia and Belarus. The agreement spells out every leg of the evacuees’ trip except the last one home.
Promised discharge, but no trust: Why Ukraine’s new military contracts are struggling. Only 8,600 Ukrainians have signed the army’s new fixed-term contracts in four months.
Ukraine may already be pushing Operation Vivaldi across the Zherebets River. It’s a risky gamble. Two mappers put Ukrainian troops on the river’s eastern bank this week, including at Terny, where Russia crossed in 2024 and kept pushing until Vivaldi drove it back.
Nearly 5,000 tons of nitric acid for Russia’s military-industrial complex. Why did Azot plant become strategic target?. A military observer explains why Ukraine keeps striking Russia’s Azot plant.
Intelligence and technology
Ukraine finds Russia’s Geran drones fitted with a compass that works through GPS jamming, but Western electronics still at their core. Ukraine is also studying a new jamming device, and the findings go into its sanctions work.
Russian “Susanin” drone component may push Ukraine into nighttime blackouts. Roads and highways would go dark first, presidential adviser says. Ukraine may have to rethink its wartime blackouts if Russia begins mass use of drones and missiles carrying the “Susanin” optical-navigation module.
Russia is building Starlink no foreign company can switch off. Ukraine names 49 firms behind it, and 23 face no sanctions from Kyiv’s allies at all. One of them is Roscosmos, which puts the satellites in orbit.
Licensed, not banned: what China’s new rules mean for the parts inside Russia’s Shahed-type drones. Ukraine’s sanctions commissioner says Geran engines are on Beijing’s updated list and sees an opening for Kyiv.
International
Some European diplomats doubt Seoul over what they see as a tilt toward Russia during Moscow’s war on Ukraine, but Seoul says it backs ending the war, FT reports. Kyiv has already clashed with Seoul over fuel reaching Russia and two North Korean prisoners of war.
Russia’s sanctioned top diplomat heads to the US to campaign against the sanctions on its war. Moscow says Lavrov will use the G20 meeting in Atlanta to denounce sanctions, the economic pressure built to make Russia pay for invading Ukraine.
Germany holds two 19-year-olds over Bulgaria’s Starlink arson, and Sofia says they also attacked the network Ukraine fights with elsewhere in the EU. Bulgaria wants them extradited, and their lawyers say they will fight the warrant.
“I really don’t want this to be Yalta 2, 3, 4”: Zelenskyy fears Trump-Xi-Putin meeting could redivide world, with Ukraine on agenda. Great powers may sit down to redraw the world’s spheres of influence again.
Russia abducts Ukrainian children, and the Netherlands now funds UN search for them as part of new €1.2 billion aid package. Dutch companies get a way into rebuilding Ukraine: €136 million for partnerships and more export insurance in a new aid package.
Humanitarian and social impact
Classrooms in Sumy Oblast are moving underground due to Russian shelling: 13 such schools are already operating, nine are under construction, and another 14 are at the design stage. Russian attacks have damaged 165 schools in Sumy Oblast since the start of the full-scale invasion.
Demining complete, humanitarian convoy ready: Oleshky mission advances as ceasefire holds and Lubinets heads to occupied city. Ukrainian, Russian, and US delegations are coordinating a humanitarian operation in occupied Oleshky after mine clearance along designated routes. The mission aims to bring aid to civilians and facilitate their safe departure.
Six lanes and metro line under fire: Kyiv prepares about $22 million for backup river crossings after Russian strike on Southern Bridge. The bridges are of critical importance. About 600,000 vehicles cross the Dnipro River in Kyiv every day.
Russia may not give Oleshky evacuees a free choice to return to Ukraine, ISW warns, after Putin called the town a “Russian settlement”. Those who choose Ukraine will likely have to travel through Russia first, with no public guarantees that they will be let go.
Political and legal developments
Ankara tells Washington it’s ready to help revive Ukraine-Russia talks—but names no date or venue. Moscow claims a contact is near but that talk of Abu Dhabi is premature while it is still preparing. Kyiv wants that round before a summit without Ukraine.
€100 million at stake: what Ukrainians could save by joining Europe’s euro-payment zone, if parliament votes before November. Ukrainian small businesses pay for every euro transfer in paperwork and days of waiting.
Ukraine wants its Abu Dhabi talks with Russia before a proposed Trump-Putin-Xi summit. Tusk pointed to a first Abu Dhabi round after 4 November. Kyiv says the meeting now depends on Washington.

articles.title: An armored capsule instead of an open platform: Ukraine develops an evacuation module for the Murakha UGV
articles.body:
Ukrainian company Robotic Complexes is developing CASEEVAK, an armored module that lets the Murakha unmanned ground vehicle carry wounded soldiers off the battlefield, the company told Militarnyi on 28 October. The casualty rides in a closed capsule with ventilation, heating, lighting, and a first-aid kit, and side and rear doors let medics load and reach the soldier from any side.
Drones that can fly long distances pose a threat to both wounded soldiers and the crews evacuating them, making transportation the main challenge, said Ukrainian military medic Daryna Boiko, The Independent reported. Developers are looking for new ways to counter this threat. The current Murakha model is being equipped with passive anti-drone protection elements, the developers say.
An armored capsule that keeps the wounded connected
After a wounded soldier is loaded onto an evacuation platform, it is important not only to transport them to a safe location but also to protect them and monitor their condition during transit.
The module is built around a closed armored capsule made of 3.5 mm-thick Armox 500T steel with an inner lining of HDPE 1000, the media outlet reports. Side and rear doors allow the wounded to be loaded from different directions and accessed during evacuation.
To enable the operator to monitor the person inside and maintain contact with them, the capsule is equipped with a camera with day and night channels and two-way audio communication. The system can be controlled via ELRS, LTE, Starlink, or fiber-optic communications. Militarnyi reports that even if the capsule is detached from the main platform, it retains two independent communication channels.
The developers are also working to integrate vital-signs monitoring systems intended to provide medical personnel with information about the wounded person’s condition during transport.
An electric platform and protection against FPV drones
The evacuation module requires a platform capable of carrying it as it moves through dangerous areas. The Murakha is equipped with two electric motors, delivering a combined torque of 1,600 N·m, and a 35 kWh battery. The system’s stated range is up to 80 km, according to the media outlet.
Another area of development is protection against drones. Measures intended to protect the system include net launchers and electronic warfare (EW) equipment. However, work on a protective cage against FPV drones is still ongoing, according to the report.
The company has already conducted ballistic tests of the armor steel at a distance of 50 meters, using ammunition of various calibers, Militarnyi reports.
The Murakha-Mini logistics platform
The same company previously developed the Murakha-Mini logistics platform. Ukrainian military personnel began using it on the front line to deliver equipment, provisions and other supplies, Militarnyi reported on 24 October 2025.
The UGV can carry up to 250 kg and travel up to 40 km on a single charge, the media outlet reported. During one combat mission, it transported 150 kg of cargo and towed a six-metre platform carrying another drone and provisions, covering 16 km in one direction, Militarnyi reported.

Zelensky: Russia fired 17 ballistic missiles overnight, took no steps toward de-escalation in energy sector
According to Ukrinform, the head of state stated this in his nightly video address.

"Unfortunately, Dnipro came under repeated strikes throughout the day, including again this evening. The energy infrastructure was hit, and the railway station was hit again as well. Unfortunately, additional emergency power outages have been introduced. We have the personnel and equipment needed for restoration. In Kyiv and the region, in the Chernihiv region, Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv and Sumy regions – restoration work must proceed promptly everywhere. Today, Russian ballistic missiles also struck the Poltava region. Kremenchuk. Our oil refining infrastructure was targeted. The Russians have not taken a single step toward energy de-escalation. They continue to carry out terrorist strikes against our cities," Zelensky said.
At the same time, he stressed that Ukraine would continue working with all its partners to strengthen air defense and secure ammunition for F-16 fighter jets.
"We are preparing new decisions in the near future," the head of state said.
As reported, Russian attacks caused extensive damage to energy infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region and the Dnipropetrovsk region. It will take time to fully restore electricity supplies, the Ukrainian Energy Ministry said.

articles.title: Swiss components also found in new Russian weapons
articles.body:
Swiss components also found in new Russian weapons
Ukraine has now named 11 Swiss companies whose components have been found in Russian drones and missiles.
What new discoveries have the Ukrainian authorities made?
The Ukrainian military intelligence service, HUR, regularly publishes details of electronic components found in the wreckage of Russian weapon systems in a publicly accessible database. Findings from spring, September and October of this year show that Swiss components continue to be used in new or upgraded Russian drones, missiles and cruise missiles. Ukraine has identified components from 11 Swiss companies. Swiss components have also been found in North Korean ballistic missiles fired at Ukraine.
How important are these parts for Russian weapon systems?
Very important, says Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the Ukrainian president’s adviser on international sanctions, speaking to Swiss public broadcaster SRF. According to Vlasiuk, 95% of Russian drones and missiles contain parts from Swiss companies. The electronic components supplied by Swiss firms are mass-produced industrial goods. They are used as microcontrollers in the control systems of missiles and drones, in the processing of satellite navigation data, as voltage converters, as sensors or as memory chips.
These components are not military equipment, nor are they dual-use items
And yet these electronic components are of military use. Countries are still struggling to define these goods in a uniform manner, as they have hitherto regarded them as civilian products. With changes in the nature of warfare – for example, the widespread use of low-cost drones – these mass-produced goods are becoming strategically significant. Together with the G7 countries, the EU has placed these goods on a joint sanctions list. Switzerland has adopted this sanctions list. As a result, Swiss companies are also no longer permitted to sell them to Russia.
What is Switzerland being accused of?
Switzerland is not doing enough to prevent shipments to Russia. This is the criticism levelled by Vladyslav Vlasiuk, an adviser to the Ukrainian president. He is calling on the Swiss government to involve the law enforcement authorities and to strengthen the export control bodies. He is dissatisfied with Switzerland’s responses to date. Sanctions regimes have evolved, as has Russia’s ability to circumvent them, he says, adding that Switzerland cannot simply stick to the logic that there are no production facilities in Switzerland and that it does not export to Russia. That is not enough.
More
Swiss Army combines horses and high-tech drones
What does the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) say?
SECO is aware of the issue regarding the components, the State Secretariat stated in response to an enquiry. It explains that, in most cases, the goods are not produced in Switzerland. Consequently, no exports take place. The export of these goods from Switzerland – including indirectly – to Russia is prohibited. Swiss companies are obliged to comply with certain due diligence requirements. This includes, in the case of exports or sales to third countries, contractually prohibiting the re-export of these goods to Russia. The effective and comprehensive enforcement of sanctions against Russia is a priority for the government, SECO writes.
What is required of companies?
They should take a closer look. Particularly when selecting their distribution partners and intermediaries, says Vladyslav Vlasiuk. He cites the example of the Dutch company NXP. A few years ago, this company attracted even more negative attention than the Swiss firms. By 2026, NXP electronic components were almost entirely absent from Russian weapons.
The Ukrainian government lists 11 manufacturers based in Switzerland, two of which belong to the same group. We have asked the four companies with the most entries in the Ukrainian database for their comments:
STMicroelectronics: The company is headquartered in Plan-les-Ouates (canton Geneva). It emphasises that the use of its products for purposes other than those for which they are intended is neither authorised nor tolerated. The company has a comprehensive global compliance programme that includes training, procedures and guidelines for all sales channels. Since the end of February 2022, STMicroelectronics has taken measures to implement all sanctions packages and export control measures imposed by the EU, the US and other partner countries against Russia and Belarus. The company says it no longer conducts any business in Russia.
u-blox: In its statement, the Thalwil (canton Zurich)-based company condemns Russia’s attack on Ukraine in the strongest possible terms. Upon the outbreak of war, the company suspended all cooperation and deliveries to Russia and Belarus; sales to countries in the Eurasian Economic Union were subsequently halted as well. Since 2021, u-blox has also been working with the organisation Conflict Armament Research (CAR) to investigate how its own components ended up in drones used in the war in Ukraine. On the basis of this collaboration, it says several companies involved have been identified and blacklisted.
Traco Power: The company, based in Baar (canton Zug), points out that its products are electronic components for civilian industrial applications which are not listed in any dual-use regulation and are not intended for military purposes. Until the sanctions came into force, the company had supplied the Russian market exclusively via closely monitored authorised distribution partners. With immediate effect from February 28, 2022, Traco Power says it ceased all deliveries and business relations with Russia – including those via third countries. Any of the company’s components that may be found could therefore under no circumstances have originated from deliveries made after the sanctions came into force. The company says it conscientiously and strictly complies with all applicable regulations, embargoes and sanctions.
TE Connectivity (Schaffner / Axicom): TE Connectivity states that it complies with all export controls and sanctions applicable worldwide and has therefore fully complied with all sanctions imposed following the Russian invasion. Since these came into force in March 2022, the company has not supplied any products to Russia from any of its sites. TE Connectivity says it is committed to a business policy that excludes both direct and indirect deliveries to Russia or other sanctioned countries. These guidelines are communicated to its distribution partners, who are also expected to comply strictly with them.
So why are Swiss components still finding their way into Russia?
There are many indications pointing to China. Research and investigations by thinktanks, NGOs and the media show that intermediaries and distribution partners from China are supplying the goods to Russia. Some Swiss companies have their products manufactured in China.

articles.title: Satellite photos confirm Ukraine destroyed two Russian Su-34s
articles.body:
- Satellite imagery shows two Su-34 fighter-bombers destroyed at Russia’s Marinovka air base after a Ukrainian Neptune missile strike on Oct. 29.
- Ukraine’s Navy says the jets belonged to the 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment; Russia has not confirmed any losses at the Volgograd region base.
Satellite imagery shows the wreckage of two Su-34 fighter-bombers destroyed at Russia’s Marinovka air base in the Volgograd region, confirming Ukraine’s claim that its Neptune cruise missiles knocked out the jets on Oct. 29, open-source analysts said.
The open-source monitoring group CyberBoroshno said the post-strike image shows the effects of hits in two parking spaces where Su-34s were stationed, with the remains of the aircraft visible. It compared the image with a Sentinel satellite picture taken on Oct. 28, which shows a Su-34 standing at the same spot, a sign the location was the aircraft’s regular parking position.
“This confirms that the strike hit the places where the aircraft were based, not random points on the airfield,” CyberBoroshno said.
The Russian aviation-focused account Avivector also published satellite frames showing the destroyed aircraft, writing that the Ukrainian Navy’s Oct. 29 strike on Marinovka “destroyed two Su-34 fighter-bombers.” Russia has not publicly confirmed any losses at the base.
The Ukrainian Navy said on Oct. 29 that its units hit the base near the settlement of Oktyabrsky with a coastal Neptune missile system, in what it called a “Long Neptune” strike, the extended-range land-attack version of the Ukrainian-made cruise missile. The Navy said the two Su-34s belonged to the 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment of Russia’s 4th Air and Air Defense Forces Army, Ukrainska Pravda reported. President Volodymyr Zelensky later confirmed the result. NASA’s FIRMS satellite fire-detection system picked up a fire at the airfield on the night of the attack, and the base lies more than 400 km (250 miles) from Ukrainian-controlled territory.
The Su-34 is the main aircraft Russia uses to drop glide bombs, known in Ukraine as KABs, on Ukrainian cities, frontline positions and the troops holding them. Each jet can carry up to 8 metric tons of weapons. Russia had about 140 Su-34s in service as of Oct. 22, Ukrinform reported, and Ukraine’s military intelligence agency HUR has estimated that Russian industry can build only 14 to 18 of the aircraft a year.
Marinovka has been hit before. In June 2025, Ukrainian drones struck the base, and Ukraine’s General Staff said four Su-34s and a maintenance area were hit, with a Russian air force-linked Telegram channel later acknowledging losses. Earlier this month, on Oct. 15, Ukraine said Neptune missiles struck Su-34s at Borisoglebsk airfield in the Voronezh region, and satellite imagery of that base also showed destruction.
Ukraine has not said how many Neptune missiles it fired at Marinovka or whether other aircraft at the base were damaged in the strike.

articles.title: Houthis continue to engage in ‘fierce battles’ in mountains near Aden, Taiz - report
articles.body:
The Houthis continue to attack Saudi Arabia and are also continuing to engage in “fierce battles” in Yemen. This is an important issue because any talks with Iran, which appear to be happening, will take the Houthis into account. Arab News in Saudi Arabia said on October 30 that the “Saudi-led coalition said on Friday it intercepted and destroyed in the Makkah region a drone fired by Yemen’s Houthis.”
According to the Saudis, “a drone launched by the terrorist Houthi militia has been intercepted and destroyed in the Makkah region.” The report noted that “the Iran-backed militia has for weeks targeted airports, energy infrastructure and cities across the Kingdom with drones and missiles.”
Now, Al-Ain media in the UAE also says that “dozens of government forces and Houthis were killed and wounded on Friday in fierce battles in Al-Maqatra district of Lahj, following a large-scale attack by the militias.”
Sources in Yemen told Al-Ain News that the Houthi militias launched a large-scale ground attack on government forces’ positions in Al-Maqatirah district, the northern gateway to Lahj, in an attempt to make progress on the ground and control key mountain ranges in the area.
This is an area in southern Yemen where the Houthis are fighting a tough and complex war against the Yemeni government and also other factions aligned with the government. Some of these factions were linked to the Southern Transitional Council, which had been backed by the UAE.
The UAE has excellent sources in this area.
“The sources confirmed that the Houthi militias aim, through the attack, to control the ‘Al-Muqatara Tunnel’ area and the strategically important Al-Muqatara mountain fortress, as well as to reach the Al-Rubu’ market located in the Heijah Al-Abd valley, where the main road linking Taiz and Aden is located.” The sources explained that the battles extended to the Haifan front, where the militias are trying to reach Mount An’an, which overlooks large areas between Haifan and Al-Maqatirah.
Events in Yemen could affect Iran, UAE, Qatar, US
This area appears to be only around 40 to 50 miles from Aden. This means the battles in these mountains, amid palm trees and scrub brush and steep terrain, could determine the next moves in Yemen. What happens here, could also matter in Tehran, Doha, Riyadh and Washington.
Let’s recall why the Houthis matters. The Iran-backed Houthis have emerged as one of the most important armed terrorist armies in the Middle East, using Yemen as a base to threaten Saudi Arabia, Israel and international shipping. The movement, also known as Ansar Allah, emerged from northern Yemen's Zaydi Shi'ite community and seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014.
In early 2015, Houthi forces advanced south toward Aden, forcing Yemen's internationally recognized government to flee. Saudi Arabia intervened in March 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition seeking to restore the government and prevent the Houthis from consolidating control over Yemen.
The war devastated the country but failed to defeat the Houthis. Iran's support helped the movement develop an increasingly sophisticated arsenal of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones. These weapons enabled the Houthis to strike Saudi Arabia and eventually target Israel.
Following the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, the Houthis began launching missiles and drones toward Israel and attacking commercial shipping in the Red Sea. Israel, the United States and Britain subsequently carried out strikes against Houthi targets. The Houthis resumed attacks on Israel during the 2026 conflict involving Iran.
Yemen's war escalated again in July 2026, when the Houthis renewed attacks on Saudi targets and shipping. In September, Houthi forces advanced along the Red Sea coast, capturing Mocha and reaching the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait. The strait connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is a vital route for international trade and energy shipments.
Fighting has also intensified around Taiz, where the Houthis have sought to threaten the road linking the city to Aden, the internationally recognized government's main base.
The renewed conflict illustrates how Yemen's civil war has become intertwined with the wider regional confrontation involving Iran, Saudi Arabia and Israel. Control of territory around Bab al-Mandab gives the Houthis additional leverage over regional security and international commerce.
Al-Ain says that as the battles in the mountains have continued, “warplanes launched a series of raids on Houthi positions and gatherings to repel the militia's attack on Al-Maqatirah district in Lahj governorate.” Al-Ain concludes that “by attacking Al-Maqatirah, the Houthi militias are trying to reach Tur Al-Bahah district in Lahj, a coastal province that is the main gateway to the capital, Aden.”
Yemen has been witnessing fierce battles since the beginning of last September, following a large-scale, multi-pronged attack launched by the Houthis on areas of the western coast, Bab al-Mandab and Taiz, which resulted in thousands of deaths and injuries.
Houthis lay seige to Taiz
The Houthis are also laying siege to the city of Taiz in the mountains. Arab News says that the Houthis are also facing growing international criticism over their detention of United Nations personnel and the worsening humanitarian crisis in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city.
According to Arab News, the Houthis are holding 71 UN staff members, severely restricting the organization's ability to operate in areas under their control. “These actions render the delivery of humanitarian aid in areas under the control of the Houthis untenable at this time,” Shirin Yaseen, associate spokesperson for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, told Arab News.
The reports indicate that the humanitarian situation has deteriorated further around Taiz, where more than 800,000 people have been cut off from essential supplies. The Houthis intensified their siege in early October after seizing the road connecting Taiz with Aden, the seat of Yemen's internationally recognized government. According to the World Food Programme, approximately three-quarters of the affected population depend on humanitarian assistance. Taiz has faced varying degrees of Houthi siege since 2015.

articles.title: “The enemy has changed tactics”: Zaporizhzhia faces record number of Russian FPV drone attacks, hitting public transport 3 times in one day
articles.body:
Zaporizhzhia experienced a record number of Russian FPV drone attacks on 29 October, injuring 14 people, including a 14-year-old boy, regional authorities said.
Russian forces used FPV drones and multiple-launch rocket systems to attack civilian infrastructure, targeting municipal transport and damaging residential buildings, warehouses, and cars, prosecutors said.
Zaporizhzhia reports record FPV drone attacks
Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration head Mykhailo Semikin said Zaporizhzhia had experienced a record number of FPV drone attacks on Thursday. After meeting with military officials, he said the authorities were aware of the situation and relevant services and Ukrainian defenders were responding.
He said Russian forces had “changed their tactics and modified their drones,” adding that Ukrainian military personnel were working on countermeasures to address the new threats.
Semikin urged residents to remain calm, heed air raid alerts, and exercise particular caution.
Russian drones target municipal transport
The attacks included strikes on a municipal bus, a minibus, and a trolleybus, according to Semikin.
In the morning, a Russian FPV drone struck a municipal bus, injuring four people.
In a separate attack, Russian forces struck 15 vehicles, a warehouse building, and a power line, sparking a fire and damaging a nearby apartment building. Two men, aged 41 and 66, were injured.
At around midday, another FPV drone hit a minibus in central Zaporizhzhia, injuring one person.
Later, a Russian drone struck a municipal trolleybus, critically injuring a 56-year-old woman and lightly injuring two other women, aged 71 and 66.
Zaporizhzhia’s proximity to the front line
Zaporizhzhia lies relatively close to the front line in southern Ukraine, leaving the city exposed to Russian attacks with weapons that can be used at shorter ranges, including FPV drones and multiple-launch rocket systems.
The proximity allows Russian forces to threaten civilian infrastructure more easily without relying solely on long-range missiles or drones.
Prosecutors investigate suspected war crime
The Zaporizhzhia Regional Prosecutor’s Office said it had opened a war crimes investigation. Investigators from the Security Service of Ukraine’s regional directorate are conducting the pretrial investigation.
The casualty count and damage reports were preliminary, and authorities said information was still being updated as the attacks continued.
Russian attacks kill civilians in several Ukrainian cities
Zaporizhzhia was not the only major city hit by Russian attacks on 29 October. In Dnipro, a Russian strike on the railway station killed at least 14 people.
In Chernihiv, two teenage girls were killed and 23 people injured, including four children. In Kremenchuk, Poltava Oblast, three people were killed and 15 injured, including three children.
The attacks damaged residential buildings and civilian infrastructure in all three cities.

articles.title: “We were told brigade couldn’t be saved”: Ukraine’s 125th grew its manning 430% and won back 1,500 absent soldiers in one year
articles.body:
A year ago, Ukraine’s 125th heavy mechanized brigade was written off as beyond saving, manned at 17% with not a single tank, gun, or drone crew to its name. A year on, the brigade says it now ranks first among the army’s heavy brigades and that 1,500 soldiers who had gone absent without leave have returned to serve.
The 125th, part of Ukraine’s Third Army Corps, drew the comparison as it summed up its first year under new command. It comes as Ukraine struggles with a force-wide shortage of soldiers and leans on the Third Army Corps, the formation the 125th now fights under, for its counterattacks around Lyman.
The figures behind a brigade rebuilt from 17% strength
In the unit’s telling, the collapse was never the whole story.
“We were told the brigade couldn’t be saved. But they didn’t account for the main thing, people,” the brigade recalls.
By its own count, manning has risen 430% over the year, and its main units now stand at 95-100%. The crews that grew fastest were the ones flying drones: the number of aerial-reconnaissance teams is up 1200%, FPV crews 950%, heavy-bomber crews 1400%, and fixed-wing drone crews 600%.
The brigade also built units of uncrewed ground vehicles from scratch and stood up its own training, air defense, electronic warfare, reconnaissance, and medical structures.
Now, it is among the most effective brigades for destroying Russians, mining, artillery, air defense, ground robots, and reconnaissance, and for three months running it has placed first among the army’s heavy mechanized brigades on those combined measures.
From two pickups and a minibus to Bradleys and Leopards
The starting point was close to empty. At the beginning of the reform, the brigade had almost no combat equipment, its commander, Volodymyr Fokin, told ArmyInform in June.
“For the whole brigade we had two pickups and one minibus,” he said.
In the first six months, he added, the brigade replaced about 90% of its commanders in key posts and stood up a tank battalion, a drone battalion and a ground-robotics company.
Today it fields American Bradley infantry fighting vehicles, German Leopard tanks and artillery of various calibers.
A captain with the callsign “Skamer” told ArmyFM in July that the new equipment came with new ways of running the brigade, with more authority given to commanders who had real combat experience.

articles.title: The Pentagon wants NATO’s eastern flank to be quiet about Russia while Washington courts Moscow
articles.body:
In recent weeks, the Pentagon has urged several NATO allies, among them Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, to tone down their public warnings about the threat from Russia, four people familiar with the matter told Reuters. Pentagon officials argued that some European statements undermined Europe's security, the sources said. Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby recently advised a Baltic official against any "poking" of the Russians, one of the people said.
Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine is in its fifth year, and Moscow has spread a deniable arson and sabotage campaign across Europe. As Washington offers Moscow sanctions relief and presses Kyiv to stop hitting Russian energy, the restraint it seeks appears to fall on those Russia threatens, first Ukraine and now NATO's eastern flank.
An Estonian delegation was told to be "measured"
As an example of unhelpful rhetoric, Colby cited Europeans' public suggestions that Russia was "cornered like a rat," the person said. Reuters could not determine whose words he meant. In late September, Estonia said Russia had ordered the arson at Milrem Robotics, a Tallinn company supplying ground robots to Ukraine, and Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal likened Putin to a "rat in the corner." Michal said Putin was stepping up activity in Europe to erode the West's backing for Kyiv, and that the surest deterrent was to "back Ukraine."
At another meeting, Pentagon officials asked an Estonian delegation to keep its communications "measured," a person briefed on the encounter said. Another European official described the Pentagon's private messaging this way:
"We are helping you. The Americans are there… Just don't be loud. Don't make noise."
One European official called the advice cordial but baffling, since the Baltic states' own intelligence services have repeatedly judged it unlikely in recent months that Russia would test NATO's mutual defense provisions.
Deals with dictators lead to hell: Estonia’s PM urges Europe to help Ukraine destroy Russia’s refineries after Washington eased sanctions on diesel
The Pentagon refused to discuss "private conversations among allies," and the Baltic defense ministries did not reply.
One messenger is a key figure in the review of US troops in Europe
Colby is a key figure in the Pentagon's ongoing review of US force posture in Europe, which could lead to a sharp troop drawdown. In September, the Pentagon was weighing pulling up to 40,000 troops from Europe.
Russia has lately stepped up its deniable attacks on NATO members, Western intelligence officials say. Its suspected arson campaign against Starlink sites serving Ukraine has reached Lithuania, and on 28 October German prosecutors announced the arrest of two Belarusians suspected of plotting arson near Nuremberg. Russia denies running a sabotage campaign. Meanwhile, US officials have discussed business deals with Russia, which many European officials oppose.

articles.title: Most Russian missiles fired at Ukraine ‘contain Swiss parts’
articles.body:
Most Russian missiles fired at Ukraine ‘contain Swiss parts’
Almost all Russian drones and missiles fired at Ukraine contain electronic components from Swiss companies, according to the Ukrainian intelligence service.
Ukraine says it has identified parts made by 11 Swiss companies that play a crucial role in missiles, such as microcontrollers, navigational data processors, voltage converters, sensors and memory chips.
The Ukrainian military intelligence service HUR regularly publishes an inventory of electronic components found in the wreckage of Russian weapons. Swiss components have also reportedly been found in North Korean ballistic missiles fired at Ukraine.
More
Switzerland leads Europe in technology found in Russia’s weapons
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, advisor to the Ukrainian president on international sanctions, told Swiss public broadcaster SRF that 95% of Russian drones and missiles contain mass-produced industrial parts from Swiss companies.
+ Russia’s killer drones still boast Swiss components
It is thought that many of the components find their way into Russian hands via Chinese intermediaries. Some of the Swiss companies manufacture in China.
Vlasiuk has called on Switzerland to better enforce international sanctions to prevent Swiss components from being used by the Russian military.
The Swiss State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) told SRF that Swiss companies are obliged to conduct due diligence on customers. They must contractually prohibit the re-export of goods to Russia when exporting or selling to third countries.
An effective and comprehensive enforcement of sanctions against Russia is a priority for the Swiss government, SECO told SRF.
