articles.title: Vance offers to meet with former IRGC commander Rezaei as Pentagon preps new attack - report
articles.body:
The White House believes Mohsen Rezaei, one of the Iranian regime’s staunchest hardliners, could be the key to an agreement that would prevent renewed war between the US and Iran, Washington Post columnist David Ignatius reported Thursday evening.
Ignatius, a veteran Washington journalist who covers foreign affairs and national security, cited conversations with a US official familiar with the negotiations, providing new details about the Trump administration’s latest effort to reach an agreement with Tehran.
Previous reports revealed that Vice President JD Vance sent a personal letter last week to Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council and a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. In the letter, Vance expressed willingness to meet with him personally to discuss ending the war through negotiations.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the letter’s existence. Ignatius disclosed additional details about its contents and why the White House chose to approach a senior member of Tehran’s hardline camp.
According to the US official who spoke with Ignatius, the letter emphasized putting both countries’ national interests at the center of negotiations. Vance made clear that Washington’s primary interest was ensuring Iran did not acquire nuclear weapons.
He also pointed to Iran’s interest in rebuilding its economy, which has been severely damaged by the war and sanctions, and preserving its national sovereignty. Vance stressed that Iran must send representatives with the authority to negotiate the nuclear issue and reach binding agreements.
Rezaei the only person capable of building support for deal, US official says
A central finding in Ignatius’s report concerns US intelligence assessments of Rezaei’s influence within the Iranian regime. According to the US official, the Trump administration has concluded that Rezaei is its most important negotiating contact in Tehran and effectively the only person capable of building broad support for an agreement limiting Iran’s nuclear program.
US intelligence officials assess that Rezaei maintains regular contact with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. The two are believed to have spoken in recent days, after the American letter arrived.
Rezaei, who commanded the Revolutionary Guards for years, is believed by US officials to retain the trust of commanders who previously served under him. Over the past year, he has also strengthened his position by reorganizing the Supreme National Security Council and appointing allies to influential posts.
He maintains close ties with senior officials responsible for Iran’s economy, which has been severely damaged by the naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz and economic sanctions.
The Trump administration believes Rezaei understands the severity of Iran’s situation. His standing among hardliners could enable him to persuade opponents of compromise to accept an agreement.
If the two sides agree to meet, Istanbul or the Qatari capital, Doha, would be the most likely locations.
Ignatius noted that Vance has already played a central role in US efforts to reach an agreement with Iran. In April, he traveled to Islamabad, Pakistan’s capital, and met with Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.
During those talks, the administration offered to lift economic sanctions on Iran and pursue broad economic cooperation, an approach Trump officials called the “golden bridge,” in exchange for a binding nuclear agreement.
Ghalibaf, however, failed to secure support from the regime’s leadership in Tehran. The two countries signed a limited, vaguely worded memorandum of understanding, but it collapsed after exchanges of fire resumed in the Strait of Hormuz.
Since then, according to Ignatius, US intelligence has concluded that the Iranian regime’s real power rests with Rezaei, rather than necessarily with those who have led the formal negotiations.
Qatar continues to play a central role as a mediator, with its representatives maintaining regular contact with Rezaei and other senior Iranian officials.
Iran sees Vance's letter as respectful gesture
According to the report, Iran’s leadership viewed Vance’s personal outreach as a respectful gesture. However, there is still no indication that Iranian officials have softened their positions on the nuclear issue, which remains the main obstacle to an agreement.
The report comes as military tensions surrounding Iran rise and the Pentagon prepares for the possibility of renewed, large-scale combat operations.
Earlier Thursday, US Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper reportedly visited the White House and presented Trump with options for further military action against Iran. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine also attended the meeting.
Ignatius wrote that White House officials fear time is running out to reach an agreement without resuming the war.
He also highlighted a significant difference between Washington’s and Jerusalem’s approaches. According to Ignatius, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pushing for regime change in Iran, believing it is the only way to eliminate the threat once and for all.
Trump, meanwhile, continues to say he wants to “finish the job” in Iran as additional US forces deploy to the region. In Ignatius’s assessment, however, Trump and Vance clearly prefer a diplomatic agreement to another round of fighting.
Even as the US military prepares for a possible attack, a significant diplomatic effort is underway to reach an agreement with one of the figures most closely associated with the Iranian regime’s anti-American stance.
Ignatius, who has covered US foreign policy and the intelligence community for decades, expressed skepticism about the initiative’s prospects. He noted that Rezaei has effectively built his entire career on staunch opposition to the US and Israel.
Although Rezaei has the political influence needed to secure an agreement with Washington, doing so would represent a dramatic change of direction for him.
The initiative also illustrates Vance’s growing role in leading diplomatic efforts with Iran and his reservations about continuing a war that lacks broad support among the American public.
According to Ignatius, the political timing also matters. The initiative comes just days before the November 3 congressional midterm elections, as the Trump administration faces public criticism over the war and its economic consequences.
Beyond those political considerations, however, Ignatius concluded that pursuing a diplomatic solution is a worthwhile alternative to another round of fighting.
It remains to be seen whether Rezaei, whom Washington identifies as Tehran’s true center of power, will take the step US officials hope for: moving from decades of opposition to any agreement with the US to becoming the person capable of bringing the war to an end.

articles.title: Russian oil refinery suffers major drone attack
articles.body:
This photograph shows a general view of the oil terminal, in the port of Saint Petersburg, on September, 26, 2025. | Olga Maltseva/AFP via Getty Images
KYIV — The local governor of Russia’s Samara region blamed Ukraine for an early morning drone attack that struck an oil refinery in Novokuibyshevsk city.
“In the course of terrorist attacks on the civil infrastructure of our region and country, the vile enemy from Kyiv launched a record number of drones. There were no casualties, which is the most important thing,” Samara Governor Viacheslav Fedorischev said in a statement on Russian state messaging app Max.
Russian air defense forces shot down 1,043 Ukrainian drones over Samara, and 18 other Russian regions overnight, Moscow’s Ministry of Defense reported Friday.
Advertisement
Fedorischev asked locals not to reveal what was struck, but independent Russian media channel Astra reported a fire at the local oil refinery, which produces jet fuel for the Russian army. Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery can produce about 8.8 million metric tons of oil per year, according to Russian oil company Rosneft.
The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that Kyiv had agreed to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump. The unofficial halt is expected, according to the report, to last until after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3. Ukraine had paused drone strikes on Russian oil refineries for 72 hours when Trump announced an energy ceasefire earlier this month. But the Kremlin kept bombarding Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
“That didn’t help. There was all kinds of rhetoric, and no one thanked us for those three days,” Zelenskyy told reporters in Kyiv earlier this week.
As of Friday morning, Ukraine has not taken responsibility for the latest strike — though there was some trolling from the Ukrainian military-industrial complex.
“Little drone, how did you end up there? The Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery welcomes guests from Ukraine,” Ukrainian defense company Fire Point — which produces long-range drones used by Kyiv to bomb targets in Russia — said in a morning Telegram post.
Russia also attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles and more than 100 drones overnight, killing one person in Kyiv and leaving 350,000 people without electricity in Dnipro.

articles.title: Fire Point says its drones hit a Russian refinery’s diesel unit hours after WSJ reported Ukraine had paused such strikes under Trump’s pressure
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defense Forces hit the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in Russia's Samara Oblast with FP-1 drones early on 30 October, Ukrainian drone maker Fire Point said, adding that one of the units hit hydrotreats diesel fuel. The strike came hours after WSJ reported that Ukraine had paused strikes on Russian refineries under pressure from US President Donald Trump until after the US midterm elections on 3 November.
Russia is pounding Ukraine's power grid and cities ahead of winter, with a mounting civilian toll, including 14 people killed on a Dnipro railway platform on 29 October. Ukraine's long-range drone strikes on Russian refineries, one of its most effective operations against Moscow, target the oil money that pays for that war. Trump has pressed Kyiv for weeks to stop them, blaming them for high global fuel prices, and Ukraine went quiet without saying so and without getting what it asked for in return, WSJ reported. The Samara strike is the first on Russian oil since then. Kyiv has not said whether the pause is over.
Fires spread across a refinery that makes jet fuel for Russia's military
Residents of Novokuibyshevsk reported drones, explosions, and a fire before dawn. Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ posted the first photos on Telegram at 05:24 Kyiv time, and Russian Telegram channel Astra geolocated the fire to the refinery, citing its open-source analysis of residents' photos.
By morning, Exilenova+ counted at least 11 separate fires at the refinery. Samara Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said air defense and mobile fire groups were repelling an attack, Astra reported. The region had declared a drone alert and closed its airport.
Fire Point said its FP-1 drones scored numerous hits on the refinery grounds, and that one of the units hit hydrotreats diesel fuel. The footage published so far shows several smoke columns over the plant but does not show which units burned. The Rosneft-owned refinery has a design capacity of 8.8 million tons of oil a year and is one of the main producers of jet fuel, according to its website. Astra says it supplies jet fuel to Russia's military. The plant lies about 910 km from the front line. Ukraine's General Staff has not commented.
Ukrainian drones have hit the plant before. Ukraine's military said its forces hit it in August and caused a fire.
It is the first fire at a Russian refinery since 15 October, when Ryazan's governor reported one at the city's refinery. It is also the first reported strike on Russia's oil industry since 20 October, when Ukrainian drones hit a Druzhba pipeline pumping station in Tambov Oblast. WSJ called that strike the last before the pause.
All three Rosneft Samara refineries now offline or reduced as drones halt Kuibyshevsky operations yesterday
WSJ claims: Ukraine paused refinery strikes until after the US midterms
Ukraine's military paused its strikes on Russian refineries after weeks of pressure from Trump shook Kyiv's confidence in US support, people with knowledge of the operations told WSJ. The unofficial pause began early last week and is expected to last until after the midterms, and possibly deeper into November. Units carrying out long-range strikes were told in mid-October that the refinery campaign was effectively on hold once missions already under way were completed, two military officials said. Hours after the report, the Novokuibyshevsk strike called that account into question.
Ukraine's government has not announced a pause. Zelenskyy told reporters in Kyiv on 27 October that “our guys tried to be a little more careful during these days. But they do not have an order” not to hit refineries, according to WSJ. He said drone units were hitting other kinds of targets in Russia.
Trump's envoy Jared Kushner repeated the demand to stop the strikes at a meeting with Zelenskyy in Oslo on 20 October, two US officials told WSJ. One of them called the conversation “very tough.” Kushner, who joined remotely, said he and envoy Steve Witkoff were spending a lot of time, energy, and jet fuel on mediating with Moscow, and that a 30-day pause on refineries would be a way for Ukraine to show gratitude, the official said.
Energy truce with strings attached: Kyiv reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms
Zelenskyy had asked for something in return, WSJ reported: a mutual energy ceasefire with Russia, Patriot missiles for Ukraine's grid, or permission to use Starlink inside Russia so drones could destroy Russian missile launchers. None of those ideas got far. Some of Kyiv's European backers also nudged Zelenskyy to pause until after the midterms, a senior European official said.
The pause showed in Russia's oil industry. Russian refinery utilization at the end of October was 25% higher than at the start of the month as drone attacks subsided, Reuters reported, according to The Moscow Times.
Russia claims over 1,000 drones for a second night as Moscow's airports close again
Russia's Defense Ministry said it downed 1,043 Ukrainian drones overnight over 19 regions, including Samara Oblast, the Moscow region, and Tatarstan. The night before, it claimed 1,214.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin stated that 862 drones flew toward the Moscow region between 20:30 on 29 October and 07:30 on 30 October, that most were downed on the far approaches, and that 170 were downed on approach to the capital. Russia's aviation agency restricted flights at all four Moscow airports, Astra reported. A day earlier, more than 460 flights were delayed or canceled at Moscow and St. Petersburg airports, Astra counted.
In Starodub, in Russia's Bryansk Oblast, about 35 km from the Ukrainian border, a building of the Konservsushprod plant, which makes canned food for the Russian army, appeared to be on fire in readers' photos and videos, Astra reported, saying the plant was presumably attacked and that its open-source analyst had not verified the footage. The Atesh partisan movement reported a blast in Aleksandrovka in Rostov Oblast, and air defense fire and an explosion in Orel.

articles.title: Deal or war? US sees Iran's hardline power broker as 'greatest hope for peace'
articles.body:
The United States is making a potentially final diplomatic push to reach an agreement with Iran, with Vice President JD Vance offering to meet personally with one of Tehran's most powerful hard-line figures as President Donald Trump weighs renewed military action against the Islamic Republic.
Vance sent a message last week to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, expressing his willingness to hold direct talks on an agreement to end the war. The message described Rezaei as the greatest hope for peace, according to reports.
The diplomatic overture comes as Washington considers resuming large-scale military operations against Iran. Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, presented Trump with military options for action against Iran on Wednesday during an unusual personal visit to the White House, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The disclosure of Vance's letter to Rezaei first emerged earlier this week. On Thursday, a U.S. official familiar with the negotiations told The Washington Post that the message sought to emphasize the central importance of both countries' national interests in reaching an agreement.
American officials close to the negotiations believe the confrontation with Iran is approaching a decisive moment and have sought to convince Tehran's hard-line leadership that Vance's diplomatic initiative is serious.
According to one official, Vance identified Washington's overriding objective as ensuring that Iran does not acquire nuclear weapons.
He described Iran's principal interests as rebuilding an economy severely damaged by war and sanctions while preserving its national sovereignty.
Vance also stressed that Iran must send representatives authorized to negotiate nuclear issues, the official said.
The White House believes the window for reaching an agreement without returning to war may be closing. Vance's outreach reflects the Trump administration's assessment that Rezaei has become the central power broker in Tehran and may be the only figure capable of assembling sufficient political support for an agreement to halt Iran's nuclear program.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Rezaei maintains regular contact with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and that the two have spoken in recent days, following the arrival of Vance's letter.
Should a meeting take place, Istanbul or Doha, Qatar, would be the most likely venues, the American official said.
Washington turns to Rezaei after earlier talks collapse
Vance has been leading the administration's diplomatic efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict with Iran.
In April, he traveled to Islamabad, Pakistan, where he met Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and proposed lifting U.S. economic sanctions in exchange for a binding nuclear agreement.
The proposal also envisioned extensive economic cooperation, which Trump's negotiating team described as a "golden bridge" toward a more stable relationship between Washington and Tehran.
Ghalibaf, however, was unable to secure support for the proposed agreement among Iran's leadership.
A narrower memorandum of understanding was subsequently signed, but it quickly unraveled when hostilities resumed in the Strait of Hormuz, the strategically vital waterway through which a substantial share of the world's oil supplies passes.
Since the Islamabad meeting, U.S. intelligence agencies have increasingly concluded that Rezaei occupies a pivotal position within Iran's political and security establishment.
The former Revolutionary Guards commander retains considerable influence among his former colleagues in the military organization, which plays a central role in Iran's security apparatus and political system.
He has also consolidated his authority by reorganizing the Supreme National Security Council and appointing loyalists to influential positions within the body.
The council is one of Iran's most important decision-making institutions, coordinating national security and defense policy across the country's political and military leadership.
Rezaei's influence extends beyond security matters. He works closely with officials responsible for overseeing Iran's economy, which has been severely weakened by the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and increasingly stringent international sanctions.
American officials believe his familiarity with both the security establishment and the country's economic difficulties could make him particularly influential in determining whether Tehran accepts a negotiated settlement.
One U.S. official said Rezaei "understands the gravity of the situation."
Qatar maintains contact with Iranian leadership
Qatar has emerged as the principal mediator in the conflict, with its envoys maintaining regular communication with Rezaei and other senior Iranian officials.
The Gulf state has played a central role in facilitating indirect contacts between Washington and Tehran, making Doha a possible location for direct negotiations if both sides agree to meet.
According to reports, Iranian leaders interpreted Vance's decision to approach Rezaei personally as a gesture of respect, suggesting Washington recognizes his standing within the country's leadership.
However, there has been no indication that Tehran has softened its position on the nuclear issue.
The lack of movement underscores the uncertainty surrounding the latest diplomatic initiative, even as the United States attempts to identify an Iranian official capable of delivering a deal that the country's leadership would accept.
For the Trump administration, the immediate challenge is determining whether Rezaei can translate his political influence into meaningful concessions before Washington concludes that diplomacy has run its course.
With military options once again under consideration at the White House, the outreach to Rezaei represents an effort to test whether an agreement remains possible before the confrontation enters another phase of fighting.

articles.title: Russia strikes energy facilities in Kyiv as aid convoy heads for besieged town of Oleshky
articles.body:
Ukraine war live: Residents leave Russian-occupied Oleshky in evacuation operation
Residents evacuated from Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky have left for the Russia's Anapa city with a Ukrainian delegation, senior official David Arakhamia said Friday. They are expected to fly to Belarus before returning to Ukraine by bus. Meanwhile, more than 200,000 people remain without power in Ukraine's central Dnipropetrovsk region following deadly Russian attacks. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
Closure of independent Russian paper a 'devastating blow', UN says
The United Nations said the closure of Novaya Gazeta was yet another "devastating blow" for independent media in Russia.
"I am deeply concerned – and saddened – by the announcement today by the highly respected and fiercely independent Novaya Gazeta newspaper that it is being forced to close, in yet another devastating blow for remaining independent media in the Russian Federation," UN rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement.
"Independent journalism in the country has faced mounting restrictions and pressure for many years, but these have intensified significantly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, through increasingly restrictive legislation, tighter state controls and the harassment and persecution of journalists."
"I call on the Russian authorities to stop applying measures which stifle reporting on serious issues of legitimate public concern, and to allow full and free debate with a diversity of voices, including in the media and across the public square, in line with international standards."
EXCLUSIVE: Ukrainian minister insists Kyiv has no choice but to fight for motherland amid aid uncertainty
Ukrainian Minister for Veterans' Affairs Vitalii Kim spoke to FRANCE 24's François Picard in an exclusive interview.
"If Europe will not support us, we also will fight because it's our motherland," Kim said, insisting that Ukraine's determination to resist Russian aggression will endure regardless of the outcome of negotiations over European financial assistance.
Watch the whole interview by clicking the link below ⬇️
🎥 Stranded locals use rare truce to leave Moscow-occupied town in Ukraine
Some residents of Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in southern Ukraine ravaged by food and medicine shortages, left on Friday during a rare ceasefire brokered by the United States – due to end on Sunday evening.
Ukrainian and Russian officials visited the town together, delivering aid and marshalling those who wanted to leave.
Canada set to contribute to EU support loan for Ukraine
Canada will provide €500 million to the European Union's Ukraine support loan, Canadian Prime Minister Carney said at the conclusion of a two-day Canada-EU summit held in Montreal.
Sweden calls on EU to tighten visa rules for Russian athletes
Sweden's government on Friday called on the European Union to tighten visa rules for athletes representing Russia and Belarus, arguing there should be no normalisation of their participation in sporting events as long as the war in Ukraine continued.
The Stockholm government said in a statement that it had sent a letter to the EU commission to ask it to review "visa rules for Russian citizens participating in international sporting events."
"The aim is to ensure a more consistent and restrictive application within the EU towards individuals representing Russia and also Belarus," the statement said.
📸 In pictures: People attend an evacuation from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky
People attended an evacuation from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region.
Russia confirms humanitarian convoy from Oleshky has reached Crimea
A humanitarian convoy carrying evacuated residents from Russian-controlled Oleshky in Ukraine has reached Crimea, Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova said.
"We are concluding our humanitarian mission in Oleshky. We are currently in the territory of Armyansk (in northern Crimea), where we are organising into convoys," Lantratova posted on social media.
One convoy was carrying people bound for Ukraine, the other for Russia, she said, adding that the operation had taken place "without incidents".
EU Commission sets up framework for EU countries to approve remaining Ukraine loan by 2027
The European Commission said it had set up a framework for European countries to approve the remaining €45 billion ($50.39 billion) in loans to Ukraine to be disbursed by the end of 2027.
- The European Union has approved a loan programme for Ukraine worth €90 billion by the end of 2027. Half of the amount is set to be disbursed in 2026
- "With today's proposal, we are providing Ukraine with much-needed predictability and helping maintain essential public services," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said
- The Commission issued a positive assessment of Ukraine's financing strategy
- €13.3 billion of the amount to be disbursed next year is set to go in budget support, while the remaining €31.7 billion is earmarked to finance the Ukrainian defence industrial capacity ($1 = 0.8930 euros)
Convoy carrying evacuees from Russian-controlled Oleshky reaches Crimea, witnesses say
A humanitarian convoy carrying residents evacuated from the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky in Ukraine has reached the Russian-annexed Crimean peninsula, witnesses said.
They said the convoy of buses crossed into Crimea from the Kherson region of Ukraine.
Evacuated residents of Moscow-occupied Oleshky have left with Ukraine delegation
Evacuees from the Russian-occupied southern Ukrainian town of Oleshky in have left for the Russian city of Anapa, a senior Ukrainian official said.
Writing on the Telegram app, David Arakhamia, head of President Volodymyr Zelenkiy's parliamentary faction, said they would then fly to Belarus before travelling back to Ukraine by bus.
FRANCE 24’s Ukraine correspondent Emmanuelle Chaze reports.
Nobel committee urges Russia to 'end repression' after closure of newspaper
The Norwegian Nobel Prize Committee called on Russian authorities to "end their repression of independent media" following the closure of the newspaper Novaya Gazeta.
"The closure is a grave blow to freedom of expression and the public's right to information," committee president Jorgen Watne Frydnes said.
The publication's founder and former editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov is a Nobel Peace Prize winner.
Kremlin says Ukrainian refinery attacks do not affect upcoming peace talks
The current Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries do not jeopardise the planned trilateral negotiations on peace in Ukraine, Russia's agency Interfax cites Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying.
Moscow accuses Ukraine of resuming attacks on oil refineries
Ukraine has resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries after pausing them for a period of time, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said.
"We had a lull that lasted a certain time, but today the attacks on oil refineries resumed," Novak told a reporter from state television, amid reports of a fire at an oil facility.
Russia earlier said it had targeted energy infrastructure in and around Kyiv during overnight strikes.
Ukraine begins erecting backup bridges in Kyiv after Russian strikes
Ukraine has begun building new bridges over the Dnipro river in Kyiv, its transport minister has said.
The Ukrainian capital of around three million people has seen its bridges repeatedly struck by Russian drones, suspending traffic and stranding citizens in long traffic jams.
Ukraine's Transport Minister Mykola Kalashnyk said the government has approved the "rapid construction of alternative bridge crossings over rivers, including across the Dnipro".
A Russian drone strikes one of Kyiv's bridges on October 2, 2026. © Valentyn Ogirenko, Reuters
"In total, the implementation of 21 bridge crossings is planned. Work in Kyiv has already begun," Kalashnyk told lawmakers on Friday.
"The first bridges will become operational at the beginning of the year".
Russian attacks leave over 200,000 without power in central Ukraine
More than 200,000 people remain without power in Ukraine's central Dnipropetrovsk region following Russian attacks, authorities said Friday, a day after a deadly Russian drone strike on a train station there.
Ukraine's air force said Russia had used ballistic missiles and drones to attack several regions overnight, including Dnipropetrovsk, causing a widespread blackout in Dnipro city.
Power company DTEK said grid operator Ukrenergo had ordered emergency power cuts across the city, as well as in adjacent districts and in parts of Pavlohrad district.
"Equipment in the region has been seriously damaged due to enemy attacks," it said, adding that energy workers had worked through the night and were still busy trying to "restore power to critical infrastructure facilities".
Dnipropetrovsk regional governor Oleksandr Ganzha said on Telegram that power engineers in the region had restored electricity supply to most consumers but that "more than 200,000 subscribers remain without power".
Novaya Gazeta closure part of Russia's 'giant military campaign'
The closure of Russia's flagship independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta is part of Russia's "giant military campaign" in Ukraine, the publication's founder and former editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov has told AFP.
The paper, whose closure was announced earlier today, was "killed" because as "we are staunch opponents of war in any form" the Muratov said in an interview, charging that the move was part of "the dismantling of (Russia's) constitution".
Muratov was a joint recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021. Click on the player below to watch his interview with FRANCE 24 in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Two killed after drone strike on Russia's Samara region, governor says
Two men died after a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's Samara region, while clearing up the aftermath of the strike, the governor, Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, said in a statement on the MAX messenger.
Samara region hosts three major oil refineries and military factories.
Kremlin says European participation will be needed at some stage of peace talks, Interfax reports
Participation of European representatives in the planned peace negotiations between
Russia, Ukraine and the United States will be needed at some stage, Russian agency Interfax quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying on Friday.
Peskov said there were no detailed discussions about such participation at present.
Ukraine official posts video of Oleshky residents preparing to evacuate
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets has posted videos of himself talking to locals in Oleshky, several of them crying and wiping tears from their eyes.
Groups of residents can be seen waiting outside their buildings with bags of belongings ready to leave.
Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova has also posted a video showing groups of people waiting to board buses.
Officials from both countries have said some in the city may choose to stay, even if the fighting resumes.
The population of Oleshky has dropped from 24,000 before the war to about 2,000. Locals have faced food, water and medicine shortages for months, with some being forced to hunt and eat pigeons, former residents told AFP.
Number of residents leaving Oleshky still unclear, Kyiv says
The number of residents planning to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky for Ukrainian-held territory is still being determined, Kyiv's prime minister has said.
In a statement, Sergiy Koretskyi retracted a remark he made to parliament earlier that 527 people were planning to leave Oleshky.
"There are no exact figures at the moment. The rescue operation is ongoing, and the data is changing," he wrote on the Telegram app.
Yesterday's main developments
- A Russian drone slammed into a busy railway platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro on Thursday, killing at least 14 people in what President Volodymyr Zelensky called a "horrific" attack that demands action by Kyiv's allies.
- A localised truce between Kyiv and Moscow held for a third day in the Russian-held town of Oleshky, where a humanitarian mission was expected to arrive on Friday, according to officials from both countries.

articles.title: Russia Strikes Kyiv With Ballistic Missiles, Sparking Fires
articles.body:
Russian forces struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles late Thursday, Oct. 29, killing at least one person and setting warehouse buildings ablaze on the city’s left bank, Ukrainian officials reported.
The attack began around 10:45 p.m. local time, when Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko reported the first explosions. Shortly afterward, officials confirmed that warehouses in the Darnytskyi district had been hit.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Kyiv City Military Administration confirmed one death at 11:48 p.m. local time. Authorities had not immediately released further details about the victim.
Several hours earlier, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that new intelligence indicated Russia was preparing further ballistic missile strikes.
The latest strike followed earlier daytime attacks that left 20 people dead and at least 109 injured.
Store partially destroyed in Dnyprovskyi district
In the neighboring Dniprovskyi district, missile debris fell near a residential complex and caught fire in its courtyard, Klitschko said. The debris partially destroyed a store building, setting it on fire, though the blaze was later contained.
At two separate, undisclosed locations, blast waves blew out windows in residential buildings, damaging private vehicles parked in one of the courtyards.
Emergency services were dispatched to the affected sites as authorities assessed the extent of the damage.
Missiles launched from the north
The Ukrainian Air Force warned of a ballistic missile threat from the north at 10:40 p.m. Kyiv time, reporting a missile over Chernihiv region heading toward Kyiv.
Ukraine's Neptune Missiles Destroy 2 Russian Su-34 Bombers in Volgograd Region
Within minutes, it said at least two ballistic missiles were flying toward the capital, followed by more. The threat was declared over at 11:23 p.m.
Russian jet-powered attack drones were also active over the region throughout the evening.
One flew toward eastern Kyiv via Brovary, while another, tracked later in the night, headed west toward Fastiv in the Kyiv region, according to the Air Force.

articles.title: Russia used everything but nuclear weapons against civilians in Ukraine’s Kherson Oblast, its governor says. Drones strike up to 6,500 times weekly
articles.body:
Russia has fired more than 925,000 shells at Ukraine’s Kherson Oblast since late 2022 and now sends up to 6,500 drone attacks against it every week. Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the Kherson regional military administration, set out the toll at the Council of Europe’s Congress of Local and Regional Authorities in Strasbourg.
Approximately 70% of Kherson Oblast remains under Russian military occupation, primarily across the left (east) bank of the Dnipro River, while Ukrainian forces control and have liberated the right bank, including the regional center of Kherson city.
“Everything except nuclear weapons”: the toll Kherson carried to Strasbourg
Prokudin told European partners that his region has spent nearly five years at the epicenter of the war, a few kilometers from Russian positions.
“It used everything except nuclear weapons. A separate danger is the ‘drone safari,’ today up to 6,500 drone attacks a week. This is deliberate, targeted terror against civilians, children, medics and rescuers. But we stayed, adapted and learned to counter this terror,” Prokudin said.
What nine European countries are now coming to learn
The region has answers that are already keeping 140,000 residents alive, he said: coordination among local authorities, the military, emergency services and volunteers; underground schools and hospitals; the pace of demining in deoccupied areas; and anti-drone defenses that let Ukraine’s forces bring down most of the incoming UAVs.
“We paid an extremely high price for this knowledge. That is why our unique experience of civil-military administration is already being studied by nine European countries, from the Baltics and Scandinavia to Germany and Poland,” he stressed.
His central message, he added, was that a large-scale crisis leaves no time to prepare, and that Europe must ready its communities, energy, medicine and local government, not only its armies, while it still holds the one thing Ukrainians lacked in February 2022, which is time.
“Our pain must gain meaning, and our lessons must save thousands of lives,” Prokudin added.
He thanked the Council of Europe and international partners for their solidarity with the region.

articles.title: Classrooms in Sumy Oblast are moving underground due to Russian shelling: 13 such schools are already operating, nine are under construction, and another 14 are at the design stage
articles.body:
Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, Russian forces have damaged 165 schools in Sumy Oblast and destroyed 21 beyond repair, according to the head of the regional administration. The administration’s answer is to move classrooms underground. Design documentation for 14 new underground schools has already been prepared, Oleh Hryhorov, head of the Sumy Oblast Military Administration, said in an interview with Ukrinform published on 28 October 2026. In addition, 13 such schools are already operating in Sumy region, while nine more are under construction, the media outlet reported.
Sumy region is one of the areas regularly shelled by the Russian military, making it dangerous to hold classes in above-ground school buildings. Of the region’s 280 schools, 225 have shelters, mostly basic ones, while more than 70 have radiation-protective shelters, Hryhorov noted.
“The process is ongoing and is being scaled up as much as possible,” he said, adding that the region is bringing in partners.
Underground classrooms provide a safer learning environment in Sumy Oblast
The construction of new underground schools is primarily focused on the larger cities of Sumy Oblast, where most schoolchildren are concentrated, Hryhorov explained.
The learning process at such a school differs from the usual format. This was explained by Oleksandr Vaniushenko, the principal of one of the first underground schools in Sumy, Suspilne reported on 23 December 2025.
“We have the first shift—entirely younger children, and fifth- and sixth-graders also go out to the open locations. The second shift brings in just as many more children. The total number studying per day is 360–370,” Vaniushenko noted.
The shelter has backup power supplies, allowing children to continue their lessons during air raid alerts and power outages, according to the project, media reported.
Currently, 22 schools operate entirely in person, while 193 use a hybrid learning format, the head of the regional administration said. A total of 75,000 children are currently attending school in Sumy Oblast, he noted.
A Russian bomb hit a Sumy school during lessons in September
On 29 September, Russia struck a school in Sumy with a 250-kilogram aerial bomb while children in grades 1 to 4 were there, Serhii Kryvosheienko, head of the Sumy City Military Administration, reported. He said the Russians aimed the bomb at the school on purpose. About 40 students were in the school’s shelter when the bomb hit, a school employee told Suspilne.
"With no pity or compassion whatsoever, they strike at children? There is nothing human in the enemy! He is not fighting on the battlefield—he is destroying a nation," Kryvosheienko said.

articles.title: Trump receives rare Iran strike briefing as US weighs renewed war
articles.body:
The top U.S. military commander in the Middle East presented President Donald Trump with options for renewed strikes against Iran during an unusual face-to-face meeting at the White House on Thursday, as Washington considers launching another major military campaign against Tehran, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing U.S. officials and others with direct knowledge of the discussions.
Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), was joined by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine and other Cabinet officials. The meeting also covered matters beyond Iran, according to the report.
Cooper rarely briefs Trump in person, making Thursday's meeting particularly significant as the U.S. military prepares for the possibility of renewed fighting. The admiral previously met Trump in July, when he joined Hegseth and Caine aboard Air Force One in Delaware. The Journal said the unusual visit could indicate that Washington is moving closer to significant military operations.
The meeting followed discussions at the White House on Wednesday, when senior military officers met Vice President JD Vance. At the same time, the administration has continued efforts to reopen diplomatic channels with Tehran. The Journal previously reported that Vance had reached out to a senior Iranian hardliner in an attempt to revive negotiations.
The diplomatic contacts are taking place alongside preparations for a possible military confrontation. According to earlier reporting by the Journal, Trump administration officials have advised Arab Gulf countries to prepare for a short but intense military campaign following the U.S. midterm elections next week.
The Pentagon has also increased its military presence and defensive capabilities in the Middle East in recent weeks, sending additional air defense systems, ammunition and supplies to the region. U.S. forces have been relocated from certain bases considered particularly vulnerable to Iranian retaliation, according to the report.
Trump himself raised the possibility of renewed military action during a rally last week, referring to the major U.S.-Israeli bombing campaign against Iran earlier this year, known as Operation Epic Fury.
"We may do another little Epic Fury," Trump said. "Or they'll agree."
Iran, meanwhile, has warned both publicly and through private diplomatic communications that it would respond to any new American attack by striking U.S. military positions and targets in Gulf countries.
According to the Journal, Tehran has also resumed producing ballistic missiles using components stored in underground facilities and intensified efforts to target American personnel stationed across the Middle East.
The possibility of another military campaign has raised concerns among some lawmakers in Washington. Sen. Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat who said he had previously received classified briefings on some of the planning, sharply criticized the prospect of renewed hostilities.
Speaking Wednesday at the Middle East Institute, Murphy described the plans as "insane."
"It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law," he said.
A Pentagon spokesperson and a spokesperson for CENTCOM declined to comment on the White House meeting, according to the Journal. While the administration continues to examine military options, the renewed diplomatic contacts and regional military preparations leave open whether Trump will pursue another agreement with Tehran or authorize a new round of strikes.

articles.title: North Korean leader outlines new measures to advance drones, AI development — agency
articles.body:
PYONGYANG, October 30. /TASS/. The development of unmanned aerial vehicles and the incorporation of artificial intelligence into weapons systems will be key priorities for the modernization of the North Korean military, DPRK leader Kim Jong Un said at the Unmanned Aeronautical Technology Development 2026 exhibition, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) reported.
"The drive for absolute superiority in the field of unmanned aerial vehicles is an inevitable choice determined by the changing nature of modern warfare," Kim Jong Un stressed. According to the agency, he outlined the Korean Workers’ Party’s defense strategy, which envisages the accelerated development of unmanned aviation, and announced key state initiatives to carry it out.
The DPRK leader called for top priority to be placed on improving key technologies, incorporating artificial intelligence into unmanned weapon systems, and broadening their combat capabilities. He noted that unmanned technology is becoming one of the main tools of military operations, and its range of uses is constantly expanding.
Kim Jong Un urged the country’s scientific community to deliver breakthrough results in the fields of unmanned aviation and military artificial intelligence. He emphasized that progress in these areas must match North Korea’s successes in developing its nuclear capabilities and modernizing its conventional armed forces.
The exhibition was held on October 29. It showcased multipurpose drones for strategic and operational-tactical missions, kamikaze strike drones, and other combat systems. Kim Jong Un visited the exhibition and voiced satisfaction with the achievements of the defense industry.

articles.title: Gulf War Air Campaign Map Featured in New Smithsonian Exhibit
articles.body:
A map pinned to the wall in a basement 36 years ago will go on display in November at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum.
The map, used to identify strategic targets across Iraq in the fall of 1990, was used in the planning of Operation Desert Storm, and will be included in the museum’s new “Modern Military Aviation” gallery in Washington D.C., tracing advances in airpower from the Korean War to the present.
The exhibit seeks to expose visitors to the advances that changed the nature of warfare.
The map is one of two created at the time by now-retired Lt. Gen. David Deptula, Dean of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies. Deptula was the principal air attack planner for Operation Desert Storm—identifying strategic targets across Iraq and developing the blueprint for the coalition air campaign.
Two Gulf War maps remain in Deptula’s possession, and both are on display at AFA’s headquarters in Arlington: one depicting Baghdad hangs in AFA’s Heritage Hall, while a larger map of Iraq hangs in Deptula’s office, surrounded by other mementos and artifacts from throughout his career.
A reproduction of the map will be displayed as a large-format graphic panel at the Smithsonian. Dr. Michael Hankins, the Smithsonian’s Curator of U.S. Air Force, Navy, and Marine Corps post-World War II Aviation, learned about the maps during a chance conversation with the Mitchell Institute’s Executive Director Doug Birkey. Hankins was aware the maps had existed, but did not know they had been carried back from Saudi Arabia after the war.
Hankins immediately recognized the narrative the maps could tell and saw them as a perfect bridge for the exhibit he was creating, one that could help tell the story of the evolution from conventional airpower to the age of stealth and precision bombing that has defined military strike operations ever since.
Given the map’s fragility and size, Hankins decided a reproduction would be more accessible to visitors at the Smithsonian.
“As we were planning the layouts for some of these different labels, we had an opportunity, particularly in that section, to have a large-scale photo as an introduction to the Desert Storm section of the gallery,” Hankins said. “What better visual image to use than this to speak to that? … [It shows] how the thought process of using military aviation was different in 1991 than it might have been in previous conflicts.”
The Map, Deptula, and the Black Hole
While the map tells the story of Operation Desert Storm, it is also a pivotal artifact in the career of the officer who led the planning of that operation over countless 20-hour days in a basement room in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, that came to be known as “the Black Hole.” On Aug. 2, 1990, Iraqi forces under dictator Saddam Hussein invaded neighboring Kuwait and conquered the country within days. In response, a coalition led by the United States was formed to eject Saddam’s forces from Kuwait.
Deptula, then a lieutenant colonel working in the Office of the Secretary of the Air Force, was pulled into a Pentagon strategic planning cell known as “Checkmate,” led by Col. John Warden III. The Checkmate team had been developing a new strategic air doctrine for the post-Cold War era when it was tasked to create an operational concept for countering Iraq’s invasion with airpower. They dubbed their plan “Instant Thunder.” After briefing Army Gen. Norman Schwarzkopf, who as commander of U.S. Central Command would oversee the operation, as well as Gen. Colin Powell, then the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, Warden, Deptula and a couple of others flew to Saudi Arabia to brief Gen. Chuck Horner, the top air commander for the theater, on the plan.
Horner, unconvinced of Warden’s ability to lead the actual planning, accepted Warden’s concept, but sent Warden back to Washington, while retaining the others. Among them, only Deptula stayed long term, becoming the principal target planner for the entire campaign.
Based in the Royal Saudi Air Force headquarters basement, their “Black Hole” office was defined by secrecy, the sensitive political nature of American forces planning offensive operations on Saudi soil, and the punishing hours demanded of its occupants—and, Deptula recalled, once “someone was allowed to come into it, they were never allowed to go out.”
Here Deptula created his map and the Master Air Attack Plan that would ultimately orchestrate every strike of the campaign. On the map, Deptula and his team pinpointed strategic targets, coded by category: air defense, leadership, military bases, Scud ballistic missile launchers, command and control systems, and electricity and telecommunications networks.
The map helped planners to identify relationships between targets, coordinate force packages across multiple objectives simultaneously, and find gaps in Iraqi defenses that a list of coordinates alone could not reveal. For example, the map revealed a gap in Iraqi border monitoring stations that allowed Deptula to safely route F-15E attack aircraft to strike Scud launchers in western Iraq before they could fire on Israel. “It wasn’t just a pretty map that hung on the wall in our planning cell,” Deptula said. “That’s what the visualization of a map does that a bunch of target coordinates and names doesn’t.”
Underlying the Instant Thunder concept was the conviction that airpower could systematically dismantle Iraq’s war-making ability. Each mark aimed to take a specific capability off the table. It was a deliberate break from what Deptula called “an attritional, intelligence-based philosophy” that had defined air campaigns in Vietnam, where success was measured by the percentage of damage inflicted rather than by what capability had actually been removed.
Using the F-117 Nighthawk’s stealth capability to lead the attack, and precision munitions to ensure rapid success, coalition air forces disabled Iraq’s command and control almost instantly, and took away other war-making capabilities within weeks—all while greatly minimizing overall infrastructure damage across the country.
By targeting electrical transformer yards, rather than power plants, planners saw they could shut down the electrical grid while keeping reconstruction manageable. In some cases, Deptula recalled, Iraqi power plant managers switched off their facilities, and the coalition chose not to strike them.
“By the third night of the war, there hadn’t been an electron flowing in the Iraqi power grid,” said Deptula. “So that’s the objective.” For Hankins, the map illustrated the evolution of airpower in a way no other artifact could. He said, “I think the map shows that in an interesting way, because you can see who’s targeting what, what kinds of things they are able to target, what kinds of things they were successful at. It’s different than something you would see in the sections on the Korean War or the Vietnam War.”
Serving as the visual introduction, the map opens the gallery’s Desert Storm section, which focuses on the new technologies that defined the conflict: a scale model of an F-117 stealth fighter and an interactive display explaining how stealth technology works and why it proved so decisive.
Separately, the museum’s Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center near Dulles Airport received an original F-117 in October, so Washington visitors can see the real thing up close.
The Desert Storm section will also serve as a bridge to the conflicts of the Global War on Terror that the United States has fought over the past three decades, including the Predator drone Deptula would later help pioneer as an armed platform. After the September 11 attacks, Deptula was directing the Combined Air Operations Center for the opening of the Afghanistan campaign when the United States fired a Hellfire missile from an RQ-1 Predator at al-Qaeda targets, the first combat use of an armed remotely piloted aircraft.
For Deptula, the map’s display at the Smithsonian represents an acknowledgment of a turning point in how America wages war and as validation of the campaign itself. “I think it’s recognition of the significance of the operation,” Deptula said. “It was the birth of how we conceive air operations.”
For Hankins, the map’s greatest value may be what it teaches visitors who know nothing about the Gulf War. “It’s not just let’s launch a bunch of airplanes and go drop a bunch of weapons,” he said. “It’s much more careful than that. It takes a lot of people a lot of time.”
The Modern Military Aviation gallery, the final chapter of the Smithsonian’s eight-year renovation, is scheduled to open to the public on Veterans Day, Nov. 11, 2026.

articles.title: Russia-Africa Summit: Four days of dealmaking the West wanted Africa to skip
articles.body:
Russia-Africa Summit by the numbers: What was achieved despite Western pressure
Delegations from 48 African countries, including 21 leaders, gathered in Moscow for the third Russia-Africa Summit under the motto “For Peace, Security and Development.” The gathering concluded on Thursday with a final declaration and a new cooperation plan. Organizers reported 146 documents signed across the Summit and its accompanying economic, humanitarian and media forums, comprising 92 agreements and 54 memorandums.
More than 3,500 participants from 74 countries attended, including over 1,200 business representatives from around 630 companies.The forum hosted more than 40 sessions.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has already held at least nine bilateral meetings with African leaders, including the presidents of Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Mozambique, Namibia, the Republic of the Congo, Burundi, and Kenya, as well as Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Libya’s Presidential Council Chairman Mohamed Al-Menfi.
Bilateral talks continued on Friday, with the day’s lineup including the leaders of Sudan, Madagascar, Ghana, Mali, South Sudan, the Central African Republic, DR Congo, and Eritrea, as well as Togo’s prime minister.
The October 28-29 summit capped four days of events, beginning with Monday’s media forum and including Tuesday’s separate gas exporters’ summit. Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told RT that Western governments had tried to discourage African leaders from attending.
An overnight Ukrainian drone attack also prompted temporary restrictions at three Moscow airports before Thursday’s proceedings. Mayor Sergey Sobyanin reported 231 drones destroyed on the approaches to the capital. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov questioned the timing during an international gathering and praised air defenses.
Here are the main outcomes and key moments.
A framework through 2029
Putin and Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the African Union chair, co-chaired Wednesday's and Thursday’s proceedings. Leaders addressed a plenary session in Kremlin before continuing over a working breakfast.
They adopted the Moscow Declaration, a Russia-Africa Partnership Forum action plan for 2027-2029 and a declaration on civilian applications of artificial intelligence.
The political declaration backed greater African representation in international institutions, opposed unlawful unilateral sanctions, and supported efforts to address colonial-era damage. It also called for South Africa’s full G20 participation to be restored, following its exclusion from meetings under the US presidency. Pretoria remains a member.
At their closing press conference, Putin emphasized the potential for further cooperation, while Ndayishimiye pressed for measurable benefits. Another summit will follow, with its date and location to be agreed.
Partnership: ‘Africa has not come to ask for aid’
Russia and Africa are “natural allies in building a multipolar, genuinely democratic world order,” Putin told the plenary. He backed stronger African representation in global decision-making and described Russian businesses as partners investing in host countries rather than pursuing colonial exploitation.
African leaders also stressed that cooperation should strengthen their ability to make independent decisions and develop their economies.
“Contrary to what malevolent forces might think, Africa has not come to ask for aid,” Ndayishimiye told the Kremlin plenary. He called for commitments to become concrete investment programs and for international cooperation to follow African priorities.
Democratic Republic of Congo President Felix Tshisekedi made a similar distinction. “Diversifying our partnerships is not about choosing sides: it is about strengthening our freedom of decision-making in the service of our populations,” he said.
Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa highlighted the need to turn agreements into action while processing more minerals domestically. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi presented his country’s cooperation with Russia, including the El Dabaa nuclear plant and planned Suez Canal industrial zone, as a model for wider partnerships.
Russia also signed several documents to deepen cooperation with African regional organizations. These included memorandums with the East African Community, the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa, and the African Continental Free Trade Area Secretariat, alongside an action plan with the African Union Commission.
Sergey Lavrov met counterparts from 41 African states.
Ghanaian Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa said Lavrov pledged support for Accra’s application for BRICS partner status and would seek consensus among founding members.
Peskov said Putin presented country-specific cooperation roadmaps during bilateral meetings. Putin also highlighted expanding diplomatic representation: eight Russian embassies have opened in Africa since 2023, bringing the total to 48. Six trade missions cover 16 countries, while Botswana, Seychelles, and Togo plan embassies in Moscow.
Financing and nuclear cooperation
Signings included a Wednesday memorandum between Russia’s development institution VEB.RF and BCID-AES, the joint investment bank serving Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, to identify and assess development and integration projects.
Rosatom also signed a peaceful nuclear cooperation memorandum with Togo, establishing working groups to examine potential projects and training. Floating nuclear power units are among the possibilities.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed sought priority for nuclear cooperation, including financing, engineering training and medical isotopes. A roadmap for Ethiopia’s first nuclear plant was signed in March, Rosatom chief Aleksey Likhachev said in an interview published Friday. Site-selection preparations are underway. Burundi expressed interest in small modular reactors. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi highlighted El Dabaa and the planned Russian industrial zone near the Suez Canal as examples of bilateral cooperation.
Trade and technology at Gostiny Dvor
Wednesday’s Economic and Humanitarian Forum at Gostiny Dvor in the Russian capital set much of the practical agenda. Putin proposed at least doubling Russia-Africa trade to more than $50 billion. On Thursday, he reported that the ruble accounted for up to 85% of commercial transactions between the two sides.
Putin and African leaders toured the “Platform for Sovereign Development” exhibition, showcasing energy, healthcare, agricultural, and digital technologies.
Elsewhere, Kenyan President William Ruto visited Sberbank’s smart city development and highlighted potential AI cooperation in healthcare and education.
Gas diplomacy alongside the summit
Tuesday’s eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit adopted its own Moscow Declaration, separate from the Russia-Africa documents. It reaffirmed sovereign rights over gas resources and supported supply security, investment, and a balanced transition toward lower-carbon energy.
At Monday’s ministerial meeting, Russian Energy Minister Sergey Tsivilev promoted a proposed gas bank for long-term infrastructure financing, including in Africa. The initiative remained under discussion.
Media cooperation and liberation legacies
The Russia-Africa Media Forum ran from Monday to Thursday, organized by RT alongside Sputnik and TASS. Organizers welcomed more than 200 participants from 46 African countries for discussions on reporting, professional cooperation, and media sovereignty.
The forum also produced several media partnerships. These included Ethiopia’s Fana renewing its agreement with RT and Libya’s national news agency signing with RT Arabic. Rossiya Segodnya concluded partnerships with outlets in Algeria, Chad, Morocco, Ghana, and Zimbabwe, as well as Ethiopia’s Debre Markos University and Niger’s Higher School of Journalism and Communication.
RT’s Thursday session, “Forging Independence: Lessons from the Founders of African Nations,” featured descendants of African liberation leaders. Samia Nkrumah, daughter of Ghana’s first president Kwame Nkrumah, credited Russian support during Africa’s independence struggles, saying, “We are all here in Russia for a reason.” Ndileka Mandela, granddaughter of South Africa’s Nelson Mandela, recalled first meeting him through a prison window on Robben Island in 1981, aged 16: “I touched the window on one side and he touched on the other.”
Education and healthcare commitments
Putin extended Russia’s epidemic-control assistance program for Africa through 2029.
Eight countries have received 15 mobile laboratories, and around 450 African specialists have been trained under the program, he said.
Among the healthcare agreements was a five-year memorandum with DR Congo covering training, research, maternal and child health, nuclear medicine, and digital healthcare.
Nearly 40,000 Africans study at Russian universities, up 50% since 2020, according to Putin. Government-funded scholarship places have nearly tripled over that period, reaching 5,500 for 2026-2027. Announced initiatives include ten centers helping African applicants enter Russian universities and vocational training programs.
Andrey Maslov, director of HSE University’s Center for African Studies, told RT that extended visits by African leaders and their separate business programs showed political ties with Moscow are gaining practical substance.

articles.title: New Humvee-type air defense vehicle spotted in China
articles.body:
- Images show an upgraded Yitian-L air defense vehicle carrying two six-round missile packs, up from the four TY-90 missiles on the standard version.
- NORINCO has not commented, and it remains unclear whether the vehicle is for the Chinese military or for export.
An upgraded version of China’s Yitian-L short-range air defense system has been spotted on the move with two six-round missile packs, apparently tripling its ready-to-fire load to 12 missiles from the four carried by the production model, images shared on social media show.
The vehicle was photographed while being transported, and the images show a reworked launcher on the platform of the Dongfeng Mengshi 4×4, the Chinese equivalent of the Humvee, with two boxes of six launch tubes each in place of the four separate canisters on earlier Yitian-Ls. It was not clear where or when the photos were taken, whether the vehicle belongs to the Chinese military or is an export version, and whether the missiles are the standard TY-90 or a smaller derivative. NORINCO, which builds the Yitian family, has not publicly commented on the new configuration.
The Yitian-L is a lightweight version of China’s Yitian air defense system, meant to protect troops and fixed sites from low-flying helicopters, drones and cruise missiles. In its known form, it carries four TY-90 infrared-guided missiles and a folding 3D X-band radar on the roof. NORINCO says the radar can detect targets at up to 18 km (11 miles) and the TY-90 can hit them from 500 m out to 6 km (3.7 miles) and at altitudes of up to 4 km, Janes reported. Two operators run the system from inside the vehicle using a joystick-based digital console.
The TY-90 was originally developed as a short-range air-to-air missile for Chinese helicopters before being adapted for ground launch. It homes in on the heat from its target, so it can be fired and left to guide itself without the launcher keeping a radar beam on the target. That passive guidance also means the vehicle does not give away its position by emitting radar signals during the engagement.
Packing more missiles onto a single light vehicle addresses a problem air defense units have faced in Ukraine and the Middle East, where small drones arrive in large numbers and a four-missile launcher can empty quickly. The original Yitian and the newer Yitian II, both mounted on armored personnel carriers, carry eight TY-90s each, so a 12-round Yitian-L would carry more missiles than either of the heavier versions.
The Yitian-L has so far been an export product. Mauritania was the first known operator, displaying eight systems in June 2024, and Mali received Yitian-L systems earlier this year under a 2024 contract with NORINCO. In 2025, NORINCO also showed another lightweight Yitian variant on a Yema 4×4 chassis. The Chinese army has meanwhile fielded its own Mengshi-based short-range system, believed to be designated HQ-13, armed with FB-10A missiles.
The images do not show whether the upgraded Yitian-L keeps the same radar and fire control, whether the extra missiles cost it range or performance.

articles.title: Ukraine Requests Emergency UN Security Council Meeting Over Russian Strikes
articles.body:
Ukraine requested an emergency meeting of the United Nations (UN) Security Council on Friday, Oct. 30, over Russia’s latest wave of missile and drone attacks that left at least 25 people dead and 110 wounded nationwide.
“From Dnipro and Chernihiv to Kremenchuk and Kyiv, the scale and geography of the strikes show that no part of Ukraine is beyond the reach of Russian terror,” Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry stated, noting that the strikes targeted children, private homes, civilian infrastructure and railway facilities.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Moscow accused of blocking the UN
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, who described the strikes as another gross violation of international law and the UN charter, accused Russia of undermining international peace.
He reiterated that Russia is exploiting its status as a permanent member of the Security Council to prevent the body from carrying out its mandate. As one of the council’s five permanent members, Russia holds veto power over its final resolutions, allowing Moscow to block action on its own war against Ukraine.
As early as December 2022, Kyiv called for Russia’s removal from the Security Council.
In its latest statement, Kyiv has once again called on partners to provide Ukraine with more air-defense capabilities, to increase pressure and impose tougher sanctions on Moscow.
“Russia must understand that its campaign of terror leads only to consequences, not concessions,” Sybiha said, adding that Russia must be held accountable for the “crimes it has committed.”
Dnipro Station Hit Again as Russian Strikes Spark Fire
His remarks came as the Trump administration continues to ease economic pressure on Moscow.
On Oct. 9, US President Donald Trump struck an abrupt diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, after which Washington formally authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
The move came just three weeks after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which was intended to target Russia’s energy and defense sectors.
The Russian Direct Investment Fund, which helped arrange the diesel shipments, is now also seeking the removal of US sanctions against it, The New York Times reported.
On Oct. 21, senior US envoy Steve Witkoff publicly confirmed that Washington and Moscow are discussing future economic and trade cooperation, alongside negotiations to end the war.
He also revealed that the US Treasury Department is working directly with Kremlin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev, the fund’s chief executive, who has emerged as an increasingly prominent intermediary in Washington’s efforts to end Russia’s war through economic engagement.
A day of terror
Russia’s deadly attack on Thursday, Oct. 29 hit a railway platform in Dnipro, where a Russian jet-powered drone killed 14 people waiting near a Dnipro-Zaporizhzhia passenger train.
Russian forces struck the city’s railway station again on Friday, injuring a woman, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
In Chernihiv, a Russian Banderol strike on the city center killed two 15-year-old girls and injured 27 people, among them a 10-month-old girl.
In Kremenchuk, attacks on two locations, including an area where a boarding school was damaged, killed three people and injured 32, six of them children.
Russian guided aerial bombs (KABs) also hit an apartment building in Izium, Kharkiv region, while late in the evening, ballistic missiles struck Kyiv, setting warehouses on fire and damaging residential buildings.
In the evening of that same day, Russian forces attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles.
During the 81st UN General Assembly (UNGA) in New York late September, 51 UN member states signed a joint statement backing Ukraine and urging Russia to agree to a full ceasefire and enter meaningful negotiations.
On that same day, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the UN Security Council that Russia will not halt its aggression against Ukraine even during negotiations, rejecting growing international calls for a ceasefire.

articles.title: ‘I Won’t Hold Back’: Estonian PM Refuses to Soften Criticism of Putin
articles.body:
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said on Friday, Oct. 30, that he would not soften his criticism of Russian President Vladimir Putin after a report that Pentagon officials had urged Baltic allies to tone down their rhetoric about Russia.
Speaking to Delfi, Michal said Estonia would maintain its position and continue speaking openly about the Russian threat.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I won’t hold back. Putin is a dictator who kills women and children,” he said.
Michal added that Putin would continue doing so until he was forced to change course.
Appeasing dictators brings humiliation without preserving freedom, Michal argued. Estonia and its Baltic neighbors would continue warning about the threat posed by Russia, he said.
Michal said he had not personally received a US request to moderate his language. The issue did not arise when he last met President Donald Trump in Ankara during the summer, he added.
He noted that domestic critics accused his government of being insufficiently assertive, even as reports suggested the US wanted greater restraint.
Pentagon reportedly urges restraint
Reuters reported that Pentagon officials had privately asked several NATO allies, including Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, to tone down their rhetoric about Russia.
Four people familiar with the discussions told Reuters the requests were made during bilateral meetings in recent weeks. Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby was among the officials involved.
Zelensky Ready to Discuss Territory With Putin, Sybiha Says
One source said Colby advised a Baltic official against “poking” Russia and cited descriptions of Moscow as cornered and increasingly desperate.
Michal had called Putin a rat in a corner in September, linking Russia’s difficulties in Ukraine to suspected sabotage in Europe. Reuters could not establish whether Colby was referring specifically to those remarks.
The sources described the conversations as cordial. The Pentagon declined to discuss private exchanges between allies, and NATO also declined to comment.
The reported appeals to Baltic governments come as Washington reviews its military presence in Europe and presses European allies to take greater responsibility for their defense.
Estonia backs continued pressure on Russia
At an October summit in Brussels, Michal backed Ukrainian refinery strikes despite US pressure on Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil production.
“The faster all the Russian refineries and ability to sell energy will be blown to smithereens the better,” Michal said at the time.
His comments came as European leaders discussed additional financial support for Ukraine and relations between Kyiv and Washington deteriorated following Trump’s diesel agreement with Russia.
On July 7, President Volodymyr Zelensky and Michal signed a Drone Deal agreement on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara. Zelensky thanked Estonia for its military and humanitarian assistance, as well as its diplomatic support for Ukraine’s EU and NATO ambitions.
Allies debate how to describe the threat
Some believe emphasizing it risks amplifying the fear Moscow seeks to spread; others argue that frank warnings help explain the need for greater defense spending and continued support for Ukraine.
Western intelligence officials have warned of an expanding Russian sabotage campaign in Europe. Moscow denies conducting such a campaign.
Michal said a clear assessment of the threat was essential to preparedness and warned that Ukraine faced a difficult winter.
