articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Outrage in Europe after Russian drone kills 14 on rail platform in Dnipro
articles.body:
- European leaders have reacted with outrage to a deadly attack by a Russian drone that slammed into a busy railway platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro on Thursday, as Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Ukraine had intelligence about more ballistic missile strikes to come. French President Emmanuel Macron stressed the need for “far more than a localised ceasefire”, referencing the current truce in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky. The EU council president, António Costa, who described the Dnipro attacks as “cruel and devastating”, called for greater pressure on Russia after the latest strikes against civilians. “The EU will continue to increase the pressure on Russia and to support Ukraine until a just and lasting peace is achieved,” he added. “We call on all our international partners to do the same.”
- Later on Thursday, Russian forces launched an attack on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv with ballistic missiles, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram, hitting warehouses and triggering a fire. Emergency services were headed to the scene on the east side of the Dnipro River, he said.
- Describing the Dnipro train station attack – which killed at least 14 people and injured another 14 – as “horrific”, the president of Ukraine insisted “sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be eased for as long as this Russian war continues”. Zelenskyy warned also that Ukraine had intelligence about preparations by the Russians of new ballistic missile strikes. “We need the means to take out all this Russian evil. We are expecting relevant decisions,” he said. Another attack on Dnipro hit a student dormitory, setting it ablaze, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said, adding the assaults had cut power to 350,000 households.
- The strikes came as Ukraine and Russia kept to a fragile local ceasefire in the ravaged city of Oleshky and prepared to send a humanitarian convoy to the southern Ukrainian city under Russian occupation since 2022 and where residents have faced months of food, water and medicine shortages. Russia’s human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova said on Friday that local residents had until 2 pm local time (1100 GMT) on 30 October to evacuate, Russian news agency Interfax reported. Two people, including one sapper, were killed while de-mining in Oleshky, she said.
- Meanwhile, Ukraine’s military has paused its strikes on Russian oil refineries after pressure from US President Donald Trump, according to a report in the Wall Street Journal on Thursday, citing people with knowledge of the operations. Ukrainian units carrying out long-range strikes were told in mid-October that the campaign against refineries was effectively on hold once missions already in motion were completed, the Journal reported. The unofficial pause is expected to last until after the US midterm elections and potentially deeper into November, the newspaper said.
- After the Dnipro attack, Zelenskyy renewed his criticism of a deal struck between Trump and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin to ease some US sanctions on Russia allowing Moscow to release diesel on to global markets. “How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and the energy sector, instead of de-escalating?” he asked.
- Late on Thursday, Putin said he supported any steps aimed at restoring relations with European countries, saying the outbreak of any conflict would leave a situation with no winners. Commenting on his phone call this week with the leaders of Norway and Finland, Putin told reporters after hosting a summit with African leaders: “And if anyone wants it, let them prepare, but right now they have not achieved their goal – to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia. And if things go too far, there will be no winners at all. .”

articles.title: North Korea tests drones, tactical cruise missiles as it pledges to deter threats
articles.body:
North Korea has vowed to “deter threats” after testing suicide attack drones, tactical cruise missiles and multiple rocket launchers, state media reported on Friday.
The display of military capabilities came as South Korea and Japan reported on Thursday that North Korea had fired ballistic missiles. South Korea said the North launched around 10 missiles in its first ballistic missile test since October 12.
North Korea’s state-run KCNA said on Friday that leader Kim Jong-un attended an exhibition titled “Unmanned Aeronautical Technology Development-2026” in Pyongyang, where the capabilities and firepower of various drones and major weapon systems were showcased.
“Tactical suicide attack drones, air-to-surface missiles from multi-purpose drones and cruise missiles hit the islet target with 100 percent accuracy,” the report said.
“The 600mm-caliber ultra-precision multiple rocket launcher, which is called ‘sniper,’ opened fire before the public for the first time,” it added.
Kim called for “absolute superiority” in drone technology, saying it was “an indispensable option in light of the ever-changing patterns of modern warfare”.
Separately, North Korea’s defence ministry criticised joint air drills between South Korea and the United States.
“The frequent military moves of the enemy states at the doorstep” of North Korea “are increasing the danger of inviting an unexpected armed conflict that will result in catastrophic consequences,” the ministry warned.
It added that the “most obvious confrontational intention is bound to invite the most obvious will to respond to it”.
“Our armed forces will thoroughly deter threats with force and only act in such manner that the enemy states can understand,” the ministry said.

articles.title: Trade, sovereignty and reform: key Russia-Africa Summit 2026 takeaways
articles.body:
Trade, sovereignty and reform: key Russia-Africa Summit 2026 takeaways
Russia and African countries have agreed to deepen economic cooperation, strengthen political coordination, and push for reforms of global institutions, Russian President Vladimir Putin and African Union chair Evariste Ndayishimiye said in a joint press statement on Thursday.
Speaking at the conclusion of the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, the two leaders outlined the results of the October 28–29 gathering, which brought together senior delegations from 48 African countries, including 21 led by heads of state.
The gathering resulted in the adoption of three documents: the Declaration of the 3rd Russia-Africa Summit, the Declaration of Cooperation in the Civilian Application of Artificial Intelligence Technologies, and the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum Action Plan for 2027–2029.
Turning political solidarity into economic cooperation
Ndayishimiye said African countries are seeking to diversify their international partnerships and strengthen their sovereignty, with Russia playing a role in accelerating economic development and regional integration.
Speaking about the summit’s three-year action plan, he said that the leaders “outlined priorities, financing mechanisms, implementation schedules and areas of responsibility, and set dates by which expect to see results.”
The African Union chair called for greater Russian investment to help African countries create added value locally. He also stressed that African youth expected tangible results, including more scholarships, reliable energy supplies, and digital solutions.
Expanding trade and financial independence
Putin said Russia-Africa trade currently stood at $27 billion but remained well below its potential, and called to double it.
The Russian president noted national currencies, including the ruble, now accounted for 85% of settlements in commercial transactions between Russia and African countries.
Reducing technological dependence
Ndayishimiye called for reducing Africa’s technological dependence. He stressed the summit had adopted a separate declaration on artificial intelligence, advocating equitable international cooperation with a central role for the United Nations.
Putin said Russia and African countries had signed agreements aimed at introducing Russian digital solutions, including AI-based technologies, in African economies and public administration.
Africa must choose its own partners
Asked whether Africa risked becoming an arena for competition between major powers, Putin rejected the suggestion that Moscow viewed African countries as objects of geopolitical rivalry.
“We have not pursued any colonial policies. It is the opposite: we helped them to liberate themselves from the neo-colonial yoke,” he stated.
Ndayishimiye similarly stressed that African nations were no longer in a position where outside powers could determine their partnerships.
Reforming global institutions
Putin backed permanent African representation on the UN Security Council. “I am absolutely convinced that Africa must be represented there on a permanent basis, including in the Security Council,” he said.
Ndayishimiye reaffirmed Africa’s position on UN reform, while calling for greater representation in global financial institutions and closer cooperation with BRICS.
Strengthening security and humanitarian cooperation
Putin said Russia would continue consultations with parties involved in African conflicts and expressed hope that Moscow’s diplomatic efforts could help prevent further escalation.
He also pledged to expand cooperation in healthcare and education, including medicine supplies, mobile laboratories, and training for African students.
Russia’s epidemic-control assistance program for African countries has been extended through 2029, Putin said, adding that African partners supported expanding Russian university branches and educational centers on the continent.
Moscow Declaration sets out common political positions
The 101-point declaration, adopted in Moscow on October 29, is divided into five sections covering political and legal cooperation, security, economic ties, humanitarian cooperation, and environmental protection and climate issues. Here are its key points.
- Maritime security: Oppose the unjustified detention, seizure or arrest of civilian vessels, including African-flagged ships, in violation of international law. The document warns that such actions against commercial vessels turn maritime trade into “a tool of economic and political pressure.”
- Sanctions: Oppose unilateral coercive measures that violate international law, including measures imposed outside the UN Security Council, and strengthen coordination to reduce their impact on trade, energy, healthcare and food security.
- Sovereign assets: Oppose the freezing and attempted confiscation of sovereign assets, as well as political and economic coercion against sovereign states.
- Colonial reparations: Pursue legal mechanisms to assess and compensate for damage inflicted on African countries during the colonial era, alongside efforts to complete the continent’s decolonization.
- International justice: Counter the politicization and misuse of international criminal justice mechanisms, including their use to exert neocolonial pressure on African states, and strengthen cooperation to ensure the independence and impartiality of international courts.
- UN reform: Work toward reforming the Security Council to increase African representation, taking into account the continent’s common position under the Ezulwini Consensus and the 2005 Sirte Declaration.
- Counterterrorism: Strengthen cooperation against terrorist groups’ use of drones, encrypted platforms, and digital finance, while also addressing terrorist financing, organized crime, and maritime piracy.
- Arms control: Oppose the politicization of international arms control, disarmament, and nuclear nonproliferation mechanisms, and support compliance with existing treaties governing nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons.
- IMF and World Bank: Push for reforms to give African countries greater representation in the leadership of both institutions and more influence over decision-making.
- G20: Call for South Africa’s full and active participation in the group to be restored as soon as possible, while strengthening the voice of African countries and the wider Global South.
- Cultural heritage: Support the return of cultural objects and historical artifacts removed from African countries during colonial rule, alongside efforts to protect cultural heritage from illicit trafficking.
- Space cooperation: Expand cooperation in peaceful space exploration, satellite communications, Earth observation, and joint research, including spacecraft technologies and equipment.
- Trade and infrastructure: Expand cooperation in precious metals, strengthen industrial value chains, and develop maritime, river, road, rail, and aviation infrastructure. Remove trade barriers, increase African exports of value-added products and establish reliable financial settlement mechanisms to support trade and investment.
- Energy cooperation: Expand cooperation across oil and gas, nuclear, hydropower, hydrogen, and renewable energy to strengthen energy security and improve access to electricity.
- Education and healthcare: Expand academic exchanges, Russian-language education and joint research, while strengthening healthcare systems through medical training, laboratory development, and epidemic preparedness.
- Media cooperation: Strengthen ties between Russian and African media through the opening of representative offices, journalist training, information exchanges, and joint media projects.
- Climate policy: Oppose discriminatory protectionist measures introduced under the pretext of combating climate change, while expanding cooperation on climate adaptation and environmental projects that take national priorities into account.
- Sovereignty: Counter neocolonial practices that undermine states’ independence, restrict their decision-making, or facilitate the exploitation of natural resources, while upholding countries’ right to determine their own development paths.
- Conflict resolution: Support African-led efforts to resolve and prevent conflicts on the continent, guided by the principle of “African solutions to African problems.”

articles.title: Destinus says it now makes more cruise missiles a month than Europe did a year before 2022, but engines are what Ukraine’s strike programs are short of
articles.body:
Destinus has completed 1,750 Ruta B1 cruise missiles and reached monthly output of nearly 300, the company said on 29 October, telling Reuters this exceeds Europe’s annual cruise-missile production before Russia’s full-scale invasion.
That gives a date for easing a shortage. A looming shortage of mini jet engines threatened to hold back Ukraine’s deep-strike drones, Reuters reported in April. Czech maker ZofiTech was then producing about 200 a month, nearly all for Ukraine, and expected demand to reach thousands within months. Both Ruta versions use the 1.5-kN engines Destinus is promising. Ukraine plans to build more jet drones and cruise missiles, so engine output next year will have to keep up, Defense Express notes.
Destinus builds its own engines, but hasn’t said how many
Destinus CEO Mikhail Kokorich said the company already produces turbojets in the roughly 1.5-kilonewton class in series, supplying them both for its own missiles and to other manufacturers. The Ruta B1 runs on the company’s own T150 engine. In June, Destinus announced its 1,000th T150 and said the line was designed to sustain production of thousands of missile systems a year. The company has not disclosed its current engine output.
Block 2 enters production, Block 3 is due to fly in 2027
Meanwhile, Destinus said it has begun production of the larger Ruta Block 2, designed to carry a 250-kg payload more than 700 km. Unlike the roughly 300-km Block 1, Block 2 is designed to be stored, transported, and launched from the same container. A third version, Block 3, is planned with a 2,000-km range, with flight tests scheduled for 2027.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy acknowledged the Ruta’s combat use in October 2025. Days later, he said Ukraine expected mass production of Ruta and Flamingo missiles by the end of that year. In June 2026, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said the Netherlands was ready to finance about 700 Rutas for Ukraine, without specifying the version.
Deterrence takes “tens of thousands of missiles”
At the same time, Kokorich said Europe’s problem is shifting from production to integration.
“To have sufficient deterrence, you need to have tens of thousands of missiles,” he said.
European customers, he added, still need to build the military units and logistics to operate missiles in such numbers. Those arsenals would also need storage, transport, maintenance, and targeting infrastructure, he said, and European militaries would need to rethink how they stockpile and deploy precision-strike weapons.
No Chinese parts, and a bet on cheaper, shorter-range missiles
Kokorich said Destinus uses no Chinese components, unlike wartime production in Ukraine, and said access to Chinese suppliers would make manufacturing cheaper, faster, and easier.
Kokorich also argued that cheaper missiles with ranges under 1,000 km would make up most future demand. Separately, Destinus is working with Rheinmetall on cruise missiles and ammunition for multiple-launch rocket systems, including a planned European equivalent of the GMLRS rockets fired by HIMARS.

articles.title: Ukrainian Air Force destroys or neutralizes three missiles and 96 enemy UAVs overnight
articles.body:
Ukraine’s defense forces neutralized 99 enemy aerial targets overnight, including three Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles and 96 unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), though enemy strikes were recorded at 17 locations, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on its Telegram channel on Friday.
"According to preliminary data, as of 07:30, air defense units had shot down or neutralized 99 enemy targets: 3 Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles and 96 enemy UAVs, including Shahed-type drones (71 of which were jet-powered), Gerbera-type drones, and other types of UAVs," the message reads.
In total, overnight into October 30 (starting from 18:00 on October 29), the enemy launched attacks using Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles from Russia’s Voronezh, Kursk, and Bryansk regions; four Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles from Russia’s Belgorod region; and 113 strike UAVs, including Shahed-type drones (83 of which were jet-powered), Gerbera-type drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones, launched from the directions of Oryol, Kursk, and Shatalovo (Russia), as well as from the temporarily occupied territories of Donetsk region and the Autonomous Republic of Crimea (Hvardiyske). The primary targets of the enemy’s strike were Kyiv, Poltava, and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
The aerial assault was countered by aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare (EW) units, drone units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
At the same time, enemy weapons were recorded striking 17 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell in five other locations.
The Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine stated: "Several attack drones remain in the air; combat operations are ongoing! ... We are holding the skies!"

articles.title: EU to fast-track €45 billion for Ukraine amid acute financial crunch
articles.body:
In 2027, the EU will provide Ukraine with €32 billion in military aid and €13 billion in budget support. But more funds will be needed as Russia escalates.
The European Union intends to accelerate the disbursement of its €90 billion support loan to Ukraine as the country faces a financial crunch amid Russia's all-out escalation and blockade in the Black Sea.
The loan is split evenly: €45 billion for 2026, with payments underway, and €45 billion for 2027. Initially, the credit was meant to last until the end of next year, but the brutality of the war has upended the calculation.
As a result, Brussels will concentrate funds in the first half of 2027 to avoid a cut-off of assistance that could have catastrophic consequences on the ground.
The second €45 billion envelope will allocate €31.7 billion for the military and €13.3 billion for the budget, according to a strategy published on Friday by the European Commission.
The €31.7 billion will be paid out gradually as Kyiv submits new contracts for weapons. The submissions can begin this year to ensure timely deliveries in 2027.
The €13.3 billion will be conditional on reforms, some of which relate to Ukraine's accession process. EU leaders have urged the country to keep the legislative pace on track.
A €3.7 billion payment has already been delayed.
"We are providing Ukraine with much-needed predictability and helping maintain essential public services," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
"Together with our allies, we must also do everything in our power to mount pressure on Russia to stop its barbaric war of aggression."
Ahead of the announcement, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked Brussels to speed up disbursements.
"The sooner we start receiving the corresponding tranches for our drone production, air defence procurement, budget support and other vital expenditures, the better our position in 2027 will be," he said.
In the meantime, the Commission is searching for ways to fill the €70 billion shortfall that Ukraine faces next year, which will require fresh funding on top of the existing loan.
Commission officials insist the bloc will cover no more than two-thirds of the gap, roughly €46 billion, with the remainder to be handled by other allies. Joint debt has quickly emerged as the frontrunnerto plug the hole.
An internal document seen by Euronews identifies three main reasons for the deficit.
First, the prolongation of the war, now well into its fifth year. When Brussels designed the €90 billion loan, it did so under the assumption the conflict would end sometime in 2026. The premise, which raised eyebrows last year, has now come apart.
Second, the intensification of Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure and the blockade of the Black Sea, which are "weakening economic activity and Ukraine's capacity to raise domestic revenues", further compounding its reliance on global donors.
Third, the decrease in assistance from non-EU allies. The document says that if all NATO allies deliver on their pledges made at the summit in July, the gap in military aid will be reduced by up to €13 billion next year.
Ukraine's financial needs, the document adds, will be "largely determined" by the ability to resist Russia's airstrikes, which need costly US-made Patriot interceptors.
Kyiv has accused Washington of delaying Patriots that have been paid for with European money. The impasse has been linked with US President Donald Trump's insistence that Ukraine cease attacks on Russia's oil refineries, claiming they raise global fuel prices.
On Friday, a Ukranian drone attack was reported at the Novokuibyshevsk refinery in Russia's Samara region.

articles.title: UK Defence Secretary warns Putin may yet turn on NATO
articles.body:
Britain has to invest and has to be ready because President Putin is waging a war in Europe while saying he has no interest in one, the Defence Secretary has said, describing investment in capability, in the defence industrial base and in alliances as the things that make war less likely, according to remarks made to reporters in Glasgow.
Wes Streeting was speaking at BAE Systems Scotstoun, where a new offsets policy was announced. Asked by this publication what his warning that Britain has around a thousand days to be ready to fight and win a war means for the armed forces and for the public, and what sacrifices the public are being asked to make to get there, he said: “Well, we’re investing in our capability, we’re investing in our defence industrial base, and we’re investing in our alliances. Those things make us stronger, and the stronger we are, the stronger our deterrence, and the less likely we are to find ourselves at war.
“We don’t seek confrontation with Russia. We have no quarrel with the Russian people. But what we can’t avoid is the hard reality that at the same time that President Putin says he’s not interested in war in Europe, he’s currently waging one, and he gave the Ukrainians those assurances that he had no plans to invade only weeks before the Russian invasion took place.
“So in that climate, we have to invest. We have to be ready. And in terms of what we’re asking of the country, as the Chancellor’s Budget showed this week, we are asking people to make that contribution right across government, and so defence is our number one duty, our number one priority, and that’s why it’s my responsibility to make sure that every penny that goes in is well spent, and that every bit of value we can extract for jobs and growth here in Scotland and right across the United Kingdom is realised. That’s my commitment.”
The contribution he describes falls across government and therefore on departmental budgets, and his answer turned on deterrence, which holds that a force strong enough to make an attack unprofitable is a force that never has to fight.
He was speaking after the announcement of a new offsets policy, under which overseas companies winning British defence contracts worth more than £50 million can be required to put benefits back into the country worth up to the full value of the contract, through jobs, apprenticeships, factories, investment in British suppliers or transfers of technology. A central Offset Authority will agree, value and monitor each arrangement, and the policy applies to a select number of procurements from April 2027. Ministers consulted industry on the approach earlier this year.
Asked what role Scotland will play in the Defence Investment Plan, John Healey, who moved from defence to the Treasury and delivered Wednesday’s Budget as Chancellor, said: “Defence is our number one priority. We also announced today the defence secretary and policy, where people have seen this is a government that will direct our defence investment first and foremost in British jobs and British businesses. But there will be things that we need to buy from abroad and from allies.
“So Norwegians, for instance, are part procuring some of this portion behind us, and they will require us because they have a policy that we’re now introducing for the first time ever in Britain, which we call an offset policy. We will buy some of the things the Norwegians produce that we can’t here.
“Now, in future, when Britain places contracts abroad, we’ll make sure that those we place those contracts with invest in Britain as well, jobs, business support, innovation, so that we can make sure that every pound of British taxpayers’ money works twice.”
Norway ordered five Type 26 frigates from Britain in a £10 billion deal supporting 2,000 jobs on the Clyde, and Oslo has run an industrial cooperation requirement of its own for decades, obliging foreign suppliers of significant equipment to place work with Norwegian firms. More than £35.2 billion has been spent with overseas industry since 2016, eleven per cent of direct departmental expenditure with industry and commerce, while 85 per cent already goes to British firms.
Streeting also attacked the Scottish National Party’s position on nuclear weapons, responding to the First Minister’s claim that the government is leaving Scotland short of defence. He said: “We’ve got HMS Prince of Wales currently out on a major exercise now, so I think it’s very visible proof that what the First Minister said is both irresponsible and unfounded. I don’t think the SNP should be playing party politics with national defence and security.
“In terms of the risk of leaving the UK with insufficient defence, one of the biggest risks facing that security is the SNP’s position on unilateral nuclear disarmament. It is by far and away the most important deterrent that we have, and it’s not just the UK’s deterrent, it’s NATO’s deterrent. So any time the SNP says that a separate Scotland can be a NATO member, they have to first explain how their white flag policy on unilateral nuclear disarmament would work under a nuclear alliance.”
The party voted narrowly in 2012 to drop its opposition to NATO membership while keeping its opposition to nuclear weapons, a position that would require an independent Scotland to join an alliance whose strategic concept describes nuclear weapons as the supreme guarantee of allied security, while removing the British deterrent from Faslane and Coulport. New members are admitted by unanimous agreement of the existing ones.
Asked whether Scotland is a target for Russia, Streeting said: “The people of Scotland and people right across the United Kingdom can draw comfort and security in the knowledge that we have some extraordinary capability at our disposal. Across our armed forces, as well as our special forces, and the protection of the NATO alliance, and that principle that an attack on one is an attack on all.
“I don’t think that Putin would be foolish enough to seek a direct war with NATO today. What I can’t be certain of is that at some point in the future he might not try, and that’s NATO’s threat assessment, and that’s why we are building our capability, building our defence industry, including here in Scotland, and building our alliances so that we are strong and therefore able to deter any potential Russian threat.”
He added that governments across the United Kingdom and local councils should play their part in national resilience, work led by the Cabinet Office through the Home Defence Programme, whose public awareness campaign launched on 22 October.
Healey rejected the Scottish government’s claim that its budget is being cut by £650 million in real terms, telling reporters: “No, they’re wrong. The Scottish budget is bigger than it’s been before.”
The Budget set a target date of 2030 for defence spending to reach three per cent of gross domestic product, with the route to the NATO commitment of three and a half per cent by 2035 left to next year’s Spending Review, and the Defence Investment Plan is backed by £298 billion over four years. The Scottish defence economy is worth £2.5 billion and directly supports 12,200 jobs, including 300 roles in Edinburgh on a £453 million Typhoon radar contract.

articles.title: Russian ballistic missiles kill a man in Kyiv, capping a day that left at least 27 civilians dead across Ukraine
articles.body:
Russia attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles late on 29 October, killing a man and injuring a 35-year-old woman, Kyiv city prosecutors said. The strikes damaged eight apartment blocks in Dniprovskyi district, a gas station, a restaurant, a dental clinic, warehouses, and cars. A warehouse building caught fire in Darnytskyi district, the city administration reported.
Overnight, Russia fired Iskander-M, S-400, and KN-23 ballistic missiles, four Kh-59/69 guided missiles, and 113 drones, 83 of them jet-powered, Ukraine's Air Force said. The attack mainly targeted Kyiv, Poltava, and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts. Air defenses downed three missiles and 96 drones, but strikes hit 17 locations.
Russia is waging its war on Ukraine's cities around the clock as winter approaches, striking homes, transport, and the power grid that keeps them running. On 29 October, including the late attack on Kyiv, Russian strikes killed at least 27 civilians and injured more than 140 across six regions, by EP's tally of regional authorities' reports. It was one of the deadliest days of the autumn. Most died in daylight, on a train platform in Dnipro, in an apartment block in Kremenchuk, in central Chernihiv, and under guided bombs in Izium.
Dnipro and Kyiv's right bank lose power
A Russian strike on Dnipro left more than 350,000 customers in the city and nearby towns without power, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast's administration said shortly after midnight. Water pumping stations switched to backup power. By morning, engineers had restored electricity to most customers in the oblast, but more than 200,000 were still without power.
It was the only transport serving a village where more than 1,600 people still live: Russian forces strike a social bus with a drone in Bilenke, killing a woman and injuring other passengers
In Kyiv, equipment damaged in earlier strikes failed on the right bank, forcing emergency outages, the city administration said. Russia attacked an industrial plant in Poltava Oblast's Kremenchuk district overnight and again in the morning, with no casualties reported, the regional administration said.
In the morning, a Russian drone hit a shopping center in Kharkiv's Kyivskyi district, injuring four women, Kharkiv Oblast Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. In Chernihiv Oblast, Russian drones destroyed the house of culture in Mena late on 29 October, and in the morning a drone hit a house in Bobrovytsia and injured a woman, the regional administration said. In Chernihiv itself, 37 people sought medical help after the 29 October strike on the city center that killed two 15-year-old girls, Yana and Mariia.
Two oblasts in mourning as the Dnipro toll rises to 15
A 40-year-old man wounded in the 29 October jet drone strike on Dnipro's railway station died in hospital, raising the toll to 15, the regional administration said. Eleven people remain in hospital. Dnipropetrovsk Oblast declared 30 October a day of mourning.
Poltava Oblast also mourns three people killed when a Russian drone hit an apartment block in Kremenchuk on 29 October. Another 32 were injured, six of them children, the regional administration said.
Russian jet drone hits Dnipro railway platform, killing 14 people next to a Zaporizhzhia-bound train
In Izium, Kharkiv Oblast, Russian guided bombs hit a five-story building on 29 October, killing four people and injuring 14, police reported. In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Russian attacks killed two people in Bilenke and injured 23 across the region, 13 of them when Russia sent seven FPV drones at vehicles and public transport in Zaporizhzhia city, police said. EP reported the city faced a record number of such attacks.

- A warehouse by day, homes by night: Russian jet drones keep hitting Kharkiv

articles.title: Exclusive-Pentagon tells Europeans to cool their rhetoric on Russia, sources say
articles.body:
By Antoni Slodkowski, Gram Slattery and Andrius Sytas
Oct 30 (Reuters) - Pentagon officials have in recent weeks asked several NATO countries to tone down their rhetoric regarding the threat posed by Russia, arguing that some statements by European leaders and officials have undermined continental security, four people familiar with the matter said.
Among the nations that have received messages urging them to keep public statements in check are Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity. It was not clear if the messages, which were delivered in bilateral meetings, were conveyed to other European governments.
The US requests come as the Trump administration restarts an effort to press for a negotiated end to the full-scale war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year. The latest push has blended incentives for Russia - including sanctions relief - with pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
Asked for comment, a Pentagon official said: “Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations.”
Among the comments that have drawn US officials’ attention are suggestions by European leaders that Russia is cornered and resorting to increasingly desperate measures as its invasion of Ukraine slows to a crawl, one of the people said.
Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, a key figure in an ongoing review of US troop levels in Europe, was one of the US officials delivering the message, the people said. Reuters could not determine what other officials were involved.
None of the people, who include three European officials and a US official, suggested the advice was communicated in a confrontational manner.
EUROPE SHOULD AVOID “POKING” RUSSIA
The US messages reflect a debate within NATO regarding how to publicly address the threat of an increasingly assertive Russia.
Some Western officials have argued that emphasizing the threat posed by Moscow could play into the hands of the Kremlin, which they say seeks to sow fear and undermine support for Ukraine.
Others argue European governments must be transparent to show their electorates that sacrifice and resources are needed to keep Moscow at bay. That is especially true as Russia appears to accelerate a covert campaign of sabotage throughout the continent.
Russia has denied that it is pursuing such a campaign.
One of the people familiar told Reuters that Colby told a Baltic official recently that there should be no “poking” directed at the Russians.
The person said Colby pointed to Europeans publicly suggesting that Russia was “cornered like a rat” as an example of unhelpful rhetoric.
It was not clear what specific statement Colby was referring to. However, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal referred to Putin as a “rat in a corner” in late September, suggesting the Russian leader was resorting to sabotage efforts in Europe as Russia had become increasingly bogged down in Ukraine.
“We are helping you. The Americans are there,” said a separate European official, describing the Pentagon’s recent private messaging. “Just don’t be loud. Don’t make noise.”
In a separate recent meeting, the Pentagon urged an Estonian delegation to be “measured” in its communications, according to a person briefed on the encounter, though the person did not say Pentagon officials complained about any specific statement.
The defense ministries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia did not respond to requests for comment, while NATO declined to comment.
MOSCOW TESTS EUROPE’S RESOLVE
One of the European officials said that the Pentagon’s advice, while cordial, was baffling, given that intelligence services in the Baltic states have in recent months consistently played down the probability of Russia testing NATO’s mutual defense provisions.
Other NATO intelligence services, by contrast, have publicly warned that Russia could dramatically ramp up its sabotage campaign in the near future.
The Pentagon messages to NATO officials come at a fraught time for European security.
Moscow has recently intensified its campaign of deniable attacks on NATO countries, Western intelligence officials have said.
On Wednesday, German prosecutors said two Belarusians were arrested for allegedly planning to set fire to a building or critical infrastructure facility in the Nuremberg area. In September, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, allegations Moscow has denied.
At the same time, US officials have been discussing potential business deals with Russia as part of the Trump administration’s push for peace in Ukraine. Those efforts have drawn mixed reactions from European officials, many of whom are pushing for the Kremlin’s continued economic isolation.
Pentagon planners, meanwhile, are reviewing Washington’s force posture in Europe, a process that could see a sharp drawdown in America’s troop presence on the continent.
US officials have said European NATO members need to assume more responsibility for their own defense, particularly as the US focuses on threats in the Middle East, Latin America and East Asia.
(Reporting by Antoni Slodkowski in New York, Gram Slattery in Washington and Andrius Sytas in Vilnius; Additional reporting by Phil Stewart in Washington; Editing by Don Durfee and Alistair Bell)

articles.title: Pakistan military 'cautiously optimistic' on Iran-US mediation
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Pakistan military 'cautiously optimistic' on Iran-US mediation
Pakistan’s military is “cautiously optimistic” about its mediation between Iran and the United States, its spokesman said on Friday in his first interview since a high-level delegation visited Tehran this week.
Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir — Pakistan's chief mediator in its efforts to de-escalate the now eight-month-old Iran war — has been to Tehran twice this month, most recently on Monday alongside Saudi and Turkish officials.
"Why would the Field Marshal be going twice if it is not for some positivity? So yes, of course," spokesman Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said when asked whether the trips were a positive sign.
Pact does not bar new members
"The word that we would use is always cautiously optimistic," added Chaudhry, director general of Inter-Services Public Relations.
There were still "powerful spoilers and detractors," who believed conflict serves them, he added without naming them.
Speaking in the garrison city of Rawalpindi, where Pakistan's armed forces are headquartered, Chaudhry declined to say what was discussed or whether the United States had backed the trip.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin joined Munir in Tehran on Monday.
Their two countries signed a joint defence pact with Pakistan on 7 August, saying an attack on any signatory will be treated as an attack on all.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement has taken on added significance as the Iran war has redrawn regional alliances and raised fears of a broader Middle East conflict.
While the three signatories say the agreement is aimed at collective deterrence and regional security, analysts see its evolution as closely tied to efforts by regional powers to manage the fallout from the Iran-US confrontation.
After Monday’s talks, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said regional security should be ensured by regional countries without foreign intervention.
The wording of the pact does not bar new members, Chaudhry said on Friday when asked whether Iran could join.
"Anyone who has a shared vision of collective deterrence and regional peace, why not? Everyone is most welcome," he said, adding that it was for the political leadership of the three principal parties to decide.
Asked whether more Pakistani troops were being sent to Saudi Arabia under the agreement, Chaudhry said that would depend on the situation and the decision of both countries' political leadership.
He said Pakistan was committed to defending Saudi Arabia and the holy sites of Mecca and Medina. "We are not part of the Yemeni conflict, which is an intra-Yemen conflict," he added.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group has been reignited by the Iran conflict, stoking fears of a wider war.
Home front
On the home front, the federal government suspended the provincial government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, led by jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), on 11 October and detained Chief Minister Sohail Afridi.
The government had accused the provincial administration of failing to tackle militancy. The PTI rejected the allegations and says its government took part in counter-terrorism efforts. PTI leaders called the move a pretext to crush protests.
Asked if there would now be larger military-led campaigns in the province, Chaudhry said that was not how the army conducted counter-terrorism.
"Our counter-terrorism operations are based on what we call IBOs, intelligence-based operations... The tempo of the freedom of action of (those) IBOs will further increase," he said.
Independents backed by Khan’s PTI won the most directly elected seats in the February 2024 election but fell short of a majority. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was the only province controlled by Khan’s party.
Khan has been in jail since 2023, and his supporters see the military behind his imprisonment and the dismantlement of the PTI. The army denies involvement in politics.

articles.title: Former US ambassadors: America must stand with Ukraine
articles.body:
Flags for the United States and Ukraine billow in the wind off an activist's bicycle on April 23, 2024 in Washington, DC. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
The United States cannot credibly defend freedom around the world while treating the survival of a democracy under attack as a bargaining chip.
Russia’s war against Ukraine is not simply a territorial dispute. It is a test of whether democratic nations will defend the principles that sustain their freedom — or allow an authoritarian aggressor to destroy these principles through military force, terror and economic coercion.
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine was unlawful. Its conduct has included attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, and in March 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova over alleged war crimes involving the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children. All grave allegations that demand accountability.
Advertisement
As Ukraine continues to fight for its survival, current U.S. policy raises a fundamental question: Does Washington understand what is at stake?
If Moscow succeeds in subjugating Ukraine, other authoritarian leaders will also ask whether military conquest can succeed. Can U.S. commitments be trusted? Will democratic nations stand together when the price becomes politically inconvenient?
Ukraine’s defense is not charity. It is a strategic investment in American and European security, Washington’s credibility and the deterrence of future conflicts.
The U.S. emerged from World War II understanding that an international order based on sovereignty, freedom and rule of law serves its interests. And successive Republican and Democratic administrations recognized that unchecked authoritarian expansion threatens both American security and the independence of its allies.
That understanding must guide U.S. policy toward Russia today.
Diplomacy is essential. Negotiations to end the war should be pursued seriously. But peace cannot mean rewarding aggression, compelling Ukraine to surrender its sovereignty or giving Moscow time to rearm for another invasion.
Advertisement
Appeasement does not necessarily prevent conflict. It can encourage aggression by convincing dictators the free world lacks the will to resist them. And a ceasefire without effective safeguards could become merely a pause before the next assault. A settlement that leaves Ukraine defenseless would postpone the conflict, not resolve it.
Peace should be measured not by the speed with which an agreement is signed, but by whether it protects Ukraine’s independence and makes another war less likely. And economic pressure is among the most important nonmilitary instruments available to the U.S. in this process, as Russia’s ability to wage war depends substantially on energy revenues, access to international markets and networks that facilitate sanctions evasion.
On Sept.18, U.S. President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 into law. Then, on Oct. 16, he issued an executive order waiving specified sanctions, restrictions and duties authorized under the legislation, citing the national interest. This order raises a legitimate question about how Washington intends to use the economic leverage Congress provided.
The measurable objectives these waivers are intended to achieve, why they serve American national security and what conditions would trigger their reconsideration need to be explained.
The U.S. needs to enforce restrictions consistently, close avenues for evasion and impose consequences when countries or companies knowingly provide material assistance to Russia’s war effort in violation of applicable law.
This does not require abandoning diplomacy. It requires a coherent policy in which economic relief advances clearly defined security objectives.
Advertisement
If Washington weakens its own pressure without obtaining meaningful concessions, it risks surrendering leverage while leaving Russia’s aggression unresolved. Every source of revenue helping Moscow sustain its military campaign has consequences for Ukrainian civilians, who bear them in destroyed homes, shattered families and lost lives.
U.S. policy should not make it easier for Russia to finance a war Washington says it wants to end.
American history has a bipartisan tradition of leadership that combines the defense of freedom with strategic judgment.
Harry Truman understood U.S. security depended on resisting authoritarian expansion. During the Cuban Missile Crisis, John F. Kennedy demonstrated that strength and diplomacy are not opposites. Ronald Reagan understood freedom must be defended against those who seek to suppress it. And George H. W. Bush knew sovereignty and alliances are essential to an international order where nations cannot redraw borders by force.
Though from different eras, the leadership of these presidents reflected a common principle: American security is strengthened when the U.S. combines military strength, alliances, diplomacy and a commitment to the independence of free nations.
A policy that pressures Ukraine more than Russia, offers Moscow economic relief without substantial concessions or asks Ukrainians to accept an insecure future is not a strategy for lasting peace. It risks rewarding aggression and inviting further conflict.
Advertisement
And above all, Ukraine’s future should not be decided over the heads of Ukrainians.
Democratic institutions can be attacked and dismantled far faster than they can be rebuilt. Ukraine’s struggle is therefore about more than one war. It is about whether the democratic world will remain a community of nations bound by common principles or become a collection of states left to negotiate individually with authoritarian regimes.
History will not judge U.S. policy solely by the immediate cost of weapons, energy or sanctions. It will judge whether America stood by a nation fighting for survival, upheld the principles it asks others to respect and helped prevent future wars by demonstrating that aggression does not pay.
Adrian Zuckerman is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (2019-2021); Mark Gitenstein is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (2009-2012) and to the EU (2022-2025); Ron Gidwitz is a former U.S. ambassador to Belgium (2018-2021) and acting U.S. ambassador to the EU (2020-2021); Jim Gilmore is a former U.S. ambassador to the OSCE (2019-2021); Kathleen Kavalec is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (2023-2025); Jim Rosapepe is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (1998-2001).
POLITICO occasionally publishes opinion pieces from guest authors to offer our readers a range of perspectives on the intersection of power and politics. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not reflect the views of POLITICO.

articles.title: MBDA expands German plant to build more missiles
articles.body:
- MBDA is expanding its Schrobenhausen site to about 100 hectares to build air defense and deep strike missiles faster and in larger numbers.
- Defense Minister Boris Pistorius visited on Oct. 29; the site will produce Patriot PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors and the Taurus Neo cruise missile.
MBDA is expanding its main German site at Schrobenhausen in Bavaria to about 100 hectares (247 acres) as it turns the plant into what it calls Germany’s “missile hub” for air defense and long-range strike weapons, MBDA Deutschland said in a post after a visit by Defense Minister Boris Pistorius on Oct. 29.
The company said the expansion adds new production areas for complex weapon systems and new manufacturing technology, so it can deliver deep precision strike and air defense weapons faster and in larger numbers. Schrobenhausen develops, builds, maintains and upgrades air defense systems, guided missiles and laser weapons for the Bundeswehr and NATO partners. MBDA did not say how much the expansion will cost, how many jobs it will add or when the new areas will be finished.
Pistorius stopped at Schrobenhausen as part of a day of visits to defense companies around Munich, which also included Airbus Defence and Space, drone maker Helsing and hypersonics startup Hypersonica, the German Defense Ministry said. Almost two years earlier, he had broken ground at the same site on a new production building for Patriot interceptors.
That building is at the center of the plant’s growth. COMLOG, a joint venture of MBDA Deutschland and Raytheon, is setting up Europe’s first production line for the Patriot PAC-2 GEM-T interceptor at Schrobenhausen, with a €250 million (about $280 million) investment covering a 31,000-square-meter (334,000-square-foot) production hall. The NATO Support and Procurement Agency has ordered up to 1,000 GEM-Ts from COMLOG for Germany, the Netherlands, Romania and Spain, and Raytheon has said the plant will help fill a $3.7 billion order for Ukraine. Pistorius said in September that production of the newer PAC-3 MSE, which destroys incoming missiles by hitting them directly, is also set to begin at Schrobenhausen later this year.
On the strike side, MBDA is preparing series production of the Taurus Neo, an upgraded version of the Taurus KEPD 350 air-launched cruise missile developed with Sweden’s Saab, after signing a contract with Germany’s procurement agency at the end of 2025. Germany aims to buy about 600 Taurus Neo missiles for around €2 billion (about $2.23 billion), Reuters has reported, with production planned from 2029.
Schrobenhausen will also build the DefendAir anti-drone missile for Rheinmetall’s Skyranger 30 air defense vehicle under a contract signed in November 2025, and it hosts a final assembly line for Brimstone 3 precision strike missiles for German Eurofighters, the first outside the U.K. The plant also produces the Enforcer shoulder-fired missile.
MBDA doubled its missile production capacity across its European sites between 2023 and 2025 and plans to invest another €2.4 billion (about $2.68 billion) between 2025 and 2029 to raise output further.

articles.title: New MOKH Module for Autonomous Navigation Appears in Geran Drones – DIU
articles.body:
Starting in late summer 2026, a new MOKH module began to be detected in Russian Geran-class attack drones. This module is designed to improve the accuracy of autonomous navigation without the use of a satellite signal.
A representative of the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) shared this information in a comment to Militarnyi.
According to him, the drone’s inertial navigation system has also changed with the introduction of the new module. Two additional sensors, located in the left and right wings, are connected to it. Together with the central module, they form a three-point measurement system that allows for more accurate determination of the drone’s motion parameters during autonomous flight.
“This creates a triangle—a measurable inertial environment—that allows for greater accuracy in autonomous navigation without satellite navigation,” explained the DIU representative.
According to him, even if other guidance systems are jammed, the drone will still be able to continue its flight to the designated area.
Accuracy in this mode will be lower, but the system should allow the drone to remain capable of striking targets without a stable satellite signal.
In this way, Russian developers are attempting to reduce the strike drones’ dependence on external navigation systems, which can be jammed by electronic warfare measures.
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) also notes that the overall trend regarding the use of foreign electronic components in Russian weaponry has not changed significantly.
In cruise and ballistic missiles, as well as in some attack drones, U.S.-manufactured components continue to account for the largest share of the foreign electronics identified.
A DIU representative named Texas Instruments and Altera among the manufacturers.
Products from STMicroelectronics and Chinese manufacturers are also found in Russian weapons systems. In certain types of Russian weapons systems, notably the Garpiya and Filin, the proportion of Chinese components already predominates.
The DIU representative also reported that Russian manufacturers are increasingly physically destroying markings on foreign electronics even during the weapons production process.
According to him, this is done on a massive scale on the assembly line to make it more difficult to determine the true origin of the components.
China remains one of the main channels through which foreign electronics enter Russia, as it is home to major distributors of Western manufacturers. Once the components are resold to local companies, it becomes much more difficult to track their subsequent movement.

articles.title: How US and Israeli money turned Latvia into a drone workshop for Ukraine
articles.body:
How US and Israeli money turned Latvia into a drone workshop for Ukraine
NATO’s aggressive eastward expansion was one of the key reasons for the initiation of the military operation in Ukraine in February 2022. This is supported by RT’s findings about a drone production cluster established by NATO-affiliated enterprises near Riga.
The Baltic states had become a hub for developing combat drones as early as 2020. According to RT’s findings, companies in Latvia generated €283 million in revenue from producing UAVs, robotics, and military aerospace systems in 2022-2025 alone. More than half of that revenue came from companies with foreign investment. The two largest factories are under US and Israeli ownership, while another is partly Ukrainian-owned. Several factories form a single industrial cluster near Riga. Experts say this suggests Latvia was preparing for a conflict with Russia well in advance.
Presently, we will focus on eight UAV production factories in Latvia that are backed by foreign investments. RT uncovered the details about these companies in financial reports, aided by the G8 OSINT team that advises the Russian Defense Ministry.
According to the data, the companies collectively earned €282.98 million from 2022 to 2025.
The bulk of the revenue came from three companies: Redwire Defense Tech Riga (€131.4 million), Belss (€77.7 million), and Brasa Defense Systems (€46.7 million). The following companies contributed lesser amounts: Origin Robotics (€10.6 million), Eraser ( €6.04 million), LV-Teh (€5.98 million), Atlas Aerospace (€3.52 million), and Natrix (€0.98 million).
The Drone Coalition, which also includes the UK, was established in 2024 at Latvia’s initiative. The aim is to collaboratively supply Ukraine with drones. Collective commitments reached €600 million, and the coalition’s fund raised €1.8 billion from investors in 2024. Since then, over 100,000 drones have already been delivered to Ukraine.
Drones abound in quiet Marupe
The heart of Latvia’s drone assembly industry is located in Marupe, a suburb of Riga. Just a couple of kilometers from the international airport, five companies form a bustling UAV production cluster: Belss, its subsidiary Eraser, Brasa Defense Systems, Origin Robotics, and Redwire Defense Tech Riga.
At the center of this cluster lies SIRIN Park Marupe, a logistics hub situated near the runway. This is where Redwire Defense Tech, the industry leader in terms of revenue, is located. The company produces Penguin drones. Since 2022, they have delivered around 250 to 300 drones to Ukraine. Smaller models start at around $20,000, while some modifications can reach up to $70,000 each. The facility employs 279 people.
Nearby, at 26 Dzirnieku Street, there is Origin Robotics, which has around 60 employees. They specialize in building BEAK portable strike drones and BLAZE autonomous drone interceptors. Both models are used in Ukraine and are also part of Latvia’s military arsenal. By the end of November 2026, Origin Robotics aims to complete the development of a cargo drone system designed for precise automated delivery of cargo (i.e. explosives). In simple terms, the Latvians plan to equip quadcopters with guided mini-munitions.
Further on, in the direction of Riga, there is Brasa Defense, which occupies around 6,000 square meters of warehouse and office space at 16 Plienciema Street. They manufacture UNHUMAN ground robotic platforms designed to support infantry on the battlefield.
Located furthest from the airport, Belss operates in Ezisi Industrial Park. It is the largest defense communications integrator in Latvia (operating since 1994). The company formerly focused on secure military communications but pivoted in 2023 to develop its own line of UAVs. By 2024, they were supplying thousands of modular military drones to Ukraine. In June 2024, Belss spun off its drone division into a separate subsidiary named Eraser.
There are no doubts as to who is the primary consumer of Belss products: Latvian and Ukrainian flags are proudly displayed at the entrance. A satellite view reveals a private runway just 100 meters from the fence, used for testing equipment.
The other production facilities are located in Riga, but the difference isn’t critical since Marupe is very close to Riga. The area is home to the NATRIX, LV-Teh, and AeroVictory Baltic factories. The latter is a Baltic subsidiary of a Ukrainian company that has relocated UAV production to Latvia and has yet to submit financial reports.
Also registered in Riga is Atlas Aerospace – a company with Ukrainian roots and Israeli ownership – producing reconnaissance drones like the AtlasPRO, Atlas UAVs, and AtlasTETHER tethered systems. These devices are supplied to Ukraine and NATO countries. The company has 43 official employees.
The choice of location is strategic, according to specialists from the G8 group. In addition to proximity to the airport, a railway runs through Marupe that will soon connect with tracks leading to Ukraine via Moldova.
The father of ‘Penguins’ in the service of NATO
Latvia has its own key figure uniting several companies backed by American and European capital: Konstantins Popiks, a serial entrepreneur in the military industry. He was introduced to aeromodeling as a child and even represented Latvia in aeromodeling competitions. After enrolling at the University of Liverpool in 2005, he graduated in 2009 with a Master’s degree in aerospace engineering.
The Penguin reconnaissance drone and its combat versions, which are in service with the Latvian military and are being sold in large quantities to Ukraine, originated as Popiks’ student project. Upon returning to his homeland, he founded UAV Factory, which produces Penguin drones. Within ten years, the company reached the international level, and in 2021, it attracted an investor from the US: AE Industrial Partners. By 2022, Popiks departed, and the factory changed ownership and rebranded as Edge Autonomy.
In June 2025, the facility announced plans to double its production footprint, enabling it to produce up to ten heavy fixed-wing UAVs per month. According to documents, there were 270 employees at the time, and the company had contracts with the Latvian Defense Ministry.
In 2025, Edge Autonomy Holdings signed a merger agreement, becoming a subsidiary of American company Redwire Corp. By March 2026, it was rebranded as Redwire Defense Tech Riga, emerging as the leading company in the sector by revenue. Its reported income of €131.4 million accounts for nearly half of the total UAV sector earnings.
This defense contract not only brought Popiks fame but also significant wealth. As RT discovered, he resides in an upscale neighborhood of Jurmala (Kapu Street), where he owns a small castle. The property is surrounded by tall Baltic pines, with the Riga seashore and a beach just beyond the backyard. The property borders the Gulf of Riga.
After selling the factory, Popiks established another company – Origin Robotics. Funds from European investors began flowing in. In 2025, Belgium’s defense minister signed a €50 million contract with the company for the procurement of BLAZE drone interceptors. Currently, Origin is experiencing remarkable growth. Revenues soared from 2023 to 2025, reaching €10.6 million.
Under the wing of the IDF
Among the entrepreneurs in this cluster is Ivan Tolchinsky, an Israeli citizen of Ukrainian descent. Born in Gorlovka, Donetsk Region, he moved to Israel at the age of 10. As an adult, he served in the special forces and took part in combat operations in Lebanon. For around five years, he worked as an engineer in Israel’s aerospace industry and spent a year in China studying mass electronics production.
In 2015, Tolchinsky relocated to Latvia, where he co-founded Atlas Dynamics with Igor Zhidanov, a fellow native of Gorlovka. Zhidanov is a seasoned engineer with 35 years of experience and holds three world records in aeromodeling. He had his own club back in Gorlovka, which Tolchinsky was also a part of.
In interviews with Latvian and Ukrainian media, Tolchinsky revealed that his production facility produces over 300 Atlas drones per month – which, he says, is five times more than in previous years. He doesn’t conceal his collaboration with the Ukrainian Armed Forces. “We have a direct contract with the Ministry of Defense, which we’ve already fulfilled. Now we are working towards another contract,” he told Ukrainian journalists.
A few years before the conflict, in 2020, Tolchinsky established a subsidiary in Ireland called Atlas Dynamics UK. Originally registered at a residential address in Moreton-on-Lugg, Herefordshire, it soon changed its legal address.
The company had Israeli roots, as indicated by its founding documents drafted in Hebrew and English by a notary from Israel.
In the 2020s, Atlas Dynamics was rebranded as Atlas Aerospace SIA. In November 2025, Tolchinsky sold the company to Israel’s Xtend Reality Expansion Ltd – a company focused on creating FPV drones for entertainment and gaming prior to its collaboration with the IDF.
Russia is identified as the main adversary
Latvian UAV factories do not publicly mention contracts with Ukraine in their annual reports. Some only mention that Ukraine is among their clients, without disclosing what portion of their profits comes from supplying Kiev.
One thing is clear: Nearly all the above-mentioned companies receive investments from the Latvian Defense Ministry and EU agencies. This is part of measures to enhance defense capabilities, with Russia identified as the chief adversary.
According to EU Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius, “Russia is outproducing Europe in key armaments.” This has been cited as a reason for increased defense spending, which is reflected in official documents.
According to reports reviewed by RT, one of the main sources of funding for SIA Belss is the European Defense Fund (EDF). In 2024-2025, the fund allocated €470,800 to the company under the European Extended Mine Countermeasures program, aimed at developing demining technologies. Earlier, RT reported on how the EU channels military expenditures through the guise of ‘humanitarian’ demining initiatives.
Even before 2022, Latvia’s drone sector was already experiencing rapid growth and consolidation. LV-Teh has been operating since 2020, while Brasa Defense Systems officially became a separate entity on September 13, 2021. Origin Robotics was registered on January 31, 2022 – just weeks before the start of the Ukraine conflict.
Belss has been in business since 1994, but significantly expanded its capabilities in 2022 and 2023. UAV Factory, known for its Penguin drones, was founded in 2009, and Atlas Aerospace emerged in 2015.
Only three new companies appeared after the start of hostilities: Natrix in February 2024, Eraser in June 2024, and AeroVictory Baltic (a company with direct Ukrainian roots) in February 2026.
In one of the reports, RT uncovered evidence of Latvia’s preparations for the conflict. In December 2021, just two months before the start of hostilities, the Latvian Defense Ministry allocated €88,000 to Belss for upgrading British infantry fighting vehicles in service with the Latvian army. This included installing automatic fire control systems on turrets, allowing operators to engage targets without exposing themselves, thereby enhancing crew survival on the modern battlefield, which is increasingly dominated by drones. This suggests that Latvians were gearing up for drone warfare well before the start of the conflict.
Long before the events of 2014 and 2022, a coalition of three countries with a firm anti-Russia stance formed in the Baltics, Vadim Avva, a Russian writer and political scientist born in Daugavpils, Latvia, says.
“The statehood of the Baltic nations led to the establishment of three sparsely-populated forts along [Russia’s] northwestern borders; their primary function is to support expanding NATO military bases and other infrastructure clearly being prepared for an operation to invade and occupy the territories of Russia and Belarus,” Avva says.
A launchpad for hatred
Avva recalled a viral video in which Estonian teenagers were asked which country should be erased from the world map, and many named Russia. He notes that during World War II, the national bourgeoisie of Latvia and Estonia “became a foundation for Latvian and Estonian SS legions,” and today, local schools are named after Lithuanian collaborators with Nazi Germany. He explains that the oppression of the Russian-speaking population in these regions began in the late 19th century and only intensified with the collapse of the Soviet Union.
“What has returned to the Baltics is not just bourgeois nationalism; it’s a blend of bourgeois Nazism and ‘brown’ [ultra-right] emigration,” Avva says. “What fate could befall this territory after the establishment of property monopoly and political monopoly and the welcoming back of the descendants of fascist collaborators? Obviously, it could only become a military launchpad.”
Latvian UAVs are occasionally identified and shot down by Russian drone interceptors. However, their share among the various models used by Ukraine remains small, according to a drone operator with the call sign ‘Baks’, who neutralizes enemy drones approaching Russian borders.
“Ukrainians definitely try out everything produced by the Balts and purchase a lot of their equipment, but it’s a question of scale and quantity. We don’t have much information on the BLAZE and BEAK models, but there is some info on ‘Penguins’ – our colleagues at Rubicon [Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies] managed to take down a few. The number of downed UAVs directly relates to their quantity. Compared to the Shark, Leleka, and other [Ukrainian drones], Latvian models represent a mere fraction [of the deployed drones].”
It’s not just Penguin drones that are being targeted, however, but their manufacturers as well. Redwire Defense Tech Riga, the company producing these drones, relocated to Sirin Park after their previous facility in Marupe unexpectedly burned down.
Similar incidents often occur at European companies that supply drones to Ukraine. In August 2026 alone, there were several incidents: A production facility belonging to Polish arms maker WB Electronics caught fire at the end of August; an explosion rocked the KNDS Ammo plant near Rome on August 13; and on August 15, unknown arsonists set fire to the building of Estonian military robotics manufacturer Milrem Robotics, which RT wrote about in the first part of its investigation.

articles.title: USA Delays Delivery of PAC-3 Missiles for Ukraine’s Patriot Systems but Continues to Supply PAC-2 Missiles
articles.body:
The United States is delaying the delivery of PAC-3 interceptor missiles to Ukraine for the Patriot air defense systems.
This was reported by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, citing an anonymous informed source within NATO.
These PAC-3 anti-aircraft missiles are primarily designed to intercept and destroy ballistic targets.
At the same time, PAC-2 interceptors, which are primarily used against aircraft and cruise missiles, continue to be delivered under the PURL program.
A well-informed source at NATO noted that the issue of the PAC-3 missile delay is currently being discussed at a high political level.
However, officials currently do not know when exactly this situation with the delivery delays will improve.
Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that the U.S. is delaying the delivery of interceptor missiles that have already been fully paid for by European allies.
According to him, part of these deliveries under the PURL program is still awaiting final approval from Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth.
At the same time, over the past 90 days, the United States has transferred only 24 anti-aircraft missiles for the Patriot systems to the Ukrainian side.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio explained the delay by the need to balance commitments to partners with the U.S.’s own needs for protecting its facilities.
At the same time, the head of the U.S. State Department assured that there was no deliberate political directive from Washington to harm Ukraine.
According to data from analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) for July 2026, U.S. PAC-3 stockpiles have decreased from over 2,300 to fewer than 830 units.

articles.title: Air defenses down three missiles, 96 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
articles.body:
Air defenses down three missiles, 96 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
The Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this in a Telegram post, Ukrinform says.
According to the report, from 18:00 on Thursday, October 29, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles, four Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles, and 113 attack drones, including Shahed-type UAVs (83 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones and Parodiya decoy drones.
The ballistic missiles were launched from Russia’s Voronezh, Kursk and Bryansk regions, while the air-launched missiles were fired from the Belgorod region. The drones were launched from the directions of the Russian settlements of Oryol, Kursk and Shatalovo, as well as from the temporarily occupied areas of Hvardiiske in the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and Donetsk.
The main targets of the attack were the Kyiv, Poltava and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
The Russian attack was repelled by Ukrainian Defense Forces aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups.
According to preliminary data, as of 7:30 on Friday, air defenses had shot down or suppressed 99 enemy aerial targets: three Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles and 96 Shahed-type drones (71 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones and UAVs of other types.
Hits by Russian aerial weapons were recorded at 17 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at five other locations.
Several Russian attack drones are still in Ukrainian airspace, and combat operations are ongoing.
As reported by Ukrinform, Russian forces attacked an industrial facility in the Kremenchuk district, Poltava region, overnight on October 30.

articles.title: Ukrainian Soldier Suspected of Passing Troop Positions to Russia
articles.body:
Ukraine’s State Bureau of Investigation (DBR) said on Monday, Oct. 26, that it had detained a serviceman suspected of passing information on Ukrainian troop positions in the southern Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions to Russia. The bureau said Russian forces used the information to direct strikes that wounded Ukrainian troops and damaged military equipment.
The DBR’s statement says the man was drafted in late 2024. After several months of service and training, he left his unit without authorization and hid in southern Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Investigators allege that he later agreed to work for Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) in exchange for money. He gathered information on the movement and locations of Ukrainian units, their weapons and military equipment, then passed it to Russian handlers.
Suspect allegedly tried to return to service
Russian forces used the information to strike Ukrainian positions, wounding troops and damaging equipment, the DBR said. The bureau did not give a casualty figure or identify the units or equipment involved.
The suspect later sought to return to military service to gain access to more information, the DBR said. Investigators and military counterintelligence officers from the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) detained him.
Suspect faces possible life sentence
The serviceman was formally notified of suspicion of wartime treason under Article 111(2) and leaving his unit without authorization during martial law under Article 407(5) of Ukraine’s Criminal Code. A court ordered him held in custody, the DBR said. He faces up to life imprisonment if convicted.
Putin Says Russia Is ‘Ready’ for War With Europe, Warns There Would Be No Winners
The bureau said the operation was carried out with assistance from the Military Law Enforcement Service. The Kherson Specialized Prosecutor’s Office in the Southern Region is overseeing the case.
The suspect’s name has not been released. The allegations have not been tested in court, and he is presumed innocent unless convicted.
The case follows other investigations into alleged Russian efforts to obtain information about Ukrainian military positions. In June, the SBU said it detained a deserter in Zaporizhzhia who allegedly mapped potential targets and sent their locations to an FSB handler.

articles.title: Destinus Is Building Nearly 300 Ruta Cruise Missiles a Month—More Than Europe Made in 2022
articles.body:
