Destinus Is Building Nearly 300 Ruta Cruise Missiles a Month—More Than Europe Made in 2022
Destinus has increased production of its Ruta cruise missile to nearly 300 units per month—a monthly output the company says now exceeds what all of Europe produced in an entire year before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
More than 1,750 Ruta Block 1 missiles have now been produced, Destinus reported on its official website on October 29.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Reaching that scale required the company to bring much of the production chain in-house, including engines, airframes, avionics, and guidance systems. That gives Destinus greater control over critical components while reducing dependence on outside suppliers.
One example is the T150 turbojet engine, which produces roughly 1.5 kN of thrust. Destinus manufactures the engine in series for the Ruta Block 1 and also supplies it to other weapons manufacturers.
The company expects its production capacity to be sufficient by 2027 to meet European demand for engines in this class, including orders connected to Ukraine.
Destinus also says its supply chain contains no Chinese components. While sourcing from China could potentially make production cheaper and faster, the company chose to organize manufacturing without Chinese suppliers.
CEO Mikhail Kokorich has said that as missile production scales up, the next challenge for European militaries will increasingly be how to employ such weapons in large numbers.
“To have sufficient deterrence, you need to have tens of thousands of missiles. But the main challenge… is that European customers still need to build the military units and logistic capabilities to operate these big numbers of systems,” Kokorich said, according to Reuters.
Destinus is simultaneously moving beyond the original Ruta.
The company has begun producing Ruta Block 2, a larger cruise missile designed to carry a payload of up to 250 kilograms and fly more than 700 kilometers.
Unlike Block 1, the new missile can be stored, transported, and launched from the same container. The approach is intended to simplify deployment and logistics, particularly when militaries need to stockpile large numbers of weapons.
The Block 2 features a box-shaped fuselage and an integrated folding-wing mechanism that allows the missile to fit inside its transport-launch container.
It also uses a solid-fuel booster to provide initial acceleration at launch.
That means Ruta Block 2 can be fired directly from its container instead of requiring a separate launch rail, making the system easier to transport, conceal, store, and deploy.
Earlier, Destinus accelerated development of the Ruta Block 3 long-range strike missile together with Rheinmetall, aiming to create a 2,000-kilometer-class precision weapon that will be tested in Ukraine.

articles.title: Shadows, roofs, job ads give Ukrainian arms plants away to Russian analysts, Ukrainian experts warn
articles.body:
Russian analysts can locate Ukrainian weapons plants from details in published photos and TV footage, Ukrainian defense outlet Oboronka reported on 29 October. Open-source researchers told the outlet how to hide those details.
Ukraine plans to build 7 million drones this year, and Russia is hunting the plants that make them. In June, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said Russia’s GRU military intelligence was gathering data to prepare air strikes on defense plants and attacks on their engineers.
A TV clip, then missiles
On 7 April 2022, Ukrainian channel 1+1 aired a report from a workshop at the Kyiv Armored Plant converting captured Russian military equipment for Ukraine’s forces. On 14 April, Rybar, an anonymous pro-Russian Telegram channel, posted the factory’s location. Russian missiles hit the workshop on 16 April, killing at least three civilians, the Centre for Information Resilience (CIR) found.
Retracing the likely method, CIR wrote that wall colors, window size, and ceiling height could single out the plant, and Google Earth imagery the workshop. InformNapalm researcher Andrii Lisitsyn told Oboronka that matching a frame with old photos, satellite images, job ads, or staff profiles quickly narrows the search.
A Gaussian blur smears pixels but keeps part of the information, Oboronka wrote. In a 2020 blog post, aerospace engineering student Gonçalo Raposo showed it can be fully reversed if the exact filter and edge handling are known. Pixelation fails too: a 2022 neural network reconstructs plausible faces from pixelated images. Lisitsyn advises cropping or fully opaque masking instead, plus checking file metadata.
Leaks beyond photos
Some Ukrainian defense enterprises still keep accounts and procurement records in Russian 1C software, Oboronka wrote. Since 6 January 2026, 1C products have been on the State Special Communications Service’s list of banned software. The ban covers systems with state information resources and critical information infrastructure owned or managed by state bodies, state enterprises, and local governments, the service said.
Oboronka also wrote that days before the full-scale invasion, Spanish journalist Pablo González photographed production lines at engine maker Motor Sich. Poland held him from February 2022 until a prisoner swap sent him to Russia in August 2024. Prosecutors then indicted him under both his names, Pablo González and Pavel Rubtsov, for spying for Russian military intelligence.

articles.title: Six Chinese Aircraft and Seven Ships Detected Around Taiwan; Five Aircraft Enter ADIZ
articles.body:
Six aircraft and seven ships from the PRC Navy were detected around Taiwan.
This was reported by Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense.
Monitoring took place from 00:00 on October 28 to 00:00 on October 29 Kyiv time (from 06:00 on October 28 to 06:00 on October 29 local time, UTC+8).
Of the six aircraft detected, five entered the island’s air defense identification zone.
The violations were recorded in the northern, central, and southwestern parts of the air defense identification zone.
In particular, four aircraft and drones crossed the median line of the Taiwan Strait.
One fighter jet was flying in the northeastern part of Taiwan’s air defense zone.
The Taiwanese Armed Forces monitored the situation and took appropriate countermeasures. To monitor air and maritime space, they deployed patrol aircraft and naval vessels.
Coastal anti-aircraft missile systems were also deployed to monitor Chinese activity.

articles.title: Belgium Deployed F-16 Fighter Jets to Reinforce NATO Mission in Baltics
articles.body:
The Belgian Air Force has joined the air defense mission in the Baltic states by deploying its aircraft.
This was reported by the Lithuanian Ministry of Defense, according to LRT.
A contingent of about 100 Belgian military personnel and six F-16 fighter jets will reinforce the Italian contingent, which is already carrying out missions in the region.
A formal welcoming ceremony for the Belgian military personnel was held at the Lithuanian Air Force base in Šiauliai.
The event was attended by Lithuanian Air Force Commander Antanas Matutis, Italian Ambassador to Lithuania Emanuele de Maigret, and Šiauliai Vice Mayor Justinas Švegžda.
In July, at the NATO summit in Ankara, a decision was made to reorganize the Air Policing mission in Europe into a full-fledged Air Defense mission.
This decision expanded the Alliance’s military command’s authority to respond more swiftly and decisively to a wide range of threats — from manned aircraft and UAVs to cruise and ballistic missiles.
In late July, the Italian contingent, with four EF-2000 (Eurofighter Typhoon) fighter jets, began the first rotation of this updated mission in Lithuania.
Milulitarnyi previously reported that the Slovak Air Force will resume defending the country’s airspace on its own in the coming days using F-16 fighter jets.
President Pellegrini emphasized that NATO membership does not exempt the country from responsibility for its own defense.
NATO will also deploy additional patrol aircraft, radar systems, and drones to the Black Sea.
The decision was made following a series of attacks on merchant ships off the coasts of NATO member states.

articles.title: Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report
articles.body:
Gulf states are going to have to reconfigure their trillion-dollar defences given the damage inflicted on their economies and the questionable continued value of US bases in the face of Iranian attack, according to a study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
The report says that in the weeks before the 8 April ceasefire, 12 regional states, overwhelmingly in the Gulf, faced 4,670 Iranian one-way attack drones and more than 1,400 ballistic missiles. Nearly half were aimed at the United Arab Emirates. Although the vast majority were repelled, one estimate of the damage to energy infrastructure cited by the report is put as high as $58bn (£43bn).
Iran would portray either a reduction or complete withdrawal of US forces from the region as “a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness, but also use it to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection”.
The report says the war also highlights another “uncomfortable truth for the Gulf states: not only has their trillion-dollar acquisition of US weapons not translated into US protection at the crucial time, but their respective militaries are also not adequately prepared for the new kind of attritional air war to which they are being exposed”.
Despite huge investment in mainly US armaments, the report identified significant shortcomings: “overwhelming reliance on US-supplied air- and missile-defence systems and munitions; a failure to achieve regional defence integration; a shortage of minesweeping capability; limited retaliatory options; and the prohibitive costs stemming from an overdependence on expensive, high-end systems to take down relatively inexpensive drones and missiles”.
The report is neutral on whether the divided Gulf states should seek a new non-aggression pact with Iran, but notes that the US-Iran war has shown longstanding defence and security partnerships with the US “have failed to ensure adequate protection against Iranian aggression”.
It adds: “If anything, US military bases and defence partnerships with the US have provided Iran with another pretext for attacks against the Gulf states.”
Public opinion on the US in the Gulf has also been shifting, it says, “from security provider to strategic liability”.
Any reduction or withdrawal of US forces from the Gulf region would be portrayed by Iran “as a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness” and would also be used “to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection,” the report notes.
The study comes after Chris Murphy, the Democrat senator and member of the senate foreign relations committee, said a debate was under way in the US military about the value of seeking to rebuild the damaged US bases in the Gulf.
Murphy said the Gulf state leadership “want us to rebuild” and “to keep a presence in the region”, but asked: “What good is it to have a base in the region to protect American interests if within 24 hours of a hot war starting, it is wiped off the map?
“We would be criminally incompetent as stewards of taxpayer dollars if we were to rebuild bases that are blown up within hours of the next war starting.
“So clearly, we are going to have to have a smaller footprint in the region, and the limiting principle on the footprint that we rebuild will be ‘what can we protect?’ because we clearly cannot protect the scope of our footprint today and if we can’t protect it, it is useless.”
Murphy suggested that, at the very least, the US may need to relocate its bases in the eastern Mediterranean further away from Iranian missiles.

articles.title: Dozens of Russian drones fell to gun turrets over Kyiv in a month, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry says
articles.body:
Automated gun turrets now serve in Ukraine’s Air Force and are destroying Russia’s jet-powered weapons, the Defense Ministry reported on 29 October. It gave no count for those jet kills, and it did not say what type of drones the turrets downed over Kyiv.
Jet drones are where Ukraine struggles most. From 1 to 26 September, Ukraine downed 55% of jet-powered drones against 90% of slower ones, partly because its interceptor drones fly at about 300 km/h, too slow to catch them. Yurii Cherevashenko, Deputy Commander of the Air Force, told a parliamentary inquiry commission on 6 October that jet-drone interceptors would arrive in the needed numbers no earlier than late November. Guns have limits too. On 5 October, Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat said turrets had already downed Geran-5s, but that their range is short because their main weapon is a machine gun.
Air Force turrets against jet weapons
According to the ministry, Brave1, a defense innovation cluster, began developing automated turrets in 2024. The systems have since “moved beyond the experimental stage and become an integral part of air defense,” it said. In Air Force service, the turrets are destroying jet-powered Banderol munitions and Geran-5 drones.
To scale up air defense without straining the front, Ukraine enlists business. In under year nearly 100 companies have joined, their crews downing 60-plus targets
Russia first used the Geran-5, a 6-meter jet-powered strike drone, in early 2026. The Banderol, a jet-powered cruise missile, flies at 520–560 km/h and can reach 650 km/h.
Private teams, a familiar number
Separately, the ministry said turrets have destroyed more than 60 targets within the private air defense project. The project lets companies form anti-drone teams that work under Air Force command.
Postal service Nova Post says it has already shot down Russian Shahed drones, as Ukrainian businesses take air defense into their own hands
Yet on 14 October, the ministry gave the same 60-plus total for all private teams. At the time, it named interceptor drones and heavy machine-gun turrets as their main weapons. Groups from six companies were on combat duty, about 50 groups had been formed in total, and some were still training. Nearly 100 companies had joined by then, up from 81 in mid-September.
The ministry says the project expands air defense “without placing an additional burden” on the military’s own air defense. It and Brave1 say they will keep integrating automated turrets into the air defense system.

- Ukraine’s private air defense has quadrupled since spring: businesses are now shooting down Shaheds over their own sites
- Ukraine just caught a Geran-5 at 425 km/h—the jet drone that has often outrun Ukrainian interceptor drones since January

articles.title: Pentagon tells Baltic hawks to stop ‘poking’ Russia – Reuters
articles.body:
Pentagon tells Baltic hawks to stop ‘poking’ Russia – Reuters
The Pentagon has privately urged the Baltic NATO states to rein in their increasingly aggressive war of words against Russia, warning that the rhetoric is undermining European security, Reuters reported on Friday, citing sources. The reported rebuke comes as the US intensifies its diplomatic push to settle the Ukraine conflict through negotiations with Moscow.
The message was delivered by Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, a key figure in an ongoing review of US troop levels in Europe, who advised a Baltic official against “poking” Moscow, four people familiar with the matter told the agency. Among the nations that received the warning were Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia – countries that have been more hawkish on Russia than most of their NATO counterparts.
“We are helping you. The Americans are there,” one European official told Reuters, describing Washington’s message. “Just don’t be loud. Don’t make noise.” The Pentagon also reportedly urged an Estonian delegation to be “measured” in its public communications. It is unclear whether other NATO nations received a similar warning.
One European official told Reuters that Washington’s advice was “baffling,” claiming that Baltic intelligence services have already played down the likelihood of a direct Russian assault on NATO. The Pentagon declined to comment on private communications with NATO allies.
The warning came after Baltic officials issued a frenzy of aggressive statements against Moscow. In September, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal likened Russian President Vladimir Putin to a “rat in a corner.” Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda made similar remarks as he warned that Ukrainian strikes deep into Russia – many of which target civilian facilities – could trigger Moscow’s retaliation. The jabs came despite Moscow’s forces making steady progress on the battlefield.
Meanwhile, Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braze went so far as to accuse Russia of “state-sponsored terrorism” over an explosives-laden drone discovered at Germany’s Leipzig airport.
Putin denied Moscow was responsible, saying that Berlin failed to provide any proof while suggesting that the incident was linked to the country’s own domestic woes. The Russian leader has also repeatedly dismissed speculation that Moscow could attack NATO and the EU, describing it as “political schizophrenia.”
The reported Pentagon intervention comes amid US President Donald Trump’s renewed diplomatic overtures to Moscow. Following an October 9 call with Putin, Washington temporarily eased sanctions to allow Russian diesel shipments to the US and global markets, with Trump suggesting the move would alleviate pressure on American truckers and farmers.
US envoy Steve Witkoff subsequently met Putin in St. Petersburg to discuss new Ukraine peace proposals, with Moscow agreeing in principle to restart trilateral talks with Washington and Kiev in November.
Trump’s deal with Putin triggered backlash from Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky, who denounced it as a “weak decision,” prompting the US president to suggest that Zelensky should be ousted to open the path to peace. Some of Ukraine’s EU backers have also sounded the alarm over the US-Russia agreement, describing it as risky and undermining NATO unity.

articles.title: Ex-Pentagon strategist accused of Iran and Ukraine leaks – Axios
articles.body:
Ex-Pentagon strategist accused of Iran and Ukraine leaks – Axios
The Pentagon’s former top military planner allegedly leaked classified information about Iran and Ukraine to journalists, Axios reported on Thursday, citing an internal investigation.
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth fired Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia as head of strategy, plans, and policy on the Joint Staff earlier this week.
Without mentioning Sylvia by name, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said on Thursday that the department has “zero tolerance for the intentional, unauthorized disclosure of classified information.” He added that the Pentagon “took necessary personnel action to protect sensitive information.”
According to Axios, Sylvia admitted to leaking information as early as June 2025, before most media outlets were barred from the Pentagon. He allegedly continued communicating with reporters through the encrypted messaging app Signal and once met a journalist at a diner to discuss military aid to Ukraine without authorization.
“He had trouble passing multiple polygraph interviews,” the report said, according to Axios.
Officials reportedly suspect that the general deliberately deleted records of his communications with a reporter, though he claimed the deletion was accidental. Sylvia also allegedly admitted to being a source for another story criticizing Pentagon leadership.
Sylvia’s departure comes amid reports that the US and Israel are preparing to resume strikes on Iran following next week’s US midterm elections. US President Donald Trump has indicated that he may take military action if Tehran refuses to accept his terms for a peace deal.
Since returning to the White House in early 2025, Trump has sought to crack down on government leaks, accusing news outlets of conducting a smear campaign against him.
In July, Hegseth said the Pentagon and Justice Department established a joint task force to “identify and prosecute leakers.”
In April 2025, Hegseth fired three senior Pentagon aides – Dan Caldwell, Darin Selnick, and Colin Carroll – amid an investigation into alleged leaks of sensitive information to the media. All three denied wrongdoing, and none was subsequently charged with a crime. Caldwell later returned to the Trump administration in a position at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

articles.title: Production of Ruta Cruise Missiles Used by Ukraine Reaches Nearly 300 per Month
articles.body:
Destinus has ramped up production of Ruta cruise missiles to nearly 300 units per month — more than the whole of Europe produced in a year before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Destinus made this announcement on the official website.
The total number of Ruta B1 missiles produced has exceeded 1,750.
To sustain this production rate, the company has established in-house manufacturing of engines, airframes, avionics and guidance systems. This allows it to independently control the key stages of the production process.
For example, the company is mass-producing T150 turbojet engines with a thrust of approximately 1.5 kN. They are used in the Ruta Block 1 and are also supplied to other weapons manufacturers.
Destinus is expected to be able to meet European market demand for propulsion systems of this class as early as 2027, including orders for Ukraine.
At the same time, no Chinese components are used in production. Although cooperation with Chinese suppliers could reduce costs and speed up missile manufacturing, the supply chain has been organised without their involvement.
Destinus CEO Mykhailo Kokorych noted that as missile production increases, the main challenge for European armed forces is their practical deployment. In particular, it is necessary to establish dedicated units and develop infrastructure for storage, maintenance and target designation. In particular, it is necessary to establish appropriate units and develop infrastructure for storage, maintenance, and targeting.
In addition to ramping up production of the base version, Destinus announced the start of production of the larger Ruta Block 2 cruise missile. According to updated company data, it is designed to carry a 250 kg payload and has a range of more than 700 km.
Unlike Block 1, the new variant can be stored, transported and launched from a single container. This simplifies logistics and deployment, particularly when large missile stockpiles need to be built up.
Militarnyi previously reported on the design changes introduced in the Ruta Block 2. The new variant features a box-shaped fuselage and an integrated wing-folding mechanism, allowing the missile to be housed in a canister.
The Ruta Block 2 is also equipped with a solid-fuel booster that provides initial acceleration during launch. This allows the missile to be launched directly from the canister without the need for a separate launch rail.
Ukraine is already using Ruta cruise missiles to strike Russian targets. In particular, in July, reports emerged that Russian forces had found debris from these missiles, providing one of the first public confirmations of their combat use.

articles.title: Putin explains why he welcomed rare call from Nordic leaders
articles.body:
Putin explains why he welcomed rare call from Nordic leaders
Russian President Vladimir Putin says he welcomed the rare phone call from the leaders of Finland and Norway, adding that Moscow has always supported efforts to normalize relations with European countries.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store spoke with Putin on Tuesday, breaking with the longstanding practice among European leaders of avoiding direct contact with Moscow since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022. The initiative drew criticism from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who questioned its effectiveness and said it was not coordinated with European partners.
At a press conference in the Kremlin on Thursday, Putin said he welcomes dialogue with Western countries despite their military support for Ukraine and sanctions on Russia.
“I believe it was the right thing to do. After all, there are people in Europe who, unlike some others, do not want to inflict a ‘strategic defeat’ on Russia but instead want to establish some kind of constructive dialogue,” he stated.
He added that Russia will support “any steps aimed at restoring full-fledged and comprehensive relations” with European countries, whether through the EU or on a bilateral basis.
Putin reiterated that Russia is not seeking a broader conflict with the EU or NATO. “We do not want any war with Europe. If some of them want one, let them prepare. But they have not achieved their goal of inflicting a ‘strategic defeat’ on Russia, and it is unlikely that this will be possible by 2030,” he said.
And if things go too far, there will be no winners at all. Let no one forget that.
The leaders of Norway and Finland said they sought to convey messages directly to Putin “regarding future negotiations to help to end the war,” ahead of US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks expected to take place in Abu Dhabi in the near future. They described the conversation as a follow-up to their meeting with Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky in Oslo on October 20.
Norway and the Kremlin disputed a report by the Financial Times claiming that Putin spent much of the call lecturing his counterparts on Russian and Slavic history.
Stubb has cultivated a close relationship with US President Donald Trump, with whom he has frequently discussed the Ukraine conflict, earning him the nickname ‘the Trump whisperer’ in the media.
The Finnish leader noted his country’s long experience of dealing with Russia. Finland shares a 1,340-kilometer border with its eastern neighbor and maintained peaceful, if sometimes uneasy, relations with Moscow throughout the Cold War.
The call came amid growing tensions between Kiev and Washington after Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports and subsequently waived additional restrictions following Zelensky’s refusal to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Trump blamed for soaring fuel prices.
Moscow has accused European leaders of sabotaging the 2022 peace talks with Ukraine and seeking to undermine Trump’s ongoing efforts to broker a deal.

articles.title: European countries fear being sidelined in Russia–Ukraine peace talks but can’t agree on how to secure a seat at the table, FT reports
articles.body:
European countries fear being sidelined in Russia–Ukraine peace talks but can’t agree on how to secure a seat at the table, FT reports
European countries fear they could be shut out of talks to end Russia’s war with Ukraine, but they cannot agree among themselves on how to secure a seat at the negotiating table, or who should represent their interests and how, the Financial Times reported.
That anxiety has grown since Washington eased sanctions on Moscow and accused Kyiv of being unwilling to end the conflict. European countries worry that, ahead of talks among the United States, Russia, and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, Washington and Moscow could reach a deal without them on issues that affect European interests, including security guarantees for Russia and restrictions on NATO.
Driven by these concerns, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke by phone with Vladimir Putin on October 27. The call drew criticism from other European countries because the Finnish and Norwegian leaders had not secured their allies’ support beforehand.
According to the newspaper’s sources — European diplomats and officials — these uncoordinated attempts at contact, and the backlash they triggered, highlight the dilemma facing Europe: how best to convey its interests to Putin and Trump.
“Before we can talk about choosing a representative [for Europe at the talks] we need a chair at the table. Putin doesn’t want to include us, he wants to talk to Trump and so to put [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelensky in a corner,” one senior European diplomat said.
The United States is still involving Europeans in the negotiating process to some extent, the Financial Times reported. Washington and Kyiv have been considering the so-called European troika — the United Kingdom, France, and Germany — as the most likely representatives of Europe at the upcoming talks, but diplomats say that option risks provoking objections from other European countries.
Pentagon officials recently asked several NATO countries to tone down their statements about the Russian threat. The countries that received these requests include the Baltic states — Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia — among others, Reuters reported.
Moscow says there is no need for European involvement. Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov, for example, commented on the possible participation of European representatives in the new round of talks:
If they buy plane tickets, fly to Abu Dhabi, and hang around there somewhere, then from time to time the same Ukrainians, or even the same Americans, might report something to them, consult with them, maybe take some points of view into account — in other words, the process there could become more complicated.
What’s happening in Oleshky, where the war has caused a humanitarian catastrophe
- Minesweeping of routes for the humanitarian mission has been completed.
- A humanitarian mission, led by the human rights ombudsmen of Russia and Ukraine, has departed for the city.
- The evacuation of residents and distribution of humanitarian aid have begun.
The war in photographs. The aftermath of Russian attacks in Ukraine’s regions.

articles.title: Kiev ‘ignoring’ Trump – Kremlin
articles.body:
Kiev ‘ignoring’ Trump – Kremlin
Ukraine, emboldened by continued European support, is ignoring US President Donald Trump’s calls to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov has said.
Three Russian oil refineries and a gas chemical complex were targeted in overnight attacks on Friday, according to Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak.
Commenting on the latest attacks, Ushakov told journalist Pavel Zarubin that Kiev had once again defied Trump. “I would even say they are simply ignoring him,” he added.
According to Novak, one of the targeted facilities sustained minor damage, but Russian air defenses largely repelled the attacks. Samara Region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said on Friday that two people involved in dealing with the aftermath of the drone strikes had been killed, while several others were injured.
Trump has repeatedly demanded that Kiev stop targeting Russian oil refineries, accusing it of worsening the global fuel crisis and driving up prices for American consumers and farmers – a sensitive issue ahead of the November 3 US midterms. Vladimir Zelensky rejected the criticism, calling Trump’s claims “totally false.”
Ushakov suggested that Kiev was emboldened by continued European support. “They would hardly have dared to do this on their own,” he said.
“Trump has been persistent on this issue and continues to be, but they are not listening,” Ushakov said. The aide noted that trilateral talks are being planned under US mediation, which he described as crucial to resolving the conflict.
Moscow agreed in principle to a fourth round of trilateral talks with the US and Ukraine following last week’s meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg. The negotiations could take place in Abu Dhabi in November, with European countries not invited, according to the Kremlin.
Ukraine’s European backers have been excluded from all three rounds of trilateral negotiations so far and have increasingly sought direct participation in the peace process. Moscow has accused the EU of acting as the principal side arming Ukraine and prolonging the conflict.
Novak said on Friday that the Russian government was preparing to extend its diesel export ban until the end of January 2027, while maintaining exemptions for certain shipments to international markets.
Tankers carrying Russian diesel have been dispatched to the US under an agreement reached between Putin and Trump following their October 9 phone call. Washington temporarily waived sanctions on Russian fuel imports to facilitate the deliveries.

articles.title: Star Wars: Has Russia's war with Ukraine gone intergalactic?
articles.body:
Star Wars: Has Russia's war with Ukraine gone intergalactic?
Russian made an unprecedented combative move this month as one of its military satellites, the Cosmos-2612, encroached upon the orbit of Ukrainian commercial satellite, Iceye-X36, in behaviour deemed "threatening" by the US State Department. Norbert Pouzin, an orbital analyst at French space tech firm, Aldoria, described the mercenary manoeuvre as the first of its kind.
Has space become a new frontier in Russia's war with Ukraine?
Russian military satellite Cosmos-2612 carried out a manoeuvre between October 15 and 18 that brought it “dangerously close” to Ukrainian commercial satellite, Iceye-X36. The move was described by US Under Secretary of State for Arms Control and International Security as "threatening".
Operated by Finnish company Iceye, Iceye-X36 is a Finnish-American civilian satellite equipped with Synthetic-aperture radar (SAR) to provide satellite images to the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
The US State Department said Russia's tactic was consistent with “in-orbit military operations”.
Analysts specialising in space surveillance have been following Cosmos-2612 since its launch in April.
"Cosmos-2612 was one of six satellites launched in total. It was immediately apparent that this wasn't a classic deployment. As soon as they took off, the satellites started changing orbit to pursue Iceye satellites,” said Norbert Pouzin, an orbital analyst at Aldoria, a French space surveillance firm.
Cosmos-2612 took off on April 6, 2026 alongside Cosmos-2609, Cosmos-2610, Cosmos-2611, Cosmos-2613 and Cosmos-2614. KeepTrack, a site specialising in satellite navigation, enables viewers to track their paths.
Orbit re-routing – as has been the case of the Cosmos satellites – is a move that consumes a lot of fuel. It’s also the first step in approaching another satellite, Pouzin explains:
 "If two satellites are travelling in the same orbit, then they don’t need as much fuel to approach one another. Changing directions in space uses a lot of fuel. But once in the same orbit as another satellite, you’ve already executed the most costly move fuel-wise, if you then want to carry out an approach.”
From a kilometre to within just a few hundred metres
As the imaging data via site, Satellite Tracker, corroborates, Cosmos-2612 diverted from its original position – around 400-500 km from Iceye-X36 – to get closer to the Finnish-American satellite.
"On October 15, Cosmos-2612 was within 5 kilometres of Iceye-X36. Its position continued to narrow in on the satellite on October 16 and 17, before finally getting to within a few hundred metres and a kilometre of Iceye-X36 ,” Pouzin said.
Satellite imaging company Vantor published a photo of the two satellites on October 22, depicting their orbits withing just 1.02 kilometres of one another.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Data from KeepTrack also revealed that Cosmos-2612 and Iceye-X36 later embarked on the same orbit, meaning the Russian satellite was “following” the Finnish-American satellite.
A bold move
So why did Cosmos-2612 carry out this “threatening” manoeuvre?
Given the lack of debris, it doesn’t appear that Iceye-X36 was the target of a “kinetic” attack – that is, a physical strike involving a collision or the launch of a projectile. But according to Pouzin, the manoeuvre by Cosmos-2612 could be interpreted as a form of exerting pressure on Ukraine, as it is the direct recipient of the data gathered by the Iceye satellite:
 "SAR satellites have unique observation plans [Editor’s note: a schedule that coordinates how radar satellites can scan specific parts of the planet.] If an operator knows about these, then he could – for a short time – disrupt the satellite’s mission, potentially causing repercussions for ground-based or maritime operations, for example."
Cosmos-2612’s move seemed to shock Western commentators, he added:
 "While Russia regularly launches military satellites in the same orbital planes as classified American military satellites; carrying out this particular kind of approach on a commercial satellite while in a low orbit is something new. Furthermore it seemed to be non-cooperative in nature: we are dealing with two actors who are not on the same side and these are satellites not operated by the same entity."
The initiative also revealed something about Russia’s capabilities, Pouzin concluded:
 "The move demonstrated a certain agility by the Russian operator, a skilled knowledge of the space domain, and a very high level of mastery in this type of navigation.”

articles.title: Ukraine destroys Iskander-M missile launcher in Russia's Kursk Oblast, General Staff says
articles.body:
Ukraine destroys Iskander-M missile launcher in Russia's Kursk Oblast, General Staff says
Ukrainian forces struck an Iskander-M missile launcher in Russia's Kursk Oblast, along with several ammunition depots and repair facilities in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories between Oct. 29 and Oct. 30, the General Staff said.
Ukraine struck the missile launcher near the town of Fatezh, at a site used to reload ballistic missiles, the General Staff said.
The Iskander-M is a short-range ballistic missile system that Russia uses to attack Ukrainian cities. During its overnight attack on Oct. 30, Russia launched ballistic missiles from Voronezh, Kursk, and Bryansk oblasts as part of a combined assault that mainly targeted Kyiv, Poltava, and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts, Ukraine's Air Force said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 5 that Ukrainian forces would prioritize strikes on Russian missile launchers as Moscow steps up its use of ballistic missiles. Zelensky also said international deliveries of air-defense interceptors to Ukraine had fallen threefold from 2025 levels.
Ukraine's military also reported strikes on Russian ammunition depots in the occupied parts of Donetsk, Kharkiv, and Luhansk oblasts.
Ukrainian forces hit several other Russian military targets in occupied Luhansk Oblast, including a logistics depot near Bilovodsk, a repair unit near Rubizhne, and a repair and recovery base near Pysarivka, the General Staff said on Oct. 30.
The General Staff did not specify which weapons were used in the strikes.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the extent of the damage.
Zelensky said on Oct. 29 that Ukraine had carried out two missile strikes, destroying an Iskander-M missile launcher and two Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber jets.
On Oct. 29, Ukraine's Navy also struck two Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber jets at the Marinovka military airfield in Russia's Volgograd Oblast using domestically produced Neptune missiles, the Navy reported.

articles.title: Slovak Prosecutor General reopens case into transfer of MiG-29 fighter jets and Kub air defense systems to Ukraine
articles.body:
Slovak Prosecutor General Maroš Žilinka has decided to reopen the case concerning the transfer of military equipment to Ukraine by the country’s previous government in 2023.
"After reviewing the case, I have concluded that the decision to close it was premature," Žilinka wrote on social media. He stated that the investigation must be resumed and that the relevant directive has been issued to the prosecutor in the city of Trenčín.
The case concerns the transfer to Ukraine of 13 MiG-29 fighter jets and Kub (SA-6 Gainful) surface-to-air missile systems that had been in service with the Slovak Armed Forces.
In February 2026, Bratislava prosecutor Rastislav Remeta, upon concluding a preliminary investigation, stated that the transferred fighter jets and air defense systems were obsolete and that their transfer to Ukraine did not constitute a criminal offense. Previously, on October 31, 2025, a police investigator had closed the criminal proceedings, and on January 26, 2026, a prosecutor rejected an appeal against that decision.
In September 2026, the Slovak Prosecutor General’s Office reported that it had reviewed the legality of the closure of the proceedings and concluded that the decisions made by the investigator and the prosecutor were lawful. Žilinka’s current decision means that the circumstances of the case are being re-examined; however, this does not, in itself, imply that a criminal offense has been established.

articles.title: Putin’s African ties: Military cooperation, “history” wars, and sanctions
articles.body:
Russia and a range of African countries have adopted declarations on political and economic cooperation following the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow. In the outcome documents, the parties agreed to counter the “rewriting of history,” the blocking of sovereign assets, and the politicization of international justice while working to foster cooperation in security, space, mineral extraction, and AI. Vladimir Putin said that Russia already has agreements on military and military-technical cooperation with 45 African nations. The Insider has compiled the main statements and agreements of the two-day summit.
The third Russia–Africa summit took place in Moscow on Oct. 28–29, with delegations from 48 of the continent’s 54 countries in attendance. Two dozen states were represented by high-level officials, with sessions co-chaired by Putin and Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, who currently heads the African Union.
As a result of the gathering, the parties adopted three main documents: the final declaration of the summit, a declaration on cooperation in the civilian use of AI, and the action plan of the Russia–Africa partnership forum for 2027–2029. In addition, more than 60 official agreements were signed at the summit and at the parallel economic and humanitarian forum, Russian presidential adviser Anton Kobyakov announced via Telegram.
Countering sanctions, “rewriting of history,” and colonial legacies
A significant part of the final declaration is devoted to international politics. Russia and the African states in attendance agreed to oppose the blocking and seizure of sovereign assets, as well as to resist outside political and economic pressure. The parties intend to coordinate their positions when it comes to sanctions against African countries.
The summit participants also agreed to counter attempts at “rewriting and falsifying history.” These and other provisions are included in the final declaration, which consists of 101 points.
Another area will be assessing the damage “inflicted on African states during the colonial period.” Russian scientists are already developing a methodology for such assessment jointly with African colleagues. Preliminary results should be presented in 2027, and a special research laboratory is expected to open in Uganda in November 2026.
In his speech on Oct. 28, Vladimir Putin accused Western countries of trying to preserve Africa’s economic dependence and impose new debt obligations on it. The Russian president claimed that Moscow is ready to transfer technology and foster production on the continent.
African Union Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf stressed in his speech that African states are interested in developing local industry and gaining access to international capital. He also called for reforming the U.N. Security Council by expanding African representation.
Military cooperation and fight against terrorism
Putin stated that Russia has intergovernmental agreements on military and military-technical cooperation in effect with 45 African states, noting that Moscow trains African servicemen and law enforcement officers at Russian educational institutions.
In the final statements, the parties reaffirmed their intention to expand cooperation in the fight against terrorism and extremism, counter the use of new technologies by terrorist organizations, and develop joint security mechanisms.
Special attention was paid to the Sahel states: Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger. Commenting on the statement of Assimi Goïta, the head of Mali’s military government, Putin stressed the global importance of resolving the situation in the Sahel.
Russia’s military presence in the region has expanded in recent years. After the Wagner Group wound down its activities following the death of founder Yevgeny Prigozhin in August 2023, Russia's state-run Africa Corps stepped in to take over the role in several African states. Russian military units currently operate in Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso, and the Central African Republic.
Two days ahead of the summit, African branches of Amnesty International appealed to its participants with a call to demand that Moscow stop the deceptive and coercive recruitment of citizens of African states to take part in the war against Ukraine. Human rights activists claim that Russia recruits foreigners under the guise of employment and then sends them to the front.
AI, space, and control over technology
The summit participants devoted a separate declaration to cooperation in AI — to promote equal and fair access to safe AI technologies, the development of joint educational programs, and capacity-building efforts. Satellite communications and the use of space were discussed separately.
According to Putin, approximately 40,000 students from African countries are studying in Russia, and Moscow is expanding training programs for foreign civil servants, including in the digitalization of public administration. Putin also characterized Russia as being one of three countries with full digital sovereignty — a claim The Insider has examined in its Antifake section.
Precious metals, nuclear power plants, and trade
The economic part of the summit focused on energy, transportation, agriculture, and the mining and processing of minerals.
Russia’s Rusal and the state-owned Ghana Integrated Aluminium Development Corporation agreed to create two joint ventures in Ghana. The companies plan to develop the Nyinahini deposit with annual output of up to 5 million metric tons of bauxite and build an alumina refinery with a capacity of 1.2 million metric tons per year, with Rusal receiving controlling stakes in both ventures. Reuters notes that the company is seeking to reduce its dependence on external suppliers of raw materials after losing part of its supplies from Ukraine and Australia in 2022.
Ghana’s President John Dramani Mahama also announced the start of negotiations with Rosatom on building the country’s first nuclear power plant.
According to Putin, Russia’s trade with African countries reached $27 billion in 2025, and since 2023 Moscow has opened eight new embassies on the continent. In the near future, Botswana, Seychelles, and Togo intend to open diplomatic missions of their own in the Russian capital.
Putin also said that in the first nine months of 2026, Russia had supplied African countries with 13 million tons of agricultural products. Deliveries of mineral fertilizers, he said, exceeded 2.2 million tons this year, compared with 1.5 million tons for all of last year.
Trade with Africa remains significantly below the level promised by Putin
Despite claims of successful cooperation, Russia’s trade with Africa has not yet reached the level that Putin promised at the first summit in 2019. As Chatham House notes, the Russian leader set a goal of bringing trade turnover to $40 billion; however, in 2025, it totaled only $27 billion. For comparison, also according to data cited by Chatham House, China’s trade with African countries reached $348 billion in 2025, and the European Union’s was about $395 billion.
At the same time, Russia continues to expand its political and military presence on the continent. Earlier, The Insider described how Moscow uses cooperation with African governments to gain access to natural resources and strengthen its influence in international organizations.
Six days before the current summit, The Insider identified a GRU officer who in April 2025 infiltrated the diplomatic residence of the African Union in Ethiopia. He turned out to be Alexander Dubikov, who worked undercover as an assistant to the Russian military attaché and is linked to hackers from the Sandworm group. The incident occurred at a compound used by the current chairperson of the African Union Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, who also took part in the Moscow summit.
Dialogue with Europe, possible war, and situation in the Baltic Sea
At the press conference following the summit, Putin took questions about relations with Europe. Commenting on his Oct. 27 phone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Putin said the European leaders themselves initiated the call, stressing that they were acting in their national capacity, not on behalf of the European Union. Despite being critical of his counterparts, Putin called the conversation the right step and supported attempts to restore dialogue with European countries.
Nevertheless, Putin said that Russia is ready for war with Europe, even if it does not seek one. He criticized statements by European politicians about the need to prepare for a possible military conflict by 2030 and expressed confidence that Russia cannot be dealt a strategic defeat. “If it goes too far, there will be no winner at all,” he commented, adding that Russia remembers the lessons of the First and Second World Wars and is doing everything it can to prevent reliving them.
Finally, Putin touched on the situation in the Baltic Sea, which he had discussed with the leaders of Finland and Norway. According to Putin, his Nordic interlocutors had invoked the need to comply with international maritime law. Putin supported their position but warned that a situation similar to what is happening in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz could develop in the Baltic. Russia, according to him, does not want such a development but is ready to respond to any challenge.

articles.title: Zelensky: Intelligence reports Russia preparing new ballistic missile strikes
articles.body:
Zelensky: Intelligence reports Russia preparing new ballistic missile strikes
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said this in his nightly video address, Ukrinform reports.
"We now have intel about the Russians preparing new ballistic missile attacks. We need the capabilities to shoot down all this Russian evil," he said.
Zelensky also said he had held a meeting of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief's Staff earlier today, with countering Russian ballistic missiles as the key issue.
"Sanctions pressure is insufficient – and we need the packages from partners that we have discussed with them. When it comes to key jurisdictions, sanctions can indeed have a significant restrictive effect, but not immediately – only over time. Sometimes this requires months of work. The longer sanctions packages targeting ballistic missiles are delayed, the longer Russia can maintain its supply schemes for the components needed for this production," he said.
He instructed the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry to accelerate this work with partners.
"We also set additional tasks for our long-range sanctions, which work much faster. For now, no public details on this, but everyone could see in recent weeks that Ukraine’s long-range capabilities are delivering results," he said.
Zelensky recalled that Ukraine had carried out two missile strikes that destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers and also hit an Iskander missile launcher.
"Thank you, guys, for the result! Glory to Ukraine!" the president said.
Photo: Office of the President of Ukraine

articles.title: NATO military chief sees no delays in Patriot deliveries to Ukraine
articles.body:
NATO military chief sees no delays in Patriot deliveries to Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
The United States continues to supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles and weapons paid for by European allies. New talks on the war will take place in the UAE.
NATO’s top military commander, General Alexus Grynkewich, said that the United States continues to supply Ukraine with air defense missiles for Patriot systems and weapons packages paid for by European allies. UNN reports this, citing Bloomberg.
Everything has been delivered; in fact, we received a shipment only during the past week. I will not go into information about the quantity or types of missiles, but the deliveries are continuing
Grynkewich said that "nothing included in the PURL package that was paid for by European allies has been delayed," referring to the NATO-led program for purchasing American weapons, financed by other members of the military alliance.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy this week urged U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to sign agreements on the transfer of Patriot missiles from third countries to Ukraine.
"Every third party that submitted a request to the U.S. government was approved," Grynkewich said. "We continue to work on the contents of future PURL packages. We are working hard."
Calls for more missiles came after a dispute between Zelenskyy and Donald Trump over the U.S. president’s decision to allow Russia to sell some diesel fuel on global markets in order to "lower prices." Both sides have sought to ease tensions in recent days and put negotiations on ending Moscow’s war back on track, the publication writes.
Trilateral talks between the United States, Ukraine, and Russia are expected to resume next month in the United Arab Emirates.

articles.title: North Korea warns South Korea with ballistic missiles as Seoul calls for talks to ease border tensions
articles.body:
Missile launches and a dispute over a landmine incident have heightened tensions between the two Koreas. Seoul is seeking military talks to prevent accidental clashes, but Pyongyang has yet to respond.
North Korea fired around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles towards the sea on Thursday, South Korea’s military said, a day after Seoul renewed its call for talks to prevent accidental clashes along their heavily fortified border.
The missiles were launched from the eastern coastal area of Wonsan at about 12.30pm local time and travelled around 250 kilometres, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff.
South Korea said it had stepped up surveillance for further launches and was sharing information with the United States and Japan.
Seoul proposed military talks on 23 October to jointly verify the location of the Military Demarcation Line, which separates the two Koreas, restore military communication lines and agree measures to prevent accidental clashes.
Unification Minister Chung Dong-young renewed the appeal on Wednesday in an address read on his behalf at a forum in Goyang, near Seoul.
“South and North Korea should align their positions on the MDL through dialogue,” Chung said, calling for communication channels to be restored so the area could be managed peacefully.
North Korea has not responded to the talks proposal.
Mine blasts deepen border tensions
The offer follows landmine explosions in the Demilitarised Zone on 21 September that injured three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously.
Seoul accused North Korean troops of planting the mines south of the demarcation line. North Korea denied responsibility and accused the South of fabricating the incident in a letter to the UN Security Council.
The US-led United Nations Command, which oversees the armistice, said a joint investigation with South Korea had identified an active North Korean mine south of the line and determined that an armistice violation had occurred.
North Korean troops have been reinforcing the border with roads, fences and landmines. South Korea says they have repeatedly crossed the demarcation line during the work, prompting warning broadcasts and warning shots.
Seoul says differing interpretations of the boundary could lead to accidental clashes. Many of the markers installed under the 1953 armistice have deteriorated or disappeared, with only about 200 of the original 1,292 still identifiable, according to Yonhap.
Direct military communication between the two Koreas remains suspended, although the command maintains a separate channel with the North Korean military.

articles.title: Russia’s Geran-5 has hit 1,000 km/h in maneuvers, and Chinese engineers help develop some technical solutions for Russia’s drones
articles.body:
Russia’s Geran-5 jet drones have sped up to 1,000 km/h while maneuvering, Ukraine’s presidential adviser on defense technology Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said in Kyiv on 29 October. He added that Chinese engineers help develop Russia’s Geran drones.
When Russia moved to faster Geran versions, Ukrainian developers had to look for new ways to intercept them, Beskrestnov said, and Ukraine must learn to stay a step ahead. From 1 to 26 September, air defenses downed only 55% of Russia’s jet-powered drones. On 29 October, one such drone hit Dnipro’s railway station, and the death toll has since risen to 15. Over the past three months, air defenses downed nearly 60% of the jet-powered Geran-4, the General Staff said on 27 October, noting a shortage of guided anti-aircraft missiles. That update gave no Geran-5 figure.
A peak well above cruise speed
That peak, about 620 mph, came during maneuvers. Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) puts the Geran-5’s cruise speed at 450–600 km/h. By Beskrestnov’s count, the earlier Geran-3 flew at 280–300 km/h.
Ukraine intercepts nearly 60% of Russia’s Geran-4 jet drones, General Staff says, as Kyiv races to counter evolving threat
Russia’s best engineers work against Ukraine, and China’s do too, Beskrestnov told journalists. Russia’s Alabuga drone plant sets Chinese engineers tasks such as work on the control module, he said. Key components inside Russia’s Shahed-type drones are Chinese, he said. Meanwhile, China will require licenses for Geran engines from 18 November, Ukraine’s sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said. Licensing is not a ban, he stressed.
Speed is the easy part
Some interceptors are being designed to match the Geran-5’s cruise speed. US firm CHAOS Industries claims a top speed of 540 km/h for its Vespid Mk 1 interceptor. On 14 October, Ukrainian defense outlet Defense Express judged that may be enough against the Geran-5’s 450–600 km/h cruise speed.
Russia equips Geran attack drones with image-based navigation using Google map imagery, reducing reliance on satellite navigation that Ukraine can jam, defense adviser warns
Ukrainian manufacturers have already shown jet-powered interceptor drones, Beskrestnov said. But they have run into problems with control, guidance, automatic target lock, and scaling up production. A model that flies fast is only one part of the job, he said, and an easy-to-use serial product is a different question entirely.

articles.title: Azov says it struck more than 100 Russian trains in occupied Donbas in four months, in part thanks to donations
articles.body:
Fighters of the 1st Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine "Azov" struck more than 100 Russian trains carrying fuel and other supplies for occupying forces, the corps reported on social media on 28 October. The strikes disabled locomotives, fuel tank cars, and other equipment, the statement said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed on 16 October that seizing all of Donetsk Oblast remains one of Russia's main tasks. Azov notes that these strikes help "destroy" Russia's offensive capabilities.
Small Ukrainian drones strike Russia's 100-ton locomotives
Azov emphasizes that neither mobile fire groups nor electronic warfare systems can protect Russian logistics routes.
"The enemy is doing its utmost to create an image of successfully capturing settlements, but is unable to protect key railway stations through which the fuel supply chain runs toward the front," Azov said.
The rail hubs hit had carried Russian military trains to the fighting in Donbas and southern Ukraine, Defense Express reported on 29 October. The count of more than 100 trains covers Azov's operations over the past four months, the outlet said.
The mass of any diesel locomotive exceeds 100 tons, yet the Ukrainian military struck these large Russian targets using small UAVs, the outlet also notes.
Donations helped make the strikes possible
Donations and the work of the Come Back Alive foundation contributed to the operation's results, Azov said. In particular, the foundation provided the military with 440 Starlink Mini terminals, the corps added.
Azov announced Operation Hell back in the summer
On 2 July, the Azov Corps announced Operation Hell and released the first footage of strikes on Russian railway equipment. The video shows a strike on a diesel locomotive that was likely used by Russian forces for military logistics.
The corps said the strike was part of a carefully planned operation and promised details soon.
